name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterms
description: CT was one of the states that sued to block Trump's order. AG  William Tong called the ruling a 'huge win for free and fair elections.'
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald J. Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots for the November midterm elections, ruling in favor of Connecticut and a coalition of other states that sought to block the U.S. Postal Service from implementing parts of the president’s executive order.
The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they’ve used for years and have accounted for nearly a third of votes cast.
It represented a stark defeat for Trump on an issue he consistently has emphasized as vital to ensuring election integrity even though there is virtually no evidence of fraud with mail ballots.
Attorney General William Tong applauded the decision by the Supreme Court Monday night and heralded it as a victory. But he warned of the president continuing to sow doubt over voting less than two months before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when the balance of power in Congress will be at stake.
By upholding the preliminary injunction from a federal judge, Tong said the ruling by the Supreme Court continues to block states like Connecticut from needing to get approval of ballot and return envelope design as well as include information on each state’s voters into a portal.
“This is a huge win for free and fair elections. Donald Trump has tried over and over again to seize control of this election, to pick and choose who gets to vote and how we cast our ballots,” Tong said in a statement issued shortly after 9 p.m. “Tonight, the United States Supreme Court sided with states and gave Donald Trump a big no. I have no illusions that this President is done trying to inject chaos and confusion into this election, but we’re going to be there at every step to fight to protect voters and our democracy.”
This year, for the first time, any voter in Connecticut can vote by absentee ballot for any reason. A state constitutional amendment approved by referendum and an act of the General Assembly ended the state’s policy of restricting absentee voting to those able to attest an inability to vote in person on election day.
States have the constitutional authority to administer their own elections. And Congress, not the president, can make changes at the federal level through legislation. But Trump, who says he wants to “nationalize the voting,” has sought to do so both through unilateral action and legislation he wants Congress to pass.
On March 31, months ahead of the November midterm election and as primary season was starting, Trump issued an executive order that could change how mail-in or absentee ballots work. He has argued it’s an attempt to crack down on noncitizen voting, which is already prohibited by federal law and rare.
His order instructed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to compile a “state citizenship list” through citizenship, naturalization and Social Security records and send that to election officials in each state. It would allow for investigating or prosecuting local officials if they provide a ballot to someone who’s ineligible to vote in a federal election.
The order also gave the U.S. Postal Service rulemaking authority on voting by mail. In response, the agency proposed a rule in early June that would require states to submit a “mail-in and absentee participation list” of voters who intend to vote by mail. If a state isn’t in compliance, the Postal Service could block the transmission of mail ballots. The executive order required USPS to submit a final rule by the end of July.
The Supreme Court majority on Monday wrote that the administration’s push to implement the restrictions this year is likely to lose in court, though the brief emergency order didn’t detail its reasoning. Two justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, publicly dissented.
The Trump administration had asked the justices, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress.
Alito wrote in his dissent that the Postal Service “has broad authority to regulate the mail” and likely does have the power to enforce Trump’s restrictions.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, meanwhile, agreed that the restrictions should not go into effect for the midterms but indicated he might rule in favor of the Trump administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time.
Lower courts agreed to block Trump’s plan, including a preliminary injunction issued by a judge nominated by the president.But the Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that federal control of the Postal Service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible.
The federal government won an early procedural decision at the Supreme Court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan.
Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Leading candidates in Alaska US House race endorse bycatch limits in fisheries debate
description: Front-runner candidates for Alaska’s sole U.S. House of Representatives seat expressed strong support for the fishing industry and coastal communities at a debate in Kodiak over the weekend.  Incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III and independent challenger Bill Hill took very similar positions on issues including fisheries bycatch, declining fish st[...]
text:
Alaska candidates for the U.S. House race incumbent Republican Nick Begich III (left) and independent challenger Bill Hill (right) squared off at a fisheries debate in Kodiak on Sep. 12, 2026. (Photo by Brian Venua/Alaska Beacon)Front-runner candidates for Alaska’s sole U.S. House of Representatives seat expressed strong support for the fishing industry and coastal communities at a debate in Kodiak over the weekend. 
Incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III and independent challenger Bill Hill took very similar positions on issues including fisheries bycatch, declining fish stocks and representation in federal fisheries management, but there were some differences. 
Begich touted his legislative record in his first two-year term as beneficial to Alaska fisheries, while Hill said his personal history as a lifelong fisherman in Bristol Bay is advantageous for representing Alaska in Congress.
Begich, a technology entrepreneur and business executive, garnered 44.6% of the vote in the primary election, while Hill, a former school superintendent and commercial fisherman, received 32.5% of the vote. Third and fourth place finishers in Alaska’s ranked choice general election include Eric Hafner — a registered Democrat serving a federal prison sentence in New York – with 3.8% of the vote, and Libertarian Jim McDermott of Fairbanks with 1.2%. 
The winner of the November election will serve a two-year term as one of the 435 members of the U.S. House of Representatives. 
Begich promoted his legislative record as a freshman in the Republican-controlled U.S. House. This spring, six bills he sponsored passed Congress to become law — a tie with another Arizona lawmaker for most bills passed as a freshman — but none of those bills directly address fisheries issues.
“I have passed more legislation than any freshman on record,” Begich said. “And those are good Alaska bills — they are bills that unlock lands for Alaskans, and they are bills that, in many cases, we’ve been working to achieve for decades.”
Hill repeatedly referenced his experience growing up subsistence and commercial fishing in Bristol Bay. “I raised three of my kids on my fishing boat, and understand the importance that state, national and international politics play in what happens on our back decks with our children, what happens in the income that we can take home, what taxation does to us, what tariffs do to us,” he said. “I’ve lived a life of fish.”
Bycatch
Several debate questions focused on bycatch, the accidental harvest of nontargeted fish. Bycatch has raised public concern around Alaska’s industrial trawl fleet, which has many vessels harbored in Kodiak, where the debate took place. 
Both candidates said they support broader representation on the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, which oversees fishing policy in federal waters, including bycatch regulations. 
Begich said he supports increasing representation for subsistence, sport fishers and small commercial operators, as well as large operators, in council decisions. He pointed to a bill he introduced, the Bycatch Reduction Act, which would require the council to implement gear performance standards to reduce bycatch, to make investments in fishing gear and fisheries research and to increase monitoring and reporting from the industry and the council, among others. 
“We need transparency — more transparency for folks who may have conflicts of interest that currently serve on the NPFMC,” Begich said. He also expressed support for a chum bycatch limit established by the council this year for the Bering Sea pollock fishery.
Hill said he supports bycatch limits to protect salmon runs, and additional seats representing subsistence and tribal groups. 
“Subsistence is sacred, and the very first thing that needs to happen, and I think you hear it from across the state — this is why there’s such a loud outcry — is because some of our subsistence users have not been able to access their resource, which is more than just protein, for quite a few years now,” he said. 
In a question about Congress’ role in reducing bycatch, debate moderators noted all fisheries produce some bycatch harvest and said “a goal of zero bycatch isn’t reasonable.”
But both candidates pushed back on that framing and said that zero bycatch should be the ultimate goal. 
The industrial trawl fleet, particularly boats that target pollock, has been the focus of public criticism because it contributes substantially to the state’s bycatch numbers for species including juvenile halibut, cod and salmon returning to spawning grounds throughout Alaska.
Begich said he agreed that every fishery produces some level of bycatch and it’s up to the council to manage each complex fishery. But he said the goal should be “aggressive.” 
“I do think the goal should be zero. It’s going to be a long road to get there. But we also have to recognize that in every single fishery, whether it be subsistence, sport, small commercial or large commercial, they have a bycatch responsibility as well,” Begich said.
Hill said the goal should be zero bycatch. “We need to work towards that. We need to work towards a very low-threshold for our trawling industry, especially the out-of-state corporate trawlers,” he said. 
And Hill expressed confidence that the trawl industry would be able to meet required limits. 
“My perspective is when you set something out for industry to accomplish, they always find a way, and we’ve seen over and over again that our trawl fleet has met the standards that are being set for them. So, can we get to 0%? That would be everybody’s desire, but should we be working towards it? Yes, we should be,” Hill said. “But those who are bad actors, you’ve got to leave the fishery.”
When asked about the primary causes of king and chum salmon run declines, Begich responded it was “largely bycatch related.”
“You look at the Yukon, you look at the Kuskokwim — those runs are way down. We’re seeing some recovery in chums. I think that the cap that we put in with NPFMC is sort of that initial shot saying, ‘Hey, we’re going to be managing these more carefully,’” Begich said. “But I think that historical bycatch is the root cause.”
Hill said he agreed, and added that climate change driven factors are affecting Alaska’s salmon runs. “Climate change is a real thing, and we need to start mitigating for that,” he said. “But yes, we need to end bycatch.” 
Processing and protecting Alaska’s fisheries
Both candidates said they would support investments in building the workforce in fishing and processing sectors, as well as more visas for hiring international workers in processing.
In a lightning round of questions, the candidates agreed on every issue. They supported science-based fisheries management, more investment in research and engaging with a wide range of fisheries interest groups prior to introducing new legislation or policies. They also agreed that rural and tribal communities should have more say in decisions affecting fish. 
When asked how they would ensure the economic value of federally-managed fisheries would not come at the expense of Alaska communities, Begich said he supports labeling rules for farmed vs. wild-caught fish.
“Alaska seafood is competing with penned fish and farmed fish, and the end consumer doesn’t know it,” Begich said. “And so, when you’re buying an Alaska seafood product, we need to make sure that it’s labeled Alaska. That’s transparent because it gives us the best price for our product and it reduces some of the pressure on our fisheries.”
Hill said he would support more investment in in-state seafood processing to diversify processors to which fishing fleets can sell their harvests. “More processing in our state that’s not a consolidated, vertically integrated type of processing,” he said. “And we need to make sure that we’re legislating to make sure that farmed fishing does not come to our seas and that we keep them off for as long as we possibly can.”
Geopolitics
Both candidates expressed support for tariffs on international seafood to protect Alaska markets.
Hill also condemned the U.S. war in Iran for driving high costs of fuel and affecting fisheries. 
“The Iran war is a terrible, terrible thing in terms of how it’s impacted our industry,” he said. “The fuel costs I paid this summer were $2 per gallon more than last year, and they were already high. And then we start talking about things like food and groceries, and the things that allow our crews to do good work for us while we’re fishing hard.”
Begich has expressed support for the Trump administration’s military action against Iran, and voted against a war powers resolution that passed Congress in June calling on President Donald Trump to remove armed forces against Iran, unless authorized by Congress or a declaration of war.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Trump nominates Pete Serrano for US attorney in western WA
description: In an unexpected move, President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Pete Serrano, a former state attorney general candidate from Pasco, to be the next U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington.  Serrano now leads the federal prosecutor’s office in eastern Washington in his dual roles of first assistant U.S. attorney and special attorney to […]
text:
Pete Serrano, who leads the federal prosecutor's office in eastern Washington, was nominated Monday to be U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington. Serrano, a Republican, lost a 2024 bid for Washington attorney general. He is shown here during a debate in Spokane, Wash., on Sept. 18, 2024.  (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)In an unexpected move, President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Pete Serrano, a former state attorney general candidate from Pasco, to be the next U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington. 
Serrano now leads the federal prosecutor’s office in eastern Washington in his dual roles of first assistant U.S. attorney and special attorney to Attorney General Todd Blanche. His appointment is the latest development in a turbulent chapter for judicial nominees in the state.
Serrano served about four months in 2025 as interim U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Washington. That appointment expired in December when Trump failed to formally nominate Serrano for the job in the face of staunch opposition from Washington’s two Democratic U.S. senators.
A Republican, Serrano ran unsuccessfully for state attorney general in 2024. He is also the founder of the conservative nonprofit Silent Majority Foundation, which has challenged Washington’s gun restrictions and COVID mandates.
The appointment of interim U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd in western Washington also ended without Trump nominating him for the job. Floyd now serves as first assistant U.S. attorney.
Judges in the western district then appointed Roger Rogoff, a former federal prosecutor and King County judge, to the post. Trump fired Rogoff an hour after the appointment, creating the vacancy that Serrano has been nominated to fill. Rogoff has sued, contending the president’s action violates a federal law that allows judges to act if the interim appointment is not confirmed.
On Monday, Serrano said he was informed of the nomination Monday and had “definitely” not spoken to the president. “It’s just another day in the Trump administration in Washington,” he said.
He also said he expects Washington’s senators will not drop their opposition. He was right.
“I will be using every tool I have to block this nomination,” Sen. Patty Murray said in a statement. “Let’s be clear about what a sham this is: After federal judges declined to appoint Serrano in Eastern Washington, this administration invented a workaround to install him anyway. Now they want to permanently install Serrano in the Western District.”
“The people of Washington state deserve a serious U.S. Attorney who will follow the law, not a political loyalist who thinks the law is whatever the President says it is,” she said.
One of those tools is the “blue slip” process, a longstanding tradition that allows senators to block nominees for U.S. attorney positions and federal judgeships in their states.
Once a president makes a nomination, a consent form, known as a blue slip, is sent by the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee to the two senators in the nominee’s home state. 
If the forms are signed and returned, the process continues. If not, it signals a lack of support and the chair will not advance the nominee.
Trump loathes the process because it has derailed some of his picks. He has called it “old and outdated” and threatened legal action to end it.
“I have a Constitutional Right to appoint Judges and U.S. Attorneys, but that RIGHT has been completely taken away from me in States that have just one Democrat United States Senator,” Trump has posted on social media.
There are 93 U.S. attorneys nationwide. They prosecute federal criminal cases and work on civil litigation involving the federal government. Serrano supervises a staff of approximately 79 prosecutors, civil litigators, and support personnel, according to the Department of Justice.
Serrano was appointed in early August 2025 as interim U.S. attorney by former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi. He could serve 120 days while awaiting confirmation. The clock expired in early December without Trump nominating him.
Originally from California, he moved to Pasco in 2015 with his family. He worked as an environmental lawyer for the U.S. Department of Energy and at Energy Northwest before founding the Silent Majority Foundation. Serrano is also the former leader of the Franklin County Republican Party.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Vance rallies support for Kansas Republicans in pointed speech interrupted by protester
description: OLATHE — Vice President JD Vance on Monday vouched for Kansas Republicans running for the U.S. Senate and the governor’s office, pushing back against Democrats who want to regain control of Congress in November. Federal and state Republicans signaled they need more Kansans on their side, encouraging the hundreds of attendees of a rally at […]
text:
Vice President JD Vance appears at a Sept. 14, 2026, rally at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)OLATHE — Vice President JD Vance on Monday vouched for Kansas Republicans running for the U.S. Senate and the governor’s office, pushing back against Democrats who want to regain control of Congress in November.
Federal and state Republicans signaled they need more Kansans on their side, encouraging the hundreds of attendees of a rally at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe “to find 10 friends” and convince them to vote Republican, or as Kansas’ GOP Party chair Danedri Herbert said it: “We need every single one of you.”
Top Kansas GOP leaders joined the vice president to campaign for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, who is running for reelection against a Democratic pastor, and state Senate President Ty Masterson, a Republican who is running for governor against fellow state Sen. Cindy Holscher, a Democrat.
Vance, surrounded by heavy machinery and sheet metal, praised Marshall’s friendship and tenure in the U.S. Senate, and cast aspersions on his opponent, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor in the Kansas City area.
Some attendees hoped for a formal announcement of a Vance 2028 presidential run, and others came interested to hear Masterson and Marshall speak. Stan and Janette Gray, a couple from Paola, said they see Vance as a “tell it like it is” leader, and they find value in the fact that “he didn’t have a cushy life” growing up.
Vance spent the rally slamming Democrats and bolstering Republicans. He said Marshall has fought for businesses and working people and been an ally to the Trump administration.
“When the lobbyists and the special interests and the far-left lunatics come and try to fight against the people in this room, Roger Marshall has been on the right side every single time,” Vance said.
Moments later, a protester interrupted his remarks about Marshall.
“He sued his patients,” the man yelled, before being pushed out by security.
Security forces out a protester at a Sept. 14, 2026, rally by Vice President JD Vance at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
The New York Times reported last week that Marshall sued hundreds of patients in central Kansas for unpaid medical debt while he was the only available OB-GYN within a roughly 60-mile radius.
Vance carried on, touting Marshall’s support for eliminating taxes on overtime income and sponsoring legislation that would cap credit card interest fees.
“The reality is that Doc Marshall has stood up for everyday Americans every single day in the United States Senate,” Vance said.
Vance disparaged Hamilton, the leader of the largest United Methodist church in the nation, who won a 10-person Democratic primary in August and will face Marshall and a libertarian candidate, David Graham.
Vance brought up some oft-repeated soundbites from Hamilton’s old sermons that without context indicate Hamilton thinks people should repent for eating meat and that white privilege is a sin. He also condemned Hamilton’s church, Resurrection, for sponsoring a local pride festival, along with dozens of other organizations.
“In this race, we have got Dr. Roger Marshall, a proud servant of this state, and a proud Christian to boot, versus a guy who would insult your faith and spit on your religion to accrue donations to himself,” Vance said.
Glynnis Harvey, a spokesperson for the Hamilton campaign, said in a statement the church in 2025 fed more than 45,000 people in need, distributed nearly 60,000 children’s books, held blood drives, led foster care support programs and built affordable housing. 
“(Hamilton) welcomes VP Vance to come visit Resurrection, instead of attacking the largest United Methodist Church in the country in an attempt to save Roger Marshall’s flailing campaign and distract from record diesel and gas prices, the war in Iran, and Roger Marshall’s usurious medical debt collection practices,” Harvey said.
Marshall, who addressed the crowd ahead of Vance, said Hamilton has “no clue” about the importance of manufacturing jobs.
“China loves him,” Marshall said, and added that Hamilton is “too woke and too weak to stand up to China.”
The rally came roughly 50 days before the November election when Marshall will compete to retain a U.S. Senate seat that’s been held by Republicans for nearly the past century. was organized by Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc.
Repeatedly, Republicans emphasized the high stakes of the election. 
Randy Sipe, a 70-year-old retiree from Waverly, said at stake in November are the continuation of “America first” policies, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran. He said he wants to see Trump remain in Iran until the U.S. accomplishes its goal.
“You’ve got to complete the game if you’re going to win,” Sipe said.
U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann, a Republican who represents Kansas’ 1st Congressional District, offered a three-pronged focus for Kansas Republicans in the lead-up to November. Republicans across the country needed to “clearly define” what they’re running against, which he said were Democratic socialists, “tie every Democrat to this insanity,” and get out and vote.
U.S. Rep. Ron Estes, a Republican who represents Kansas’ 4th Congressional District, said he has heard throughout his time campaigning across his district this year from constituents who fear that Democrats will take back control of Congress. He encouraged the crowd to vote Republican so the country doesn’t revert “to the malaise that we were in.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Homeland Security boss visits Omaha, talks tough on immigration, touts disaster response strides
description: OMAHA — The head of U.S. Homeland Security was in Omaha Monday nurturing partnerships he said helped send roughly $120 million in federal disaster aid to Nebraska since 2025, and to seek feedback on cutting costly “red tape” in the reimbursement process. At another stop in the state’s most populous city, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne […]
text:
U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is flanked by Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts on the left and the parents of Sarah Root, Michelle and Scott, on the right. Their daughter Sarah was killed in a 2016 car crash involving an undocumented migrant. Mullin was in Omaha Monday for two unrelated events. The other was to discuss his department's progress on streamlining federal disaster aid to communities. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)(Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner) OMAHA — The head of U.S. Homeland Security was in Omaha Monday nurturing partnerships he said helped send roughly $120 million in federal disaster aid to Nebraska since 2025, and to seek feedback on cutting costly “red tape” in the reimbursement process.
At another stop in the state’s most populous city, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin switched to tough-talking about illegal immigration. He hosted a press conference with the family of Sarah Root, the 21-year-old killed a decade ago in an Omaha crash with an undocumented migrant who fled the country but was found and sentenced in February to up to 22 years in prison. 
“I will hunt you down. Our agents will hunt you down and we’re going to send you back,” Mullin said during the livestreamed gathering where he and others laid out Root’s story and a 2025 law that Congress subsequently adopted.
ICE pacts rise in Nebraska
Mullin was accompanied on both Omaha stops by Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is in a high-intensity battle with nonpartisan Dan Osborn, who is seeking to unseat Ricketts.
U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen leads a roundtable discussion held at the Omaha Fire Department headquarters. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
During the Root event, held in the federal building where immigration court cases are heard, Mullin told reporters that people often complain about the tactics of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. He dismissed such concerns and lauded the 2025 law and the work of officers involved in bringing “justice” to the Root family. 
“Every single death at an illegal’s hands is 100% preventable,” said Mullin, who previously represented Oklahoma in the U.S. House and Senate.
Sworn into his current role in March, Mullin also commended Nebraska for increased enrollment in a 287(g) program in which local law enforcement agencies contract with Homeland Security to carry out certain ICE functions. Local agencies that participate receive training and reimbursement by the feds. Mullin said the pacts lead to more arrests and deportations of migrants in the country illegally.
Seven Nebraska agencies launched 287(g) pacts this year, according to the Homeland Security website. They formed after a Nebraska lawmaker this past February unsuccessfully sought new local requirements for 287(g) agreements that drew opposition from Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration. At that time, a handful of agencies had a partnership with ICE. 
The Nebraska State Patrol is among participants, having started its pact in August 2025 with six troopers trained for the program. The number of troopers on the task force has grown to 16, a patrol spokesman told the Nebraska Examiner last month.
Asked by a reporter about community concerns that such ICE partnerships lead to more intense scrutiny and traffic stops of brown-skinned people, Mullin was quick to react.
“It’s a lie,” he said before noting that he is Cherokee. “There’s nothing racist about enforcing the nation’s laws.”
Sarah’s Law
Michelle and Scott Root, Sarah’s parents, told reporters that earlier in the day they met three federal agents who helped capture Eswin Mejia, who investigators said was speeding and had a blood alcohol content three times over the legal limit when his vehicle struck Sarah Root’s car from behind. 
The Roots have met multiple times with President Donald Trump and have attended various White House and congressional events tied to immigration policy as the circumstances of their daughter’s death have been highlighted nationally.
Col. Bryan Waugh, superintendent of the Nebraska State Patrol, at podium, speaks at a news conference with Gov. Jim Pillen on Sept. 14, 2026, detailing recent historic stops by the State Patrol. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Of the timing of Monday’s meeting, Mullin said, “We’re  not forgetting about these families … We’re making sure people hear it. They need to hear the story about what’s taking place. They need to hear that narrative.”
Michelle Root said Mejia’s sentencing a decade later does not bring back her daughter but “does close that chapter and it lifts a weight off of our shoulders because we fought long and hard to make this a reality, to get justice for Sarah.”
Though Mejia initially was arrested after the crash, he was released the following month on a $5,000 bond and fled the country. In March 2025, Homeland Security agents tracked him down and said it marked the first time Honduras had extradited someone to the U.S. for homicide.
“Sarah’s Law” was added as an amendment to the Laken Riley Act, the first piece of legislation that President Donald Trump signed into law during his second term. The act mandates federal detention of undocumented immigrants arrested for crimes including burglary, theft and any that result in the death or serious bodily injury of another person.
Opinions of the Laken Riley Act vary across policy and advocacy groups. The National Immigration Law Center has argued that the law exploits a personal tragedy to scapegoat immigrants while weakening constitutional protections without proven benefit to public safety. The American Immigration Lawyers Association emphasizes due process concerns.
Proponents view the law as necessary for accountability and public safety.
Roundtable on disaster relief 
Earlier Monday, at his first Omaha appearance, Mullin joined a roundtable discussion at the Omaha Fire Department that included Ricketts, Fire Chief Kathy Bossman, representatives of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and local emergency management administrators.
Both ICE and FEMA, which coordinates the federal government’s response to natural and man-made disasters, are under the auspices of Homeland Security. 
Mullen said he has held such sessions across the country to strengthen partnerships and hear suggestions that can improve the flow and efficiency of federal emergency disaster recovery dollars. He said his agency is seeking to cut unnecessary and expensive bureaucracy. 
“If we can get that dollar to the local governments, allow them to spend it, allow them to contract it, it’ll go farther and be more efficient.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and others at a roundtable discussion watch firefighters sliding down a pole as they head to an emergency. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Too often, Mullin said, disagreements erupt between agencies despite having a common goal. He said the Trump administration’s goal is to change old ways, which he described as the federal government coming in to “tell everybody how to do it our way.”
“We’re trying to change that focus and saying we’re going to give you the ability to do it your way. You know your town. You know where the hot spots are …,” Mullin said.
He expects better response if agencies are confident “knowing that the money is going to come in.” And he encouraged the panel and local and state officials to provide feedback. 
“We can’t fix it if we don’t know about it. And don’t think you’re going to get punished or get your hands slapped for doing it,” said Mullin.
Bossman said fire officials, in responding to emergencies, establish procedures and coordinate with outside agencies so that the most effective equipment is on site.
“We can feel confident that we can go ahead and perform at our highest level using the equipment that is most appropriate for the rescue or response knowing we can trust our state and federal partners to support us,” she said.
Mullin touted his personal and professional relationship with Ricketts, and encouraged local officials to turn to such elected officials as they seek federal emergency recovery aid.
“Relationships matter,” he said.

(Foto de Jill Hummels para Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
HUTCHINSON — Los candidatos a gobernador se enzarzaron en una verdadera pelea a puño limpio cuando subieron al escenario el sábado en la Feria Estatal de Kansas para un debate marcado por los cánticos y abucheos de una multitud entusiasta de seguidores en duelo.
El presidente del Senado de Kansas, Ty Masterson, el candidato republicano, y la senadora estatal Cindy Holscher, la candidata demócrata, en gran medida evitaron las preguntas directas de un panel de medios mientras discutían quién era más extremo y cómo hacer que la vida fuera asequible para los residentes del estado.
La multitud que llenó el Pabellón de la Cooperativa de Crédito Heartland, en ocasiones, silenció a los candidatos. Los seguidores de Holscher llevaban carteles que se burlaban del trabajo “ausente” de Masterson en la Universidad Estatal de Wichita, donde recibió casi un millón de dólares desde 2017 como director de “GoCreate, una Colaborativa Koch.” Los seguidores de Masterson ondeaban carteles que decían “Cue card Cindy”, en alusión a la preferencia de Holscher por llevar notas consigo en el escenario durante el debate.
Masterson, de Andover, dijo que se postulaba para gobernador para asegurarse de que las familias trabajadoras pudieran costearse vivir en Kansas y evitar que las personas fueran forzadas a salir de sus hogares.
“Seré el gobernador más pro-agricultura, pro-negocios, pro-petróleo y pro-gas que este estado haya visto”, dijo. “Así es como traemos oportunidades a nuestra gente.”
Definió repetidamente a Holscher como socialista y como la “progresista liberal más radical que jamás haya estado en una fórmula” en Kansas.
“No soy socialista”, respondió ella. “Pero Ty sigue diciendo ‘socialista’ y ‘extremo’.’ ¿Sabes qué es extremo? Oponerse a la atención médica cuando la gente sufre. Eso es extremismo. ¿Qué más es extremo? Oponerse a subir el salario mínimo para nuestra gente mientras él cobra un millón de dólares por un trabajo fantasma. Eso es extremo.”
Greg Akagi, de WIBW 580 Radio, moderó el debate con preguntas publicadas por el reportero senior de Kansas Reflector, Tim Carpenter, y por Michael Schwanke, de KWCH-TV, y la editora de Gras and Grain, Donna Sullivan.
Holcher, de Overland Park, dijo que se postulaba para gobernadora debido a la crisis de asequibilidad que golpea a todo el estado. Dijo que los impuestos a la propiedad son tan altos porque una legislatura encabezada por Masterson sigue otorgando exenciones fiscales a corporaciones y a los ricos. Señaló que Masterson ha liderado el Senado estatal durante seis años, con una supermayoría republicana, y lo culpó de no haber reducido los impuestos prediales.
“O no quiere hacer esto o no sabe cómo”, dijo ella. “Lo haré.”
También pidió que el estado invierta más en las escuelas públicas para aliviar la carga fiscal local.
“Solo escucha las palabras que salen de su boca”, dijo Masterson. “¿Crees que la respuesta a la asequibilidad es más gasto gubernamental? ¿Crees que esa es la respuesta? Eso es lo opuesto a la verdad. La verdad es que tus impuestos son tan altos porque personas como Cindy no han conocido uno de tus impuestos que no quería gastar dos.”
Holscher dijo que había una “diferencia muy grande” entre ambos en materia de política fiscal. Masterson dijo que está a favor de exenciones fiscales para sus donantes, mientras que ella favorece exenciones fiscales para la gente trabajadora. Prometió invertir más en las comunidades.
Masterson, en ocasiones, provocó un coro de abucheos entre los seguidores de Holscher.
“¿Creen que van a tener mayor asequibilidad con impuestos más altos?” dijo. “O sea, procesen eso con su cerebro.”
 
El republicano Ty Masterson ataca la postura de la demócrata Cindy Holscher sobre la política fiscal durante el debate de la feria estatal del 12 de septiembre de 2026 en Hutchinson. (Foto por Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Derechos al aborto
Masterson afirmó durante el debate que la enmienda constitucional que los votantes rechazaron en agosto no trataba del aborto. La enmienda habría hecho que los jueces de la Corte Suprema de Kansas fueran funcionarios electos, y Masterson previamente argumentó a favor de la enmienda porque sostuvo que permitiría a la corte revocar los derechos de aborto en Kansas.
La afirmación adicional de Masterson de que “el aborto es un tema 80-20” fue recibida con cánticos de “mentiroso, mentiroso” por los seguidores de Holscher. Dijo que la gente quiere menos abortos, que no haya abortos en etapas avanzadas y que no haya abortos financiados por los contribuyentes.
Holscher dijo que los votantes de Kansas dejaron clara su postura en 2022, cuando rechazaron una enmienda constitucional distinta que buscaba únicamente eliminar el derecho a interrumpir un embarazo. Después de que eso fracasó por un margen de 59-41, Masterson dijo que decidió intentarlo de nuevo con la enmienda de este año, que fue rechazada por un margen de 61-39.
“Sigue atacando la atención de la salud reproductiva, y eso es lo que seguirá haciendo si lo eligen gobernador”, dijo. “Los ataques serán implacables contra sus derechos.”
Masterson respondió acusando a Holscher de apoyar a los elitistas.
“Ella quiere el poder del grupo más pequeño posible”, dijo.
“¿Cuándo se convirtió el 60% en el grupo más pequeño?” respondió Holscher, refiriéndose al voto popular.
Masterson luego cambió de tema, acusando a Holscher de querer permitir que los niños se sometieran a “cirugías transgénero” sin que sus padres lo supieran. Sus seguidores abuchearon en respuesta.
“¡Está en el registro! ¡Búscalo! Mira. Eso. ¡Arriba! Gritó Masterson a la multitud, que abucheó más fuerte. “Esto no está en debate. Está en el registro. Estás negando la verdad.”
 
La demócrata Cindy Holscher dice durante el debate estatal justo del 12 de septiembre de 2026 en Hutchinson que el republicano Ty Masterson seguirá “centrándose en la atención a la salud reproductiva” si es elegido gobernador. (Foto por Jill Hummels para Kansas Reflector)
Centros de datos
Holscher, quien ha solicitado una moratoria temporal en los centros de datos, atacó a Masterson por apoyar su desarrollo. Dijo que las empresas de inteligencia artificial gastaron $800,000 en publicidad para apoyar a Masterson durante las primarias.
“Ty va a poner un centro de datos en cada esquina y en cada campo de maíz”, dijo Holscher.
Masterson dijo que su postura sobre los centros de datos nunca había cambiado, lo cual fue una crítica a Holscher, quien votó con él a favor de una legislación el año pasado que otorga una exención fiscal para grandes desarrollos de centros de datos. Dijo que los centros de datos transferirán fondos provenientes de los impuestos prediales a las comunidades.
“Que los locales tomen la decisión”, dijo.
 
De izquierda a derecha, Michael Schwanke de KWCH-TV, la editora de Grass and Grain, Donna Sullivan, y el reportero senior de Kansas Reflector, Tim Carpenter, cuestionan a los candidatos durante el debate de la feria estatal del 12 de septiembre de 2026 en Hutchinson. (Foto de Jill Hummels para Kansas Reflector)
Vales escolares
Masterson dijo que apoya los vales escolares privados porque no es justo dejar a los niños en una situación en la que su única opción es asistir a una escuela que fracasa.
“Aprenderán el bienestar generacional, o aprenderán que el crimen paga”, dijo.
Señalando a Holscher, agregó: “Todo esto es ceguera para esos niños que están atrapados.”
Holscher destacó su apoyo al fallido experimento fiscal del exgobernador Sam Brownback y a los recortes en el gasto público en educación.
“No sé qué esperarías”, dijo ella. “Desfinanciaron nuestras escuelas hasta el punto de la crisis. Ustedes son quienes dificultaron que a estos niños les fuera bien.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Mayoral candidate in Louisiana involved in illegal voting, feds say
description: A failed candidate for mayor in a small Louisiana town faces federal charges for allegedly helping a noncitizen to register and vote in her 2024 election.
text:
A candidate for  Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning StarA failed candidate for mayor in a small Louisiana town faces federal charges for allegedly helping a noncitizen to register and vote in her 2024 election.
Bridget Johnson was indicted last week and her charges made public Monday when U.S. Attorney Todd Blanche publicized six arrests in three states related to voter fraud.
According to her indictment, Johnson was running for town mayor in Cotton Valley when completed an online voter registration form in July 2024 for Michael Wedderburn, a citizen of Jamaica who lived in Webster Parish at the time. Wedderburn falsely claimed he was a U.S. citizen and voted for Johnson in the mayor’s race, which she lost. 
Johnson, 53, received just 44% of the 326 votes cast in the town of less than 800 residents.
She and Wedderburn are each charged with fraudulent voter registration, and Wedderburn is accused of voting by an alien. 
Johnson declined to comment when reached by phone Monday evening.
Wedderburn, 52, did not respond to outreach through social media nor did his attorney immediately answer a request for comment.
The Louisiana Secretary of State’s office assisted the FBI in its investigation, according to a news release from the U.S. Department of Justice. 
“One illegal vote is one too many. An illegal vote erases the voice of a lawful voter,” Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said in a statement. “When we uncover potential illegal activity, we will investigate it, refer it to the appropriate authorities and pursue accountability.” 
Landry has readily complied with calls from the Trump administration to share access to state voter rolls for the purposes of sussing out election fraud, though neither state nor federal officials have ever validated the president’s oft-repeated claims of widespread election fraud.
The other charges Blanche announced Monday included three people who allegedly paid homeless people in Los Angeles to sign petitions using stolen identities of registered voters. The signatures were reportedly used to help place initiatives on statewide ballots.
In Kansas, a Peruvian national and permanent U.S. resident faces multiple charges for allegedly voting in a federal election despite not being an American citizen, according to the Justice Department.
This is a developing story.

title: US Supreme Court blocks Trump rule limiting mail voting, sides with Dem states
text: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday kept in place a lower court’s order blocking President Donald Trump’s embattled plan to place new restrictions on mail ballots for this year’s midterm elections.The unsigned, one-paragraph order upheld a Massachusetts federal court’s injunction on a U.S. Postal Service rule until after Nov. 3 and did not decide whether the rule itself was lawful. But a majority of the court said the Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenging the rule were likely to succeed.Two of the court’s stalwart conservatives, Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, dissented from the decision. Alito wrote that the Postal Service has “broad authority to regulate the mail” and that at this preliminary stage of the suit challenging the rule, its policy should remain in place.“I express no view on whether the Government would be likely to succeed on de novo review of the Postal Service’s powers,” he wrote. “But for now, the Government has satisfied its burden of making a strong showing that the plaintiff States’ … claim is not likely to succeed.”In a brief concurrence, Justice Brett Kavanaugh said the rule, which codifies technical requirements on the envelopes carrying ballots and requires states to collect and send to the federal government lists of eligible voters, may be legal, but was unworkable for the midterm elections 50 days away.“There is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority,” he wrote. “But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious …  because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”The rule’s challengers argued, in part, that the regulations would be impossible to install ahead of Election Day. Several election administrators, pro-democracy groups and others declared to the court that they agreed with that argument. The Postal Service did not bring any evidence against those claims.Democrats and voting rights advocates also argued the rule was illegal and unconstitutional. The executive branch has virtually no role in elections administration, which is a state responsibility with congressional oversight under the U.S. Constitution, they said. The case, tried before President Barack Obama appointee U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, will continue to evaluate the legality of the rule for future elections.Challengers react The groups and officials challenging the rule, as well as other Democrats, hailed the ruling in statements.“Today’s order from our nation’s highest court makes clear that states cannot be forced to undermine their mail voting systems and risk voter disenfranchisement because of the President’s political agenda,” Massachusetts Attorney General Joy Campbell said. “Mail voting is safe, secure, and reliable, and I will continue to stand up for Massachusetts residents who rely on mail ballots to ensure that they can have their voices heard in the November election.”Virginia Kase Solomón, the president and CEO of Common Cause, one of the groups suing to block the rule, called the decision “a major win for the millions of everyday Americans,” including elderly and rural voters, and those with disabilities, who depend on vote-by-mail.“This executive order was a blatant power grab designed to silence voters and undermine our elections, but it failed because the people and the law were on our side,” she said in a statement. “Our Constitution is clear: states run our elections, and voters choose their leaders—not the other way around. No administration can strip the people of their power.”California Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose state was the lead plaintiff in the case, said the rule was part of Trump’s “attacks on democracy” for the past 20 months.“California stood up for democracy and we won,” Newsom wrote on social media. “Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law, and the American people looking to exercise their Constitutional right to vote.”Phil Weiser, Colorado’s attorney general and Democratic nominee for governor, said the court “just sent the message that President Trump and the Postal Service need to stay the hell away from our elections.”California and Colorado are among the eight states that send ballots to every registered voter.Spokespeople for the White House, Postal Service and U.S. Department of Justice, which represented the administration in the case, did not respond to emails seeking comment late Monday.In the hour following the ruling, Trump posted on his social media platform in opposition to slowing artificial intelligence development, the poor condition of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts building and his promise to send every voter $5,000 if Republicans win the upcoming midterms, but did not address the ruling.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Does Glenfarne actually need a pipeline?
description: Everyone debating the Alaska LNG project assumes the developer wants what it says it wants: to build an 800-mile natural gas pipeline. But look at Glenfarne’s deeds instead of its words, and a different possibility emerges. Glenfarne may actually be waiting to see if things work out with the pipeline because it now has an […]
text:
Glenfarne's name is displayed on May. 19, 2026, on the stairs at the Dena'ina Civic and Convention Center, the venue for the three-day Alaska Sustainable Energy Conference. Glenfarne is a major sponsor of the conference. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Everyone debating the Alaska LNG project assumes the developer wants what it says it wants: to build an 800-mile natural gas pipeline.
But look at Glenfarne’s deeds instead of its words, and a different possibility emerges. Glenfarne may actually be waiting to see if things work out with the pipeline because it now has an essentially guaranteed moneymaker in the form of a project to import LNG into Cook Inlet for local needs.
Consider the company’s position. Glenfarne paid $10 million and promised to fund the pipeline project’s development in return for 75 percent of the entity that holds the permits, the right-of-way, and a quarter-billion dollars worth of state-funded development work on the only federally-permitted LNG export project on the U.S. Pacific Coast.
In the energy industry, $10 million is sofa-cushion money. It’s not the price of an asset, it’s the price of an option on an asset. And a leaked draft of the state’s own review suggests there’s a highly favorable exit clause for Glenfarne: if Alaska ever wants to get that 75 percent back — to build the project itself or hand it over to a more credible developer — Glenfarne would name the asking price.
Then there’s what Glenfarne has done with its own money — not buying pipe for the gasline, which it promised to order and didn’t, but building an LNG import terminal in Cook Inlet with Enstar, the Southcentral gas utility, locked up as an exclusive customer. Cook Inlet gas is running low and Southcentral will need imported gas soon, pipeline or no pipeline. Imports are the one sure thing in this entire picture. And Glenfarne’s in the catbird seat.
And here’s the rub. The first phase of the pipeline, which Glenfarne now estimates to cost $13 billion to $17 billion, is meant to serve that same Southcentral market before any gas is exported. So Glenfarne is building a relatively cheap, near-term way to supply the Cook Inlet market while asking Alaska to subsidize a $13-billion-plus way to supply the same customers. Once you own a cheap solution to a hungry local market, why rush to build an expensive one and compete with yourself?
The booster answer has been that imports are merely a bridge until the pipeline is ready. But that gets the incentive backwards. A bridge you own, earning money the moment it opens, serving captive customers with no ready alternative, is not a reason to hurry toward a $50-billion megaproject. It’s a reason to relax and see what unfolds.
Now add the politics. To get the Legislature to yes on tax incentives, Glenfarne and the governor promised nearly anything, up to and including a $250 million Fairbanks spur to build political support in the Interior. Yet when the Legislature assembled a bill this year that gave Glenfarne what it said it needed — a big property tax break and an income-tax exemption — the deal collapsed. By several legislators’ accounts, Hilcorp, which controls the North Slope gas the pipeline would carry, leaned on Glenfarne to kill it over the income tax provision in the bill. The governor called that “bullshit.” Either way, the pipeline project is stalled while the LNG import project proceeds.
Put the pieces together and a coherent strategy appears. Build the import terminal, the sure thing, and start making money while Hilcorp and the Legislature duel over income taxes.
Meantime, hold onto your bargain-basement 75 percent stake in the pipeline project like the option it is. If the economics of that project ever come together, either build it yourself or sell out to someone big enough to wrangle Hilcorp and the Legislature into settling their differences. If the pipeline never goes, you’re not exposed, and you make money on LNG imports as far out as the eye can see.
We don’t know Glenfarne’s true intentions, of course. But the incentives all point the same way: the developer’s least risky and most profitable path is not to build the pipeline. It’s to build the LNG import facility, cash the checks, and wait.
That should change how Alaska reads every “almost there” and every new demand for additional concessions: the state may well be negotiating with a company who’s playing a waiting game rather than trying to build a pipeline any time soon. Trying to rush a deal with a counterparty who doesn’t need one is like pushing string.
Glenfarne has arranged its affairs so it can afford to wait. By deferring the pipeline question to next year, a new legislature, and a new governor, the Legislature has responded with precisely the right message: Alaska can wait, too.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Secretary of State responds to legislative subpoena, with pushback
description: Montana Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen responded to a legislative subpoena to disclose voter roll information her office provided to the federal government, but also objected to the demand and described it as “political theater.” For months, members of the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee have been trying to find out exactly[...]
text:
The Secretary of State’s office in the Montana State Capitol in Helena on Wednesday, April 26, 2023.  (Photo by Mike Clark for the Daily Montanan)Montana Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen responded to a legislative subpoena to disclose voter roll information her office provided to the federal government, but also objected to the demand and described it as “political theater.”
For months, members of the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee have been trying to find out exactly what information Jacobsen, a Republican, provided to the federal government in response to the U.S. Department of Justice’s demand for voter records.
Earlier this month, the committee voted 10-1 to approve the subpoena for the information.
“The subpoena was an unnecessary encroachment on the separation of powers that wasted taxpayer dollars, could have been avoided, and lacked warranted scrutiny,” said the letter from Montana Secretary of State Chief Legal Counsel Austin James.
But the response also outlined the categories of information the Secretary of State’s Office provided to the Department of Justice — to varying levels of satisfaction from members of the committee.
The Secretary of State’s Office did not share driver’s license or state identification numbers with the federal government, but it did share the last four digits of Social Security numbers — generated by the federal government — for the fraction of voters who use their Social Security numbers to register to vote, according to the response letter.
The DOJ has demanded states turn over voter lists to ensure ineligible voters are not included and has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for the records. It has lost 23 of those lawsuits to date, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
Some state legislators have worried the Secretary of State didn’t protect Montanans’ privacy in responding to the federal government, but Jacobsen has largely been absent from legislative meetings and unresponsive to the committee.
James previously told the committee the office protected the privacy of Montanans, but he declined to provide specific information to lawmakers, citing the threat of litigation.
The Sept. 11 letter in response to the subpoena said in August 2025, the Secretary of State’s Office provided the U.S. Department of Justice the public statewide voter registration list “available to any member of the public.”
It stated the type of data provided, and it included voter ID numbers, names, voter status, addresses (minus those protected from disclosure), phone numbers, birth years, precinct, other political districts, and “absentee indicator.”
“While demanded by the Department as empowered by Congress, the list provided did not contain any Montana driver’s license number or state identification card number,” the letter said.
In December 2025, the office again sent the voter registration list, but “this time with the addition of a federal identifier for a portion of voters where that information was provided as part of their voter registration application,” the letter said of partial Social Security numbers.
The Secretary of State’s Office said “a fraction” of voters who don’t have a driver’s license use their “federal identifier” instead, or the last four digits of their Social Security numbers, and in those cases, the office provided the last four digits. (The letter did not state how many voters that encompassed.)
The letter said the office keeps partial Social Security numbers “from general public distribution.”
But it said the last four digits aren’t considered a Social Security number by the U.S. Privacy Act, the federal government “routinely receives” those identifiers “that the federal government itself provided,” and they were provided under “nondisclosure requirements.”
The letter from the Secretary of State’s Office also said it did not consider the subpoena valid for a number of reasons, and it warned that such actions set up a confrontation between branches of government.
The Secretary of State’s Office cautioned legislators against any further subpoena for voter registration records. It said it considers the subpoena answered and will not produce additional information “absent a court order.”
Monday, Manzella said she is satisfied with the response from Jacobsen and believes the Secretary of State protected Montanans’ privacy.
“I believe that she is obligated to, under federal law, do what she did, and I think she both did what she could to protect our citizens’ privacy and also honor our request,” Manzella said.
Manzella said she approves of where Jacobsen drew the line because she protected state information, the driver’s license numbers, but she shared partial information the federal government itself generates.
“I personally don’t have a problem with the federal government requesting driver’s license numbers simply because we are a citizenry that moves across state lines on a daily basis,” Manzella said. “And I believe that the priority on elections needs to move from privacy to transparency and auditability.”
Rep. Kelly Kortum, a Bozeman Democrat, raised the idea to issue the subpoena, and he said he is not satisfied with the response from the Secretary of State.
However, Kortum also said he is likely to be the most aggressive voice on the committee on the issue, and he said it would be important to hear from Manzella and Rep. Marc Lee, a Democrat and committee vice chairman.
Kortum said the letter describes the information the Secretary of State says it sent the DOJ, but it does not provide the actual portion of the data file showing the categories.
He said the Secretary of State still is avoiding “showing us the top line on that spreadsheet.”
“I do believe the will of the committee is being thwarted,” Kortum said.
Lee said the letter was full of legalese, and he believes it fell short of the demand in the subpoena. He said he was anxious to speak to legislative staff to see if they could shed light on the response.
Lee also said Montanans value their privacy, and he doesn’t believe the idea that the federal government already has information is a justification for turning over data.
“Why would the federal government ask for stuff that they already have?” Lee said. “There has to be some sort of information that was provided to the federal government that they are not privy to.”
The Brennan Center for Justice, which has a mission to defend democracy, has described the demands by the Department of Justice as unprecedented and an encroachment on states’ authority to run elections.
Lee said legislative staff earlier indicated the committee was on solid ground in issuing the subpoena. He said his interest is in transparency from the Secretary of State’s Office.
“The Secretary of State forced us into this position because they weren’t willing to answer what I would consider a very basic question,” Lee said.
Manzella said the committee has a planned meeting in October, and if needed, it would schedule a special meeting about the subpoena.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Confidential records sitting in empty charter school building are now secured, state officials say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Private records from a shuttered Oklahoma City charter school are now in state hands after months of delay and dispute. Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, a charter high school known as PTPLA, formally closed on June 30, but for months afterward, paper copies of students’ educational records and financial documents needed for […]
text:
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, pictured May 19 in Oklahoma City, closed at the end of June. Obtaining hard-copy student records and financial documents from the school became a monthslong dispute. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Private records from a shuttered Oklahoma City charter school are now in state hands after months of delay and dispute.
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, a charter high school known as PTPLA, formally closed on June 30, but for months afterward, paper copies of students’ educational records and financial documents needed for a closing audit remained in its former building in southwest Oklahoma City.
The Statewide Charter School Board canceled the school’s founding charter contract and cut off its state funding over financial, operational and academic quality concerns. Board staff then sent repeated requests that PTPLA turn over the records or allow state officials entry to retrieve them, according to email correspondence Oklahoma Voice obtained. 
Disagreements with the school turned into a legal fight with the building’s landlord. The state board on Wednesday sought an emergency court order demanding access to the records, online court documents show.
A day later, the landlord, Cameron Kaspereit, voluntarily allowed board staff to enter the property, where they picked up eight to 10 boxes of paper documents, officials said during a Statewide Charter School Board meeting Monday.
Kaspereit did not immediately return a request for comment Monday.
The landlord had until then refused to release the school documents because PTPLA owed him back rent, damages and a penalty for early lease termination, the board’s court filing states. The records were his “only leverage,” and he said he wouldn’t release them without court intervention, the board claimed in its legal filing.
Further stressing the “emergency nature” of the situation, the former school building had recently been broken into, but “according to (Kaspereit) nothing appeared to be removed,” court documents state.
State board staff are now preparing to sort through the records, said Skyler Lusnia, the state board’s director of school performance. 
“We knew it was going to be challenging, and it has been challenging,” Lusnia said of the closure process. “If and possibly when this ever happens again, we’ll be ready.”
Skyler Lusnia, director of school performance for the Statewide Charter School Board, speaks to the Proud To Partner Leadership Academy board during a meeting Nov. 18 at the charter school in southwest Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Board staff on Monday presented a host of potential changes to administrative rules governing charter school closures. Among them is added clarity that the school, not the state, is responsible for completing closure tasks like document transfers.
The state has had electronic copies of students’ academic transcripts for several weeks, which allowed PTPLA students to transfer elsewhere unimpeded, board staff have said. 
The paper records are necessary to assemble hard-copy transcripts for students and ensure they receive proper credit for their scholastic efforts, according to the board’s court filing.
The financial records are needed to finish a legally required closing audit of PTPLA, Lusnia said. The state hired a third-party audit firm, which will be able to complete its review once the hard-copy records are in hand.
PTPLA “intentionally abandoned any attempt to comply with state and federal law regarding those documents,” the board contended in its court filing. 
Representatives of the school previously told Oklahoma Voice they no longer had access to the building after turning in the keys in July. They advised state officials to coordinate with the landlord to gain access, email records show.
PTPLA Board President Sharri Coleman alerted news media and state leaders last month that the documents had been sitting in the empty facility for weeks.
“I am pleased to hear (state board) reports that the records have been retrieved and secured,” she said Monday.

title: RI elections board rejects Pelino’s recount request in Republican gubernatorial primary
description: The close contest between Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial primary is not close enough to justify a manual refeeding of every ballot into a tabulating machine, the Board of Elections determined Monday. The unanimous vote by the election panel came after an hourlong back-and-forth with trailing candidate Elaine Pelino, who protested a lack of public no[...]
text:
The Rhode Island Board of Elections rejected a recount request by GOP gubernatorial candidate Elaine Pelino, seated before the panel. (Screenshot)The close contest between Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial primary is not close enough to justify a manual refeeding of every ballot into a tabulating machine, the Board of Elections determined Monday.
The unanimous vote by the election panel came after an hourlong back-and-forth with trailing candidate Elaine Pelino, who protested a lack of public notification and transparency by election administrators. Pelino acknowledged the 259 votes separating her from likely primary winner Aaron Guckian was slightly wider than the 231-vote margin needed to justify a recount under state law. 
But the determination does not cement Guckian as the GOP nominee. The margin is still close enough to allow election administrators to cross-check the memory sticks from ballot machines against the final tally.
Pelino seeks recount in close GOP gubernatorial primary

Pelino, 72, of North Smithfield, insisted the elections board should recount every ballot, rattling off a litany of problems with meeting notice requirements and details of how election administrators counted ballots.
The information Pelino presented during her 30-minute soliloquy Monday afternoon did not show any evidence of election impropriety — the only way the elections panel can agree to a recount when the race is not close enough to justify a recount based on the margin of victory.  
“These are more arguments than actual evidence, there’s no evidence,” board member David Sholes told Pelino, who was accompanied by 2022 GOP gubernatorial nominee Ashely Kalus.



Who gets a recount under Rhode Island General Laws § 17-19-37.1
20,000 or fewer total votes: trailing candidate must be down by 2% or 200 votes, whichever is fewer
20,001 to 100,000 total votes: trailing candidate must be down 1% or 500 votes, whichever is fewer
More than 100,000 total votes: trailing candidate must be down .05% or 1,500 votes, whichever is fewer  



Election administrators defended the transparency of the ballot counting process, which includes public notice and observation of mail ballot certification, opening of envelopes and correcting of potentially deficient ballots, among other steps.
“The entire process is open to the public, it is open to the representative of a candidate, and it’s the burden of the candidate to be part of that entire process from beginning to end,” Ray Marcaccio, the board’s legal counsel said.
Marcaccio later said, “Now is the time to proffer the evidence, not to say, ‘I want to start looking to see if something suspicious was happening.’” 
Pelino, a political newcomer and proud MAGA candidate, said she did not receive any communication from the elections board regarding any element of the tabulation process, and was unaware of it happening.
“Noted, and heard, and this information is also publicly available,” Chairwoman Jennie Johnson told Pelino. 
In her final plea to the elections board, Pelino stressed the importance of having all ballot information available to her.
“We’re just asking to look at the data,” she said, to which Johnson responded, “What data?”
Guckian, 50 of East Greenwich, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The self-described “compassionate conservative” gave what appeared to be a victory speech on the State House steps Monday afternoon, despite the pending recount request, The Providence Journal reported. 
Providence City Council primaries 
Separately, the board authorized a full recount in one Providence City Council Democratic primary. Councilor Juan Pichardo and his Democratic challenger Carmen Castillo each asked for the review after the tally showed Castillo trailing Pichardo by nine votes in the Ward 9 primary. The ward spans south Elmwood, Elmwood and Roger Williams Park. Castillo and Pichardo both attended the meeting but declined to comment when asked by the board.
A second Democratic Providence City Council primary, for the Ward 4 seat, qualified for a rereading of the memory sticks but not a full recount of every ballot. The initial tabulation shows Councilor Justin Roias beating challenger Joseph Casoli by 55 votes for the seat representing the Charles and Wanskuck neighborhoods. The margin would have needed to be no more than 29 votes to qualify for a recount.
Casoli attended the meeting but declined to comment.
Recounts and memory stick rereadings will begin at 9 a.m. Tuesday, and are expected to conclude by noon. The elections board will certify final results from all state primary races, including those subject to recounts, at a scheduled meeting at 5 p.m. Tuesday.
Election board members Louis DeSimone, Randy Jackvony and Michael Connors were absent from the meeting.

title: Lars Herseth, former South Dakota governor nominee from prolific political family, dies at age 80
description: Lars Herseth, a Democratic former South Dakota legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Saturday of cancer at age 80.  Herseth grew up in a politically active Democratic family in rural Houghton, where he returned to be a farmer and rancher after graduating from the University of South Dakota. His father, Ralph Herseth, was the […]
text:
Lars Herseth, a Democratic former legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Sept. 12, 2026, at age 80. He's pictured here in a 2023 oral history interview. (Screenshot courtesy of South Dakota State Archives/YouTube)Lars Herseth, a Democratic former South Dakota legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Saturday of cancer at age 80. 
Herseth grew up in a politically active Democratic family in rural Houghton, where he returned to be a farmer and rancher after graduating from the University of South Dakota. His father, Ralph Herseth, was the state’s 21st governor from 1959 to 1961, and his mother, Lorna Herseth, was South Dakota’s secretary of state from 1973 to 1979. 
Lars Herseth’s daughter, Stephanie Herseth Sandlin, served in the U.S. House from 2004 to 2011 and is now the president of Augustana University in Sioux Falls.
Republican Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen paid tribute to Lars Herseth and the Herseth family Monday in a post on Venhuizen’s personal website.
“Few South Dakota families can match that record of public service across three generations,” Venhuizen wrote.
Lars Herseth served in the state House of Representatives from 1975 until 1986, when he won the Democratic nomination for governor but lost in the general election to Republican George Mickelson, who was also the son of a former governor. Herseth then served in the state Senate from 1989 until 1996. His legislative leadership positions included House minority leader, Senate president pro tempore and Senate minority leader.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During his time in the state Senate, Herseth served with Mike Rounds, a Republican who would go on to become governor and is now a U.S. senator. Rounds wrote about Herseth in a post Monday on the social media platform X.
“Lars was a statesman and a problem solver who was willing to work with anyone if it meant bettering the lives of South Dakotans,” Rounds wrote. 
Herseth’s obituary said he focused his political career on issues including agriculture, transportation, economic development and healthcare. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, he worked with Republican Gov. Bill Janklow to preserve abandoned rail lines that were critical for transporting agricultural products.
“Lars was known for his legislative acumen, command of the issues, collegiality that knew no partisan bounds, and being true to his word,” his obituary said. “He was exceptionally fair-minded and a steadfast advocate for women’s rights and Native American issues. During his final legislative term, he spoke passionately in opposition to a bill that sought to prevent recognition of same-sex marriage.”
In his later years, Herseth was president of the American Coalition for Ethanol.
A memorial service will be at 2 p.m. Central time on Oct. 4 at the Johnson Fine Arts Center on the campus of Northern State University in Aberdeen. South Dakota Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden has ordered flags at the state Capitol in Pierre to be flown at half-staff in honor of Herseth that day.

title: Kenosha County DA’s law license suspended
description: Kenosha County District Attorney Xavier Solis had his license to practice law suspended Monday.  A memo issued by the state court system’s Office of Lawyer Regulation states that Solis’ suspension was for “willfully failing to cooperate with one or more OLR investigations into alleged misconduct.”  The memo also states that Solis violated a Wisconsin Supreme[...]
text:
Xavier Solis (photo courtesy of Xavier Solis)Kenosha County District Attorney Xavier Solis had his license to practice law suspended Monday. 
A memo issued by the state court system’s Office of Lawyer Regulation states that Solis’ suspension was for “willfully failing to cooperate with one or more OLR investigations into alleged misconduct.” 
The memo also states that Solis violated a Wisconsin Supreme Court rule that states that lawyers can have their licenses suspended if they’re under investigation by the OLR and don’t comply with deadlines to provide information. 
Solis, a Republican, was elected DA of Kenosha County in 2024 and had previously worked as a private defense attorney. 
Stephen Kelley, a spokesperson for the state court system, told the Wisconsin Examiner the only information available to the public is the rule Solis is alleged to have violated. 
State law requires district attorneys to have a valid law license, so Solis cannot currently perform the job. It’s not clear what the suspension will mean for Solis’ future in the seat. Under state court rules, an attorney suspension can be lifted if the suspended lawyer discloses what happened and cooperates with the investigation to the “reasonable satisfaction” of the regulators within 18 months. 
Deputy District Attorney Rosamaria Delgado is now serving as interim DA in Solis’ office. 
“Administrative staff of the Kenosha County District Attorney’s Office and I will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of the office,” Delgado said in a statement to 620 WTMJ. “We have reached out to the State for direction. I will take over management and/or reassignment of District Attorney Solis’ caseload until such time as District Attorney Solis’ license to practice law is reinstated or, until further direction is received from the Governor’s Office.  At this time, no other information is available.”
Solis, who had no experience as a prosecutor when he was elected in 2024, has been the subject of criticism since taking office and has struggled to fill vacancies after experienced prosecutors resigned. He was previously sanctioned by a judge for filing briefs written using the assistance of artificial intelligence which “hallucinated” fake citations.
