name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri GOP still see path for gerrymandered congressional map. Legal experts see little hope.
description: Republican officials aren’t giving up on the congressional map they pushed through the Missouri legislature last year, despite two setbacks at the U.S. Supreme Court and a state Supreme Court ruling that the map never became law. Their next chance comes Thursday before the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. But the legal path to […]
text:
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, right, speaks to reporters  on Sept. 10 after the Missouri Supreme Court found Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, center, "was in contempt" for ordering use of an illegal congressional map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent). Republican officials aren’t giving up on the congressional map they pushed through the Missouri legislature last year, despite two setbacks at the U.S. Supreme Court and a state Supreme Court ruling that the map never became law.
Their next chance comes Thursday before the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
But the legal path to getting the map back in place for November appears exceedingly narrow.
Even if the federal appeals court sides with Republicans challenging the use of Missouri’s old congressional districts, a U.S. Supreme Court order blocking the 2025 map would remain in effect unless the justices themselves lift it.
And there is another problem: The Missouri Supreme Court has already ruled that the map Republicans want to use never took effect under state law.
Former Missouri Supreme Court Judge Michael Wolff described that as an “insuperable obstacle.”
“The Supreme Court of Missouri is the final authority on what Missouri law is,” he said, “and the court has said that (the 2025 map) is not the law and never was, because it has not been approved by a vote of the people.”
For the Republican plaintiffs to prevail, he said, the 8th Circuit would effectively have to order Missouri to conduct an election using districts that the state’s highest court has determined are not legally in effect.
And even then, Wolff said, the U.S. Supreme Court’s stay would stand in the way.
“The chances,” Wolff said, “are between zero and zero.”
Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University, told the St. Louis Post-Dispatch there is virtually no chance an 8th Circuit ruling will ultimately change the map used in the November election.
“The war’s over,” he said, “but there’s still soldiers fighting.”
Republican leaders see it differently.
Gov. Mike Kehoe, who called lawmakers into a special session last year to redraw Missouri’s congressional districts at President Donald Trump’s request, said after the U.S. Supreme Court intervened last week that he still hopes the appeals court will revive the map.
“I look forward to the 8th Circuit’s consideration of the merits of the Missouri First Map and remain confident in the legal process moving forward,” Kehoe said. “Voters deserve certainty and clarity.”
The 8th Circuit has set remote oral arguments for 10 a.m. Thursday, two days before the federal deadline for Missouri to send ballots to military and overseas voters.
The case was filed by U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, state Sen. Rick Brattin and two Missouri voters after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled Sept. 3 that a referendum petition challenging the new map was legal, sufficient and timely.
That unanimous decision put the map on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition A and held that the 2025 districts never took effect because a successful referendum petition suspends the challenged law until voters decide its fate.
The practical result is unusual: Missouri held its Aug. 4 congressional primaries under the 2025 map but is now preparing to hold the general election under the districts used in 2022 and 2024. Onder, Brattin and the other plaintiffs argue that switching maps between the primary and general election violates the U.S. Constitution by effectively nullifying votes already cast in the primary.
Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark in St. Louis agreed they were likely to prevail on that argument and on Sept. 8 issued a temporary restraining order preventing Secretary of State Denny Hoskins from using any congressional map but the 2025 plan.
That set off two days of legal whiplash.
The 8th Circuit initially declined an appeal of Clark’s order, noting that appeals courts generally lack jurisdiction to review temporary restraining orders.
People Not Politicians, the group behind the referendum, then went to the U.S. Supreme Court, which Thursday morning stayed Clark’s order without any noted dissents.
The high court said its stay will remain in effect while the case is before the 8th Circuit and through any timely petition asking the justices to review the appeals court’s eventual ruling.
That means an 8th Circuit decision favoring Onder and the other plaintiffs would not, by itself, put the 2025 map back in place.
After the U.S. Supreme Court intervened, the 8th Circuit moved quickly, ordering expedited briefs and scheduling Thursday’s argument.
Hours after the U.S. Supreme Court acted, Hoskins reversed a directive he had issued to local election officials and told them to use the 2022 map. The Missouri Supreme Court found Hoskins had been in contempt of its Sept. 3 order but said he purged the contempt by reversing course.
During the contempt hearing, Chief Justice W. Brent Powell repeatedly pressed lawyers for Hoskins on a question that could hang over Thursday’s federal argument: Whatever the federal courts decide, can they change the Missouri Supreme Court’s conclusion that the 2025 map never became state law?
“(The 2025 map) never went into effect, right?” Powell asked William Seidleck, an assistant attorney general representing Hoskins.
“Per this court’s holding, yes,” Seidleck replied.
Powell returned to the point later, asking whether a future federal ruling could change the fact that the map had never taken effect.
“As a matter of state law,” Seidleck said, it could not.
Chuck Hatfield, an attorney for People Not Politicians, told the judges he believed the U.S. Supreme Court’s intervention had largely eliminated the immediate stakes of the federal appeal.
“I think we’re done, judge, as a practical matter,” Hatfield said, though he acknowledged the litigation could continue.
One of the biggest unanswered questions heading into Thursday is what position Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office will take.
Hanaway represents Missouri and Hoskins in the federal litigation. Her office sided with the Republican plaintiffs before Clark and urged him to block use of the 2022 map. It later asked the U.S. Supreme Court to leave Clark’s order in place.
But after the U.S. Supreme Court stayed that order and Hoskins agreed to follow the state court’s directive, Hanaway was less definitive about what comes next.
“As far as our strategy for the 8th Circuit, I don’t know, because it’s a very confusing posture,” Hanaway told reporters last week.
Asked whether any path remained to revive the 2025 map, she told reporters: “As I stand here today, no.”
Military and overseas ballots must be sent by Sept. 19. Local election officials spent much of last week waiting for the courts to decide which congressional districts they should use before Hoskins’ Thursday directive put them back on the 2022 map.

title: Lawsuit seeks $80 million from Denny Hoskins over Missouri congressional map referendum
description: Five Missouri voters are seeking roughly $80 million from Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in a proposed class-action lawsuit alleging he violated state law in his handling of a referendum challenging Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map. The lawsuit, filed Friday in Cole County Circuit Court, asks a judge to allow the plaintiffs to represent approxima[...]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins speaks to reporters following Missouri Supreme Court arguments Sept. 2 (Annelise Hanshaw/MissouriIndependent).Five Missouri voters are seeking roughly $80 million from Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in a proposed class-action lawsuit alleging he violated state law in his handling of a referendum challenging Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map.
The lawsuit, filed Friday in Cole County Circuit Court, asks a judge to allow the plaintiffs to represent approximately 162,000 registered Missouri voters whose signatures on the referendum petition were verified by local election authorities.
At the center of the case is a Missouri law that says the secretary of state must pay between $100 and $500 to an aggrieved person if the officeholder “neglect[s] or refuse[s] to perform any of the duties enjoined on him by law.” The statute has been on the books in its current form since 1945.
Missouri Supreme Court blocks gerrymandered congressional map, orders referendum vote

The plaintiffs are asking for the maximum $500 for each member of the proposed class, which would produce a judgment of about $80 million.
Their lawsuit points to several actions Hoskins took during the months-long legal battle over the congressional map Republican lawmakers passed during a 2025 special legislative session.
More than 330,000 signatures were submitted in an effort to force a statewide referendum on the map. Hoskins ultimately declared the petition insufficient, not because it lacked enough valid signatures but because he concluded congressional redistricting was not subject to Missouri’s referendum process.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously rejected that conclusion earlier this month, ruling the petition was legal, sufficient and timely. The court ordered the referendum onto the November ballot and said the congressional districts adopted in 2022 must be used for this year’s general election.
The lawsuit alleges Hoskins violated his statutory duties both by refusing to certify the referendum and later by directing local election officials to use the 2025 map despite the state Supreme Court’s order.
It also targets Hoskins’ role in a subsequent federal lawsuit that briefly produced a conflicting order requiring use of the 2025 districts. The plaintiffs allege Hoskins improperly consented to that order, citing another Missouri law that prohibits public officials from agreeing to court orders that conflict with state election statutes.
The lawsuit characterizes the federal case as “collusive,” an allegation that has not been established by a court.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday stayed the federal order, restoring the Missouri Supreme Court’s requirement that the November election proceed under the 2022 map.
Later that day, the Missouri Supreme Court found Hoskins had been in contempt for directing election officials to use the 2025 districts. The court imposed no punishment after Hoskins reversed course and instructed local officials to use the 2022 map, finding that he had purged the contempt.
The new lawsuit does not seek to change which map will be used in November. Instead, it seeks monetary damages for referendum petition signers who contend Hoskins’ actions violated duties imposed on him by state law.
A judge would first have to decide whether the case can proceed as a class action and whether the petition signers qualify as people “aggrieved” under the damages statute.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s long fight over who gets the last word
description: Fourteen Republican lawmakers sent the Missouri Supreme Court a letter last week. It was not a fan letter. Hold Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt, they wrote, and we may come for your jobs. The court held him in contempt the next day. Hoskins had told local election officials to use a gerrymandered congressional […]
text:
(Getty Images).Fourteen Republican lawmakers sent the Missouri Supreme Court a letter last week. It was not a fan letter. Hold Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt, they wrote, and we may come for your jobs.
The court held him in contempt the next day.
Hoskins had told local election officials to use a gerrymandered congressional map Republican lawmakers passed last year. The Missouri Supreme Court had ordered the old districts kept in place while voters decided the new map’s fate.
He went with the new one anyway.
His explanation was that a federal judge had told him to. The U.S. Supreme Court took that off the table Thursday morning, and by the time the state judges got around to him, Hoskins had reversed himself and told election officials to use the old districts.
The court said that was enough to purge the contempt. No punishment was imposed.
Missouri Supreme Court finds Denny Hoskins ‘was in contempt’ over congressional maps

As for the impeachment threat: It takes 82 votes in the House. Five of the 14 signers serve there. House Speaker Jon Patterson did not sound like a man about to go looking for the other 77.
“That’s not where my head is at this point,” he told the Kansas City Star.
A statewide official hauled before Missouri’s highest court was a first in living memory. The fight that put him there was not. It’s been going on for the better part of two decades, though it escalated over the last two years. And it comes down to one question: What happens when voters decide something the people running the state didn’t want decided?
The answer, so far, is that they try again. And again.
In 2024, nearly 58% of voters approved a law requiring many employers to provide paid sick leave. Republican lawmakers repealed it a few months later.
Also in 2024, voters approved Amendment 3, enshrining abortion rights into the constitution. This November they’ll vote on a new Amendment 3. This one was put on the ballot by lawmakers and would reinstate a near-total ban on abortion.
Lawmakers then asked voters to make it much harder for citizens to amend the constitution. Voters said no, 80% to 20%.
Another group of Missourians gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures for Amendment 6, which would make it far harder for lawmakers to rewrite what voters approve. Hoskins kept it off the ballot until the Missouri Supreme Court, unanimously, put it back.
And then there was the map.
Republican lawmakers passed it. Opponents collected more than 300,000 signatures for a referendum to repeal it. Hoskins waited until the last legal day, declared the referendum unconstitutional and declined to say whether the signatures were enough.
The signatures were enough.
Again, the Missouri Supreme Court overruled him. Again, unanimously. The constitution allows a referendum on “any act of the General Assembly” unless a specific exception applies. None does for congressional redistricting.
What followed was a week of emergency appeals, contradictory orders and, at the end of it, a secretary of state standing before the state’s highest court explaining why he hadn’t done what it told him to.
Here is the thing: Most of what led there was legal. Repealing a law is legal. So is proposing an amendment, appealing a ruling, arguing hard in court. The system gives elected officials plenty of ways to fight. But eventually somebody has to lose. And lately, the people in charge in Jefferson City have been treating losses as suggestions.
So what are we left with?
In November, barring a Hail Mary in federal court this week, Missourians will vote in the districts drawn in 2022. They will vote on whether to enact the map drawn last year. They will vote on whether to repeal the abortion rights they approved two years ago. And they will vote on Amendment 6, which asks how much power lawmakers should have to change what voters approve.
After everything it took to get those questions onto the ballot, Missouri is back where this started. The politicians made their arguments. The judges made their rulings.
Now the voters get their turn.

title: Missouri governor names 18 to child welfare task force amid growing scrutiny
description: With Missouri’s child welfare system under fire over foster care deaths, staff turnover and mounting investigation backlogs, Gov. Mike Kehoe has named 18 people to a new task force charged with developing common standards for how courts, caseworkers and others across the state assess a child’s safety. The Missouri Child Welfare Task Force will bring […]
text:
Jessica Bax, director of the Missouri Department of Social Services, testifies Aug. 26 to the Joint Committee on Government Accountability about issues within the Missouri Childrens Division. Bax is joined by Sara Smith, director of the Children's Division (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).With Missouri’s child welfare system under fire over foster care deaths, staff turnover and mounting investigation backlogs, Gov. Mike Kehoe has named 18 people to a new task force charged with developing common standards for how courts, caseworkers and others across the state assess a child’s safety.
The Missouri Child Welfare Task Force will bring together Children’s Division leaders, judges, lawmakers, juvenile officers, law enforcement, private providers, attorneys and advocates. Kehoe created the group by executive order Aug. 25, less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative committee held a hearing examining fatalities, foster placements and other problems inside the division. He named the members last week.
The task force is charged with developing a common definition of child safety, identifying gaps in state laws and agency policies, recommending protocols for putting those standards into practice and proposing training and quality-control measures. Its recommendations are due Nov. 15. The group will dissolve at the end of the year.
“The decisions made throughout the child welfare system are life-altering, and the standard guiding them should not depend on a child’s county, circuit, or provider,” Department of Social Services Director Jess Bax said when the task force was announced.
Missouri lawmakers press child welfare leaders on foster care deaths, staff turnover

The panel includes Children’s Division Director Sara Smith; Department of Social Services legal director Teri Armistead; State Courts Administrator Kathy Lloyd; Republican state Sen. Jill Carter; Republican state Reps. Ken Jamison and Melissa Schmidt; juvenile officers Rick Gaines of St. Louis County and Bill Prince of Greene County; and Newton County Sheriff Matthew Stewart.
Other members are Jeannette Koster of Crittenton Children’s Center, Justin Horton of Cornerstones of Care, Audrain County Associate Circuit Judge Melissa Buckman Young, attorney Tamara Veit, Missouri Network Against Child Abuse Executive Director Jessica Seitz, Children’s Trust Fund Executive Director Emily van Schenkhof, Southern District Court of Appeals Judge Joseph Hensley, Christian County Circuit Judge Jessica Kruse and Joplin school counselor Shelby Trimble.
State Sen. Mary Elizabeth Coleman, the Arnold Republican who chairs the Joint Committee on Government Accountability, told The Independent last month that she believed Kehoe’s executive order was a reaction to the hearing. Smith said the push for greater consistency grew partly out of an internal assessment conducted over the previous year.
At the hearing, lawmakers questioned Smith about the death of 17-year-old Korbin Papadopoulos, who had type 1 diabetes and autism. Macon County workers placed him nearly 300 miles away with a foster parent who was licensed only to care for relatives and who later told police he had not been trained to manage diabetes. Korbin died June 6 from diabetic ketoacidosis.
Missouri placed diabetic teen in a foster home not licensed to take him. He died 24 days later

Lawmakers repeatedly pressed Smith on who ultimately bears responsibility when the state cannot find an appropriate placement for a child with significant medical or behavioral needs.
Smith also told the committee that an internal assessment had found instances in which workers failed to respond to hotline reports before law enforcement became involved, did not refer alleged abuse victims to child advocacy centers and refused to cooperate with juvenile officers.
“This indicated to our leadership team that our workforce did not understand how to assess safety and risk,” Smith told the committee.
The division has also been struggling again with rising caseloads and delays in child abuse and neglect investigations.
Children’s Division workers are supposed to average no more than 15 open abuse and neglect cases at a time. At the end of July, workers in St. Louis County averaged 97 open cases and workers in St. Louis city averaged 58, according to state data reviewed by The Independent.
State law generally requires investigations to be completed within 45 days, though limited extensions are permitted. By July, 23 of Missouri’s 46 judicial circuits had averaged more than 45 days to close reports over the previous six months. In St. Louis County, the average was 144 days.
Frontline turnover remains about 40%, down from 55% in fiscal year 2022 but still high enough that the division loses more than a third of its frontline workforce in a year.
The division began restructuring its abuse and neglect teams this month, putting investigators under more centralized state supervision and creating specialized career tracks. Smith has said the changes are designed to improve consistency and retention.
Frontline workers interviewed by The Independent have said new requirements and increasingly prescriptive policies have made cases harder to close and reduced their discretion when working with families.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: George Ayoub: Getting petitions, elections just right
description: If you’re going to the polls — highly recommended in a democracy that prides itself on representative government — take note of a couple of recent developments. Not items on which to vote but rather on what you can cast your “yea” or “nay” and how safe it is after that. Who knew in the […]
text:
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State's Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office's Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)If you’re going to the polls — highly recommended in a democracy that prides itself on representative government — take note of a couple of recent developments. Not items on which to vote but rather on what you can cast your “yea” or “nay” and how safe it is after that. Who knew in the 250th year of this political and social journey that — without proof of any real problem with elections — we’d be choosing up sides about their processes? 
To wit: Nebraska election officials and the governor said at a news conference a couple of weeks ago that we should put the kibosh on petition circulators getting paid by the signature, what the officials referred to as a “bounty.” 
The argument goes that if we put a big enough dollar sign on the carrot, we tantalizingly shorten the stick. For further details, see Enron accounting techniques, Wells Fargo account openings and Apple backdating stock options. 
The officials’ concern — rightly — was that among the 767,000 signatures across 17 petitions during Nebraska’s political campaign season, a rather shocking number of them turned out to be stinkers. The petitions covered a gamut of attempts at redress from the Lincoln city charter to state ballot measures to candidates from a variety of political corners, so the bogus entries stretched across a number of political ideas, office contenders and government administrivia.
Cue some serious handwringing?
Well, no. That’s because Nebraska’s election system works. Quite well, in fact. County election officials got it exactly right, going line by line to ferret out problem signatures. Things got a little felonious, too, as a half-dozen circulators have been arrested. 
None of which means the Legislature might want to consider the efficacy of “bounty hunting” signatures for ballot initiatives or candidates. That is a conversation and debate worth having, given our wont to govern by referendum these days.
The more important takeaway is that Nebraskans can trust their elections despite an ongoing false narrative that something is amiss and we must “fix” it, also known as a solution looking for a problem. 
Indeed, Omahan Scott Peterson, one of the quartet vying to replace Secretary of State Bob Evnen, said Nebraska’s elections are suspect, writing on X that they are “not fully verified, not fully inspected, and not held to modern standards.” Curiously unmodern is that he wants to return to hand counts and eliminate almost all mail-in voting. Running against Peterson are Democrat Sarah Slattery of Plattsmouth, Nebraska Working People Party candidate Paul Rumbaugh of Omaha, and America First Party candidate and former state senator Bob Krist of Omaha.
We should also be aware that when circulators, paid and otherwise, show up at the DMV, outside a coffee shop or even at a local pageant or parade, they are exercising a First Amendment right: petitioning the government for redress of grievances. That said, reasonable limitations — the number of signatures required to make the ballot, verification of signatures, that sort of thing — can be in place. Most states also keep budgetary, judicial or legal matters off petitions. 
A less formal petitioning process comes in the form of lobbyists making their case in the halls of Congress, statehouses and city halls. Because so much money — there is that word again — is involved, scapegoating lobbyists for the nation’s ills has become a national sport. To further such a constitutionally protected practice as petitioning the government, citizens have also banded together in what we now call PACs and super PACs.
And so it goes … petitions, lobbyists, PACs. The First Amendment. 
Let’s also not forget the recent rush to populate voting sites with poll watchers, especially among the election-denying crowd who shout “fraud!” unless their candidate wins. Go figure. 
Poll watchers have been a part of our elections for years. What’s new seems to be that rather than observing the voting process at polling sites and reporting the rare irregularity should it occur, a new batch of beholders is coming to the task convinced (without evidence) that the fix is in. The contrast is remarkable … and potentially disruptive.
Poll-watching p’s and q’s must be minded, however. In Nebraska, you best follow the law or be tossed and charged with a Class V misdemeanor. Here’s the playbook: No interfering with, talking to or exit-polling voters unless you are 20 feet outside the polling site or, if in a large building, 100 feet from the voting booth. Stay 8 feet from the tables, booths and ballot boxes unless otherwise posted. It’s poll watching, not clandestine tradecraft.
Leave the poll workers alone, too. They’re busy. No pep rallies, political buttons, flash mobs or electioneering of any kind. I mean, duh!
All of which is … well … just right.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Reporting shows telemarketing calls came from Oklahoma prisons — so much for rehabilitation
description: Despite having my phone number on the federal Do Not Call Registry, it feels like there’s been an enormous spike in the number of telemarketers trying to sell me on everything from new roofs to insurance policies to political candidates. Ironically – as I was writing this – my phone rang, showing a number from […]
text:
An inmate at Joseph Harp Correctional Center in Lexington is pictured on Friday, Oct. 13, 2023. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)Despite having my phone number on the federal Do Not Call Registry, it feels like there’s been an enormous spike in the number of telemarketers trying to sell me on everything from new roofs to insurance policies to political candidates.
Ironically – as I was writing this – my phone rang, showing a number from the Texas Panhandle area code that my phone provider flagged as a “spam risk.” Spoiler alert: This telemarketer has been using a variety of different numbers to aggressively try to convince me to give away my personal info to purchase a scammy-sounding Medicare policy.
This continued onslaught of calls is probably why I was so annoyed to read a story from nonprofit news outlet Oklahoma Watch that found the state Department of Corrections has been operating four of its own telemarketing call centers from within prison walls.
Corrections Executive Director Justin Farris signed his name on a contract obligating  department inmates to make phone calls between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday that are political in nature or encourage people to change insurance providers.
Under the contract, the department guarantees incarcerated people will have access to computers and internet and that the agency will be responsible for any IT issues at these call centers that, as of Aug. 21, were operating at Oklahoma prisons in Helena, McLoud and Lexington.
In exchange for this work in “telemarketing and political polling activity,” the third-party vendor promised to pay the corrections department $10 per hour. Corrections has apparently been paying the inmates working in these call centers a measly $2 per hour — well below the minimum wage, according to Oklahoma Watch’s reporting.
Oklahoma inmates were making calls on behalf of this contractor in states like Connecticut, Kentucky, Ohio and Florida, according to Oklahoma Watch. They also waded into Oklahoma’s elections, asking about Republican gubernatorial candidates Gentner Drummond, Mike Mazzei, and Chip Keating. They also asked about Jon Echols, the GOP nominee for attorney general, and state Rep. Justin Humphrey, R-Lane. Humphrey is an outspoken critic of Farris, the corrections department leader, and ran unsuccessfully earlier this year for lieutenant governor.
At one prison, as many as 120 inmates each made up to 800 calls each day, and had access to information such as people’s names, addresses, phone numbers and even their current insurers, according to Oklahoma Watch.
When asked about their telemarketing contracts, the Corrections Department essentially said that what they’re doing is legal and the material complies with state and federal law.
But that’s not the point.
The point is Oklahoma taxpayers should not be footing the bill for more annoying telemarketing operations, particularly when the goal of incarceration is to rehabilitate and set inmates up for success when they are released back into society.
I fail to see how having them to do a job that is universally scorned is rehabilitative or the type we would say is contributing to society.
Rather than setting them up for success, we’re more likely getting them hung up on or cursed out.
This contract also raises safety issues. As part of their sentences, offenders are often restricted from contacting various people, including their victims. Yet we’re giving them a treasure trove of random people’s contact info. 
Giving inmate carte blanc access to people’s information and computers has already created one really bad scenario.
In 2021, an Oklahoma inmate already serving multiple life sentences for child sexual abuse, used the computer in his prison call center to download child sexual abuse material, according to Oklahoma Watch’s reporting.
After that, Oklahoma prison call centers were shut down. But lawmakers apparently never got around to abolishing them. Now they’re back with a vengeance, targeting unsuspecting Oklahomans who would already give their right arm to stop telemarketers.
So here we are, stuck with tone-deaf prison leaders who think it’s OK to make a quick buck at the taxpayer expense.
Oklahomans expected their leaders to implement policies that make all our lives better. Using the tax dollars we pay to keep the power on at prisons to run call centers does not meet that threshold.
But let’s not forget that while operating these call centers, the Corrections Department is engaging in a very controversial process of using and profiting off of captive labor.
Nationally, inmates do not have the same labor protections as the rest of us and are more vulnerable to “labor exploitation and abuse,” according to a report published by the American Civil Liberties Union’s Oklahoma chapter.
The ACLU found that while slavery and involuntary servitude is constitutionally prohibited, inmates don’t have the right to refuse to work.
About 76% of them nationwide said they were forced to work. If they refused, they faced punishments such as being placed in solitary confinement, losing visitation privileges or missing out on the ability to reduce their time for good behavior, according to the report.
They’re also not protected by minimum wage laws.
Of those surveyed nationwide, 70% reported making so little working their prison jobs that they could not afford basic necessities. The same percentage also said they received no formal training. 
What does $2 buy right now? In this economy, not much.
The incarcerated people working in Oklahoma’s call centers said they’re being punished for not meeting quotas or expectations of their supervisors, though they did not say how.
That is absolutely outrageous.
Regardless of what they were convicted of to land themselves behind bars, these are vulnerable people at the mercy of an agency that controls where they eat, sleep, are housed and exercise.
They can’t vote. They’re largely cut off from their families and the outside world.
By allowing these call centers to continue to operate, state leaders are sending their constituents a message that they think this is an appropriate way to treat inmates and use taxpayer resources.
It’s not.
The majority of those in our prisons will be released one day, and we need to give them skills to be productive and successful.
And if someone at the Corrections Department thinks call centers are a way do that, then they obviously live on a different planet than the rest of us.

title: Oil and gas leases threaten big game migration routes, lawsuit claims
description:
Energy development will kick Sublette pronghorn, Baggs mule deer and other wildlife while they’re down, conservationists assert.
The post Oil and gas leases threaten big game migration routes, lawsuit claims appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The federal government broke environmental laws when it leased 179 square miles in Wyoming for oil and gas drilling, threatening already-diminished migrating big game herds, two conservation groups assert in a lawsuit filed this week.
The Wilderness Society and Wilderness Workshop sued Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, the BLM’s acting Wyoming Director Kris Kirby and others on Tuesday asking the U.S. District Court in Colorado to revoke leases sold in Wyoming and Colorado in June. The lawsuit claims the federal agencies violated their own regulations and a slew of environmental laws by prioritizing oil and gas development over all other uses on federal public land that belongs to all Americans.
The BLM sold leases on 102 parcels in Wyoming for $34.7 million, money that is split between the federal government and the state. Conducted under last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sales collected revenue through a 12.5% royalty rate, discounted by the act from 16.67%.
The reduction makes “oil and gas development more economically attractive to industry,” the BLM said in June.
“[D]ecades-old safeguards … ensure we hand our public lands down to our children, not over to industry.” Julia Stuble
The leases threaten the Baggs mule deer and Sublette pronghorn migration corridors and other big game migrations east of Rawlins, Julia Stuble, Wyoming state director for The Wilderness Society, said in a statement. The lawsuit also challenges acreage leased in northwest Colorado, making the total contested area 430 square miles.
“This administration’s energy dominance agenda shows a flagrant disregard for the rule of law and is trampling on decades-old safeguards that ensure we hand our public lands down to our children, not over to industry,” Stuble stated.
The suit asks the court to halt any action authorized by the challenged sales, set aside the sales themselves and return the issue to the BLM for reconsideration.
In selling the leases over an area more than twice the size of the District of Columbia, the BLM prioritized oil and gas development over all other uses, said Mike Freeman, one of the conservationists’ attorneys.
“That’s just flatly illegal,” he said.
Mischaracterization?
The fossil fuel industry disputes the lawsuit’s central claims.
The lawsuit “mischaracterizes the federal oil and natural gas leasing process, which is only the first step in development on federal lands,” said Ryan McConnaughey, interim president of the Petroleum Association of Wyoming. “Actual development requires additional review and approval by the BLM,” he wrote in a statement.
The BLM “does not have a comment at this time due to current litigation,” an agency spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuit, which spans 52 pages, alleges the BLM violated its own requirements to first lease areas outside the valuable migration routes and winter ranges. Pronghorn herds in the leased areas ranged from about 37% to 66% below objectives, the suit states, and mule deer herds ranged from about 25% to 62% below.
Energy development in migration corridors curtails habitat use by wildlife by about 39%, the lawsuit says, referencing one 14-year study of mule deer in Wyoming.
An environmental analysis authorizing the lease sale claims that established BLM plans have already dealt with the effects of drilling on wildlife, the lawsuit states. But those established BLM plans themselves say the effects will be addressed in the environmental review, which does not deal with them, according to the lawsuit.
A federal environmental law “squarely prohibits playing this sort of ‘shell-game’ with impacts analysis,” the conservationists’ lawsuit states.
Leasing gives developers contractual rights, are an “irreversible commitment” of land and resources, and cannot be properly mitigated once issued, according to The Wilderness Society and Wilderness Workshop.
McConnaughey disagreed.
“The June lease sale included environmental analysis and resource-protection stipulations, and BLM’s established process provides for additional site-specific review before development can occur,” he stated. “Calling that a ‘shell game’ assumes that every environmental question must be resolved at the leasing stage, regardless of whether the specific development proposal, location, timing or impacts are even known.”
Already gone
Freeman, the conservationists’ attorney, said the BLM is supposed to balance oil and gas development with other uses. “The Trump administration has been taking the opposite approach,” he said.
In his first term, Trump and his administration tried to ignore land management plans designed to protect greater sage grouse, he said. Courts invalidated numerous lease sales because of the administration’s faulty reasoning, Freeman said.
In one instance, a court ordered the federal government to refund $109 million for illegal oil and gas leases sold in sensitive grouse habitat in 2019. Those contested leases covered 3,906 square miles in Wyoming, an area larger than Delaware.
Energy development already has affected wildlife in the Equality State, Freeman said.
“They’re in trouble in large part because of oil and gas disruption,” he said.

name: WyoFile
title: Drought leads to ‘unprecedented’ black bear conflicts in Wyoming
description:
Wildlife officials plead with homeowners to secure food and trash as black bears range into cities, campgrounds looking for sustenance.
The post Drought leads to ‘unprecedented’ black bear conflicts in Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The 5-year-old black bear had a routine. At nightfall, she would climb down out of one of Laramie’s many cottonwood trees, spend the night searching for tasty morsels in city and residential garbage cans, then by 6 a.m. she would find another tree, climb back up, and sleep off all that garbage while 60, 80 or even 100 feet off the ground. 
Pictures show her legs free floating on either side of a branch, dangling like a cartoon bear near the city’s historic train depot and across town by baseball fields. Wyoming Game and Fish Department biologists received regular reports of her whereabouts, but she was either 80 feet up a cottonwood tree — too high to dart with no branches to catch her fall — or she’d already moved on, said Lee Knox, Laramie’s Game and Fish’s regional wildlife coordinator. 
He’s guessing she spent nearly a month in Laramie before one night in late August she climbed up a spruce tree instead of a cottonwood and someone called Game and Fish in time. Knox requested help from a tree trimming service who arrived with a truck and bucket and hoisted another biologist into the air. The biologist shot the chubby bear with a tranquilizer dart and watched as she tumbled out of the spruce tree like a ball in a game of plinko, the branches slowing her fall before coming to rest in a tarp held slightly off the ground. 
This black bear spent weeks in Laramie this summer. It would sleep in trees during the day and descend at night to eat garbage. (Lee Knox)
He then checked her for injuries, gave her an ear tag to show she’d been captured and drove the sleepy bear to the nearby Snowy Range, where he released her deep in the woods hoping he wouldn’t see her again.
A black bear spending a month loitering in a town of 35,000 people was strange enough. Even weirder was that she wasn’t a young, dumb male bear — she was a 5- to 6-year-old female who had previously reared cubs. Adult females tend to be known more for their caution than recklessness, Knox said. But that’s a reflection of how bad this summer has been for bear and human conflict, not just in southeast Wyoming, but across much of the Mountain West.
“To find a bear in town once or twice a summer wouldn’t be crazy, but this summer was unprecedented,” Knox said. “There’s been an unheard-of number of conflicts. It’s at least three times as bad as the last bad year, and the majority of the conflicts have been more aggressive bear behavior.”
Why, exactly, is anyone’s guess, but one of the biggest drivers is likely an extreme drought causing a decided lack of food. And summer is not over yet.
Black bears in trouble
The Laramie region, which encompasses half of the Sierra Madre range all the way to the Nebraska border, regularly deals with black bear conflict. Several years ago, Game and Fish advised people in the Saratoga Valley and Centennial areas to lock their vehicles because black bears figured out how to open car doors for tasty rewards inside. 
This year they’re not only breaking into vehicles but also houses and cabins. Game and Fish has received at least 20 reports of black bear thieves sneaking in through screen doors and sometimes windows. They’ve also wedged themselves through doggy doors, though one bear realized too late it couldn’t get back out the doggy door and ran away with the contraption around its waist.
A black bear pads through the forest near Yellowstone National Park’s northeast entrance in May 2015. (Neal Herbert/National Park Service)
The issue is even more serious in Colorado, where portions of the state have seen a 219% rise in bear conflicts in the first seven months of the year. And in late August, a black bear broke into a home in Estes Park, Colorado, rooted around in the kitchen and then scratched and knocked over an 80-year-old woman. The woman is recovering from her wounds, according to Denver7, and the bear escaped back through the window. 
Northern Wyoming also has been struggling with problem bears, though so far they’ve largely spared houses, opting instead for chicken coops, bird feeders and garbage, said Tim Thomas, Game and Fish’s Sheridan regional wildlife coordinator. In the Bighorn Mountains, a black bear tried climbing in a tent with campers after harassing other campers a few miles away. Game and Fish caught the bear, ran DNA tests to determine it was the same one trying to steal food in campgrounds, and killed it to prevent it from an inevitably more serious conflict. 

John Hebberger Jr. submitted this photo of a black bear in Jackson to the Jackson Hole News&Guide’s “Field Notes” section in September 2024. Last year was a deadly year for Teton County black bears, which get much less attention than their cousins, the grizzly bears. (John Hebberger Jr./Jackson Hole News&Guide)

“We’re seeing issues across both gender and age classes,” Thomas said. “It’s not just young ones getting kicked off mom, they’re all looking for food resources.”
In Muddy Mountain near Casper, the Bureau of Land Management temporarily closed a campground in July after it was visited by a black bear. Because the bear had returned multiple times for food rewards, Wyoming Game and Fish made the decision to euthanize it, an agency spokesperson told Oil City News.
Colorado wildlife officials have killed nearly 300 black bears this year, according to reporting from the Colorado Sun, including an 18-year-old bear whose intestines were completely blocked by plastic garbage bags and “at least 10 nonflushable cleaning wipes.”
Looking for food in all the wrong places
Dan Thompson, Game and Fish’s large carnivore supervisor, figures he’s fielded dozens of calls from journalists this summer wondering why black bear conflict is so much higher than normal. 
The simplest answer in regions like Laramie and Sheridan is likely tied to drought and few natural foods. They’re popping up looking for food in places as far away from mountains as Torrington and Pine Bluffs, Knox said, which is not typical bear habitat.
“Hot dry conditions and lower than normal berry abundance and other things like that are contributing factors,” Thompson said. 
Berry crops failed in the Sheridan region because of a late frost, and grasses and wildflowers peaked much earlier than normal this year. But lack of food isn’t fully to blame for increased conflict. Fewer bears came into Lander this year, for example, than last year when berry bushes bowed their heads under the weight of their fruit. Last year, Thompson said, bears followed that berry abundance right into the urban-wildland interface. 
Trash overflows from a dumpster at Rob Roy Campground in the Snowies. Wildlife officials are asking the public to secure their food and trash to avoid bear conflicts. (Christine Peterson)
A larger part of the problem is the combination of scarce wild foods and more readily available human foods. If a hungry bear can’t find anything to eat, it will keep moving. If it discovers trash or other snacks, it will stick around. That’s why Game and Fish asks people year after year to bring bird and dog food into secure places, keep garbage in bear-proof cans and lock down those chicken coops. Because once a bear discovers a cache of easy, tasty food, it won’t forget, Thompson said. 
“People should let us know as soon as possible, especially if there’s any conflict activity, if they’re seeing a black bear in an area where they aren’t expecting to,” he said. “People are reluctant to call because they think we will show up and kill a bear.”
And Game and Fish has killed more black bears than normal this year, though Thompson said he wouldn’t know how many exactly until closer to winter when bears are finally in their dens. If people call early, before a bear is habituated to finding human food, Game and Fish has more luck hazing or moving the bear and helping homeowners secure food and other attractants.
“We really need people to give wildlife some grace and be as bear aware as possible,” Knox said. “If you live out of town, especially, anything is possible. It’s Wyoming and it’s a rough year.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Mixed-status immigrant households expected to lose benefits under new public charge rule
description: The rules may lead people without lawful status to forgo enrollment in public benefits for their U.S. citizen kids and other dependents.
text:
A 10-year-old Honduran immigrant who came into the United States as an unaccompanied minor carries her baby cousin in 2021 in Indiana. A new federal rule expands public charge considerations in immigrants’ applications for lawful permanent residency, a policy that could contribute to more than a million people disenrolling from public benefits. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)New rules going into effect this week allow immigrants’ enrollment in safety net resources to be taken into account for lawful immigration status applications, the latest in the Trump administration’s immigration overhaul.
The rules will have wide implications for mixed-status households, as people without lawful status may forgo enrollment in public benefits for their U.S. citizen kids and other dependents out of fear.
The new U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) guidance goes into effect Sept. 18 and affects people applying for a green card, certain visas or admission into the United States. It rescinds the Biden administration’s 2022 public charge regulations, which restricted immigration officers from considering immigrants’ use of non-cash public benefits, including many benefits for low-income families such as Medicaid, housing programs and food stamps.
When an immigration officer determines a person could become dependent on government benefits, that “public charge” is a ground for inadmissibility under federal law.
Trump’s new policy broadens immigration officers’ discretion, allowing them to consider enrollment in non-cash public benefits as public charge. That includes Medicaid, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the country’s largest food assistance program.
Those subject to public charge consideration are immigrants seeking adjustment of immigration status to lawful permanent residency, and includes those who are spouses, siblings, parents and children of U.S. citizens; widowers and widows; foreign medical school graduates; U.S. armed forces personnel; certain workers such as those with advanced degrees, and others.
USCIS specifies certain immigrant groups and classifications that are not subject to public charge. Those include asylees, refugees, Afghani and Iraqi interpreters or such nationals who worked for the U.S. government, people seeking temporary protected status, human trafficking victims, self-petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act, Indigenous people born in Canada who aren’t U.S. citizens, among other groups.
Health research group KFF this summer estimated that between 1.4 million and 4.1 million Medicaid and CHIP enrollees living in a household with a noncitizen could disenroll due to the public charge rule or another immigration-related fear.
Last November, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security acknowledged this, saying that the rule would affect U.S. citizens in mixed-status households. The agency said that federal and state spending could be reduced by almost $9 billion annually “due to disenrollment or forgone enrollment in public benefits programs by members of households that include aliens who may be receiving public benefits.”
It also acknowledged “downstream and upstream” effects for states and their economies.
“For example, the rule might result in reduced revenues for healthcare providers, such as hospitals and nonprofits, participating in Medicaid, companies that manufacture medical supplies or pharmaceuticals, grocery retailers participating in SNAP, agricultural producers who grow foods that are eligible for purchase using SNAP benefits, or landlords participating in federally funded housing programs,” the agency wrote in its proposed guidance.
Previous studies found that under the first Trump administration’s public charge rules, families were less likely to apply for food assistance or seek healthcare, a point emphasized by the American Academy of Pediatrics this week.
“When a child is hungry, it can affect every aspect of their development and lead to chronic conditions like heart disease and diabetes, even into adulthood,” said Dr. Sural Shah, chair of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health, during a news conference Thursday.
“Without accessing WIC, babies and young children will miss out on critical nutrition supports that are important for brain development in the first 1,000 days of life. Medicaid and CHIP are lifeline programs.”
In an executive order he signed a month after his inauguration, President Donald Trump wrote that his administration would “uphold the rule of law, defend against the waste of hard-earned taxpayer resources, and protect benefits for American citizens in need, including individuals with disabilities and veterans.”
Health clinicians say immigration activity has been leading to fear and isolation among families, causing delayed care and illnesses to advance among children. They also say those with disabilities and complex needs will be among those hit hardest.
The Autism Self Advocacy Network, for example, said immigrants with disabilities will be disproportionately affected, as they tend to use public benefits more than other immigrants.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming families are struggling to afford healthcare. Here are two solutions.
description:
The state must be a good steward of rural health dollars while making 12-month postpartum care permanent, writes the Healthy Wyoming Board of Directors.
The post Wyoming families are struggling to afford healthcare. Here are two solutions. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming health care is at a pivotal crossroads. With the arrival of federal Rural Health Transformation  funding, the work of state task forces, and a primary election that demonstrated voters’ clear demand for constructive governance, healthcare is dominating public debate.

Opinion

The central takeaway from all this discussion is clear. Wyoming families are paying too much for care, and healthcare costs remain among voters’ top concerns heading into the fall. Among all the difficult proposals to address this problem, two are clear and available now: Focus new federal funding on rural healthcare access, and permanently extend Medicaid care for new moms to a full year after giving birth.
For more than a decade, Healthy Wyoming has advocated for policies that make healthcare affordable and accessible. Over that time, we consistently urged lawmakers to make our state Medicaid coverage available to all low-wage citizens. That is a policy that has strengthened rural hospitals and public health in neighboring states.
Practically speaking, what can state leaders do to meet challenges as they exist today? Those challenges include new federal work-reporting rules under 2025 federal bill H.R. 1 — the so-called Big Beautiful Bill Act — shifting administrative burdens, and evolving federal budget guidelines. Broad Medicaid expansion faces real implementation and fiscal hurdles. However, Wyoming cannot afford to stand still. We must focus on tangible, immediate steps that protect access and stabilize our communities right now.
In the coming months, Healthy Wyoming will focus our advocacy on two urgent, high-impact priorities:
First, safeguarding rural investment. As Wyoming begins allocating more than $200 million in federal Rural Health Transformation dollars, Healthy Wyoming will serve as a watchdog for patients and local communities. These funds must directly protect essential local services — including rural emergency rooms, EMS transport, clinic staffing and mental health services — so families in frontier counties can access care close to home.
Second, making 12-month postpartum care permanent. In 2023, the Wyoming Legislature demonstrated genuine pro-family leadership by approving a temporary extension of postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to a full 12 months. That extension is set to expire in March. When lawmakers convene in Cheyenne this winter, Healthy Wyoming will ask them to remove that sunset and make 12-month care a permanent fixture in state law.
The medical and economic case for permanent postpartum care is overwhelming:

Clinical necessity: Nationwide, more than half of pregnancy-related complications and maternal deaths occur after the initial 60-day window, driven by cardiovascular conditions, chronic disease flares and behavioral health struggles.
Mental health in our frontier state: Between 13% and 20% of new mothers experience postpartum depression, with symptoms frequently emerging or peaking between three and nine months after delivery — long after the old 60-day cutoff. In a state facing an acute mental health provider shortage and tragic suicide rates, no new mother should be dropped from care when she is most vulnerable.
Good governance and fiscal sense: This policy does not expand eligibility to a single new group; it simply ensures mothers already enrolled receive uninterrupted care through their baby’s critical first year. The federal government covers half the cost through regular matching funds, and permanent authorization gives rural hospitals and state administrators the certainty they need to plan budgets and keep clinic doors open.

Pro-family policy is not just a slogan — it is the commitment to ensure mothers and babies survive, recover and thrive. Making 12-month postpartum coverage permanent and responsibly stewarding rural health investments are common-sense steps Wyoming can achieve together right now.
Healthy Wyoming will continue working with lawmakers, providers and local communities to build a health care system that works for every Wyomingite.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Trump gives feds 90 days to consider removing endangered species protections for wolves
description: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Sept. 4 giving the U.S. secretary of interior 90 days to decide whether to remove Endangered Species Act protections for gray wolves and Mexican wolves in the United States. The Supporting America’s Ranchers executive order calls for Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum to decide within 90 days whether […]
text:
A gray wolf in snow. (File photo courtesy of Eric Cole/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)President Donald Trump signed an executive order Sept. 4 giving the U.S. secretary of interior 90 days to decide whether to remove Endangered Species Act protections for gray wolves and Mexican wolves in the United States.
Carter’s Hope: After U.S. government killed off Western wolves, a bold experiment brought them back

The Supporting America’s Ranchers executive order calls for Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum to decide within 90 days whether gray wolves and Mexican wolves have met their recovery criteria and to begin the process of delisting or downlisting them. 
The executive order also calls for Burgum to prepare a legislative recommendation for Trump to fully delist or downlist wolves and, upon determination that recovery criteria have been met, encourage states to delist wolves and revise state standards for the killing of wolves in order to help ranchers.
 The history of the near extermination of wolves in the U.S., and their recovery

Wolves are a native species that was almost completely eliminated in the Western United States by the 1940s through a widespread government extermination campaign backed by congressional bounties and the extensive use of poisoning.
After they were nearly killed off, wolves became one of the first animals added to the Endangered Species List in 1974. Then, the U.S. government reintroduced wolves into Idaho and Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996 using wolves captured from Canada. 
Wolves were removed, or delisted, from the Endangered Species Act in Idaho, Wyoming and Montana beginning in 2011, where they can be hunted and trapped. 
U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins delivers remarks on May 27, 2026, at the USDA’s headquarters in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Christophe Paul/USDA)
But wolves are still protected under the Endangered Species Act in other parts of the United States. Those Endangered Species Act protections prevent hunting in places where wolves are still protected, but those protections could go away if wolves are removed from the Endangered Species Act as a result of Trump’s new executive order.  
“While the Biden administration chose to villainize ranching and the rural way of life under the guise of radical environmental mandates, the Trump Administration continues to focus on rebuilding the Great American Cattle Herd,” U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said in a written statement. “For the past 19 months, USDA has worked tirelessly to defend and promote our nation’s ranchers. Through our Beef Plan and the Ranchers First Initiative we are working to continue increasing our nation’s heifer retention rate. Today, the President laid out tools to better equip farmers and ranchers to deal with dangerous predators threatening their livestock, provide more transparency for consumers on where their meat originates, and expand market opportunities while maintaining our world class food safety standards. President Trump is focused on delivering an America First agenda and will do that by continuing to put our Ranchers First.”
 Wolf advocates worry Trump’s order is premature, and that wolves have not fully recovered in the U.S. 

Trump administration officials and several Republican elected officials support the executive order. 
On the other hand, wolf advocates and some conservation groups oppose the move, which they say is premature because wolf populations have not met their recovery goals across the U.S.
Collette Atkins, senior attorney and director of the carnivore conservation program at the Center for Biological Diversity, said removing wolves from Endangered Species Act protections could be devastating because wolf populations have not yet received after nearly being completely wiped during the 20th century.  
Atkins said also the Center for Biological Diversity would challenge any misguided delisting attempts in court. 
Cattle Battle: How wolves and livestock collide – and how one Idaho project offers solutions

“Trump’s new push to prematurely remove wolf protections will lead to yet another court decision that reinstates those protections while doing nothing to help ranchers,” Adkins said in a written statement. “Smart ranchers coexist with wolves by using commonsense measures like guard dogs and fencing to protect livestock. Trump should be funding these tools, not wasting taxpayer money trying to kill or illegally strip wolves of lifesaving protections.”
Carter Niemeyer, a former government trapper turned wolf advocate, called Trump’s executive order on wolves “a distraction,” saying it won’t help ranchers in Idaho, Montana and Wyoming – where wolves have already been removed from the Endangered Species List protections and can already be hunted and removed by government agencies for harassing livestock. 
“This executive order, to me, is just a distraction from other bigger issues farmers and ranchers have,” Niemeyer told the Idaho Capital Sun on Thursday.
Niemeyer, who is retired in Idaho but previously worked for the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services, said wolves kill about 200 livestock animals a year between the states of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming, where there are more than 6 million cows and cattle. 
More livestock are killed in accidents and by vehicles each year. 
“I remind people that livestock losses to wolves are less than one-tenth of 1% for cattle and sheep,” Niemeyer said. “I would think tariffs, the cost of gasoline and diesel and the lack of access to fertilizer and things like that should be way higher up the list of concerns for ranchers and farmers than wolves.”
Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials estimated that Idaho’s wolf population decreased to an estimated 1,129 wolves in 2025, a decrease of about 100 wolves compared to the year before. State officials attributed the decrease to aggressive hunting and trapping, and said the number of livestock killed by wolves is trending downward, the Sun previously reported. 
 



  Learn more about wolf recovery and wolves in the West

Check out Howl, a 2025 longform written series and podcast created by the Idaho Capital Sun and Boise State Public Radio to learn about wolf reintroduction, recovery and controversy in Idaho.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Molder and Hatcher discuss positions on renewable energy, nuclear power ahead of November election
description: District 5 candidates Charlie Hatcher, a Republican farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, and Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, share pride in Tennessee’s nuclear energy work and see renewable energy sources as tools for powering the state’s future. But they take different approaches on federal government involvement and dealing[...]
text:
Charlie Hatcher, left, and Chaz Molder, right, are campaigning to serve Tennessee's 5th Congressional District. (Photos: John Partipilo)District 5 candidates Charlie Hatcher, a Republican farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, and Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, share pride in Tennessee’s nuclear energy work and see renewable energy sources as tools for powering the state’s future.
But they take different approaches on federal government involvement and dealing with nuclear waste.
The contenders are vying for a district that spans some of the state’s most and least populated areas, including counties where local economies have ties to renewable energy sources.
The majority of the 54 solar farms in Tennessee are concentrated in West Tennessee. The 5th Congressional District includes several solar farms, including the state’s largest in rural Lake County. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The district is also home to some of Tennessee’s top agricultural counties, where corn and soybeans remain among the leading commodity crops. About 46% of Tennessee’s corn yield is used to make ethanol fuel, according to Tennessee Corn, a coalition of farmer-funded corn promotion groups. The majority of Tennessee’s soybean yield is used for animal feed, but oil extracted from the beans is also used to make biodiesel fuel.
Here’s what Molder and Hatcher told the Lookout about their positions on renewable and nuclear energy.
Federal involvement
Hatcher’s primary election campaign saw a boost from outside spending by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a political action committee funded by renewable energy investors that spent $2 million opposing incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles for his actions against renewable energy development. After Ogles’ defeat, President Donald Trump endorsed Hatcher to win the general election.
But what does Hatcher think of federal support for renewable projects?
Federal subsidies or grants can and should be used to help fledgling industries get off the ground, he said, but these should be limited in time frame.
“The federal government doesn’t need to create an artificial demand for a certain renewable energy,” Hatcher said. “It’s just not sustainable, and that’s where you get into (being) not good use of taxpayer money. If you have to subsidize renewable energy for a long period of time, I don’t like that.”
Hatcher points to agricultural subsidies as an example.
“Commonly, the USDA gives grants for value-added products, and they’re grants, but the expectation is once that project or that industry gets off the ground, then that’s … termed out,” he said. 



Quotation







The federal government doesn’t need to create an artificial demand for a certain renewable energy. It’s just not sustainable, and that’s where you get into (being) not good use of taxpayer money. 


– Charlie Hatcher, Republican nominee for the 5th Congressional District 


Hatcher also acknowledged the agriculture industry’s positive relationship with renewable fuels, which provide another use case and revenue stream for the country’s most prominent row crops.
“I’m for all forms of energy that make sense,” he said. “They have to stand alone themselves once they get off the ground.”
Molder said federal incentives for renewable energy need to be consistent, referring to the Trump administration’s abrupt reversal of Biden-era tax credits and other federal support for renewable energy programs.
“Federal policies need to be consistent and steady enough for utilities and businesses, small businesses particularly, to plan around it,” Molder said. “Constantly creating these incentives and then turning around and abruptly eliminating them makes it harder and harder for businesses to really participate in these types of renewable energy options, and frankly, make it more expensive to build and more expensive to borrow for.”
Solar power and other renewable energy can help lower costs and strengthen the grid long-term, Molder said. 
Gov predicts Tennessee will be a finalist for nuclear campus

“This is an opportunity where government can be put to work to do good by incentivizing the private sector to be innovative with respect to renewable energy opportunities instead of creating inconsistencies and causing confusion,” he said.
Going nuclear
The U.S. Department of Energy announced in early August that Tennessee is one of five states under consideration for a federal nuclear energy partnership. The state has a long history in nuclear research at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Gov. Bill Lee created a $70 million investment fund for nuclear projects and a nuclear advisory council.
The federal government is proposing a $50 billion investment in a nuclear campus involving both production and nuclear waste storage. The announcement stirred concern over where and how nuclear waste might be stored in Tennessee if the state is selected for the project.



Quotation







We’ve got to make sure we understand what we’re doing in our own state relative to nuclear energy and waste that’s being produced in our own state before we start becoming a storage site for other states’ waste.


– Chaz Molder, Democratic nominee for the 5th Congressional District 


“Nuclear energy is already our state’s biggest source of electricity,” Molder said. “We should be proud that Tennessee is leading the nation in this regard.”
Molder emphasized the growing need for electricity and said “having reliable, low-carbon power around the clock is important,” and nuclear energy will be a part of meeting that demand.
But he’s concerned about the possibility of Tennessee becoming a storage site for other states’ nuclear waste.
“We’ve got to make sure we understand what we’re doing in our own state relative to nuclear energy and waste that’s being produced in our own state before we start becoming a storage site for other states’ waste,” Molder said. “And I think, you know, being a mayor, having local control on these issues is very important for me.”
Hatcher said he’s proud of Tennessee “leading the country on nuclear energy,” including Lee’s focus on the industry. Lee appointed Hatcher to his position in the state’s agriculture department, and endorsed Hatcher’s campaign to represent the 5th District. 
Regarding nuclear waste, Hatcher said he would “just let the experts deal with that.”
“We’ve had nuclear waste in the past. I expect, as technology advances, there will be less nuclear waste and a better way to store it,” he said.
