title: Wittman, running again in VA-01, supports Trump’s $1.5 trillion defense spending budget
description: U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, is backing President Donald Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense spending budget, as the nation marks its eighth month in a war with Iran that Trump launched without congressional approval.  Wittman, who is running against Democrat Shannon Taylor to represent Virginia’s 1st Congressional District for an eighth term, a[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, speaks at a campaign event for then-Republican gubernatorial nominee Winsome Earle-Sears on Aug. 14, 2025. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, is backing President Donald Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense spending budget, as the nation marks its eighth month in a war with Iran that Trump launched without congressional approval. 
Wittman, who is running against Democrat Shannon Taylor to represent Virginia’s 1st Congressional District for an eighth term, argued that a beefed up military can help prevent and prepare for future wars, and deter other nations from picking fights. 
“We have to make sure that we are modernizing the military. The only way that we deter adversaries from acting badly is to have a strong military,” Wittman said. “The strategy of peace through strength works.”
Investment in technology, he added, can help reduce human deployment in global conflicts. 
“What we need to be looking at is making sure that we have systems out there where if we don’t have to put a human being in harm’s way, then we shouldn’t,” he said. 
An analysis from The Virginia Mercury’s parent company States Newsroom found that Virginia is among states that could benefit the most, if the $1.5 trillion spending plan is approved. 
Virginia, Texas and California have high concentrations of military bases and defense installations; each has received about $50 billion annually from the Department of Defense over the past six years, the analysis found. 

Though the funding boost could go towards technology upgrades, manufacturing and pay raises, many Democrats, including in Virginia’s congressional delegation, have so far rejected the request.
“A President who promised to end wars has transformed into one intoxicated by war,” U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said in a statement. Kaine has repeatedly referred to America’s military engagement in Iran as Trump’s “war of choice.”
The $1.5 trillion funding request would “swell the Defense budget at the very moment when Congress shows a determined unwillingness to exercise any meaningful check on how the President uses the nation’s might,” Kaine, who serves on the Senate’s version of the Armed Forces Committee, added. 
The National Defense Authorization Act is part of a series of appropriations bills Congress votes on annually to fund the federal government. Last week, however, the body passed a continuing resolution to delay funding debates until Dec. 11. 
This could help avoid a government shutdown over Trump’s funding request, like the historic 43-day shutdown that occurred last fall, and will put off the decision until Nov. 3 midterm elections conclude.
As financial deliberations continue, Wittman said he’s confident Congress can deliver at least some of Trump’s defense spending request because Republicans control both chambers and some House Democrats in swing districts have warmed to the idea. 
The House has already advanced the NDAA, totaling $1.15 trillion with an additional $350 billion that would need to go through a separate reconciliation process. The Senate has stalled in passing the full NDAA so far. 

 Midterms could advance or tank the unprecedented defense funding request

Congressional midterm elections — which occur halfway through presidential terms —  are considered a referendum on the party in power and the president. This year, Republicans are attempting to hold onto their majorities in each chamber while Democrats are seizing on “affordability” in their bid to flip seats. 
Economic issues like groceries, gas prices, healthcare access and affordability are among key voter concerns this year. The war with Iran, which is a major player in the global oil trade, has contributed to financial strains.
Whether he wins another two years in Congress or not, Wittman said, one of his main goals is securing additional defense funding. 
“The key is to make sure that we get this year’s appropriations bills done and then get the reconciliation bill done that recovers at least a portion of our readiness in these weapons accounts. And I think that’ll get us to a point that’s acceptable,” he said.
Wittman voted 60 times to undo the Affordable Care Act, then he backed extending its subsidies

If he is re-elected and Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House of Representatives, Wittman will run within his party to lead the chamber’s Armed Forces Committee. 
If Democrats flip the House, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Washington may be in line to lead the committee, as he has in the past. 
In a statement, Smith said he sees “opportunity to work together in a bipartisan manner” but said there will also be times when Democrats on the committee “will strongly disagree with the Trump Administration.”
Earlier this year, when laying out goals for the committee in the year ahead, Smith was critical of the “war of choice” in Iran and military deployment in U.S. cities. 
“These political decisions detract from the military’s core missions, reduce the Department’s readiness, threaten our country’s position at the forefront of global innovation, and erode public trust and confidence in the military,” he said. “Reining in mission creep needs to be a focus of the committee.” 
Wittman said he has continued conversations with Smith and other democratic leaders on the committee to align their visions and seek collaboration. 
“But obviously the first thing on our objective list is to make sure that we win the election this year,” he said. “We’re not taking any of that for granted.”
Early voting in the midterm elections begins Sept. 18. Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Virginia lawmakers move closer to regulating self-driving vehicles
description: Virginia is moving closer to regulating self-driving vehicles, with lawmakers and experts recently agreeing on a plan ahead of the next legislative session as the technology expands and safety concerns grow. Last year, the General Assembly directed a workgroup to consider rules for autonomous vehicles, or AVs, which have been tested in states including Arizo[...]
text:
Virginia lawmakers are considering regulations to allow for autonomous commercial vehicles, which could shift companies from using gas to electric, self-driving vehicles. Pictured are trucks parked off Interstate 95 in Virginia. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Virginia is moving closer to regulating self-driving vehicles, with lawmakers and experts recently agreeing on a plan ahead of the next legislative session as the technology expands and safety concerns grow.
Last year, the General Assembly directed a workgroup to consider rules for autonomous vehicles, or AVs, which have been tested in states including Arizona and Texas and restricted in California. Meanwhile, the federal government announced a national strategy plan to accelerate the development and deployment of self-driving vehicles across the country.
Virginia moves toward regulating self-driving vehicles amid safety and liability concerns

Leaders in the commonwealth are drafting proposals to establish a framework for implementing AV policy and create an ongoing advisory committee after the group concludes its work. The panel held its most recent meeting on Aug. 28. 
Virginia’s proposed framework would focus on commercial use rather than personal vehicles, including ride-sharing and delivery services, buses and Class 7 and 8 heavy-duty vehicles.
However, the meeting was not without disagreements over regulatory authority, various protections and workforce impacts.
“I believe what we’re doing … leading up to session, is illustrating where there’s strong consensus,” said Senate Transportation Committee Chair Lamont Bagby, D-Henrico, at the August meeting. “Folks can lobby to make amendments to legislation leading up to session or during session, but we’re just trying to… I think what I would love to see is the sort of bones of what this legislation looks like.”
On regulation, the group disagreed over whether the initial framework should cover light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, with the latter ultimately excluded from the broader motion. Members also debated how much discretion the Department of Motor Vehicles should have to suspend or revoke permits, rather than s establishing specific standards and limits in state law.
However, there was general agreement that the state should regulate AVs, with local regulation primarily applying to AVs operating as taxis.
Debate also focused on data collection, consumer and safety protections, and how to determine whether an AV pilot is safe and successful enough to continue or expand.
Specifically, members disagreed over whether to set specific safety requirements and benchmarks upfront or allow the DMV to determine whether a pilot is safe enough based on the vehicle’s operating conditions and the distance it has traveled. 
The meeting also included debate over whether to collect comprehensive, real-time operational and location data from AVs or limit reporting to non-real-time information comparable to existing federal and California requirements. 
Members also disagreed over whether legislation should protect AV customers from being forced to use arbitration to resolve disputes or leave those issues to existing consumer protection laws.
The group reached a consensus that agencies should recover administrative costs but disagreed over whether AV-specific fees should also fund worker retraining and support for displaced drivers.
Additionally, there was broad agreement that law enforcement and first responders need AV-specific training, but disagreement over whether that training should be mandatory, statewide and funded through fees or addressed separately.
Questions remain about whether AV services should receive special retail sales and use tax treatment. Lawmakers also debated whether legislation should immediately include worker retraining and support or address those issues later through separate laws and funding.
Several people, including Renee Gibson, vice president of government affairs at the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association, spoke during the August meeting about developing a regulatory framework for AVs in Virginia. 
Gibson said to the work group, ”Without a legislative framework that offers a clear path to commercial deployment, companies will simply not be able to enter the market.”
She was joined by business representatives from Uber, Tesla, Stack AV, Torc Robotics and Volkswagen, as well as labor union and organizational representatives who emphasized the need for commercial deployment pathways and labor protections.
Kevin O’Neill, a steering committee member of the DMV Drivers Alliance, was among those representing organizations, associations and unions concerned about job and income losses from AV deployment.
”Before Virginia gives companies a predictable path into this market, drivers do deserve to know what happens when autonomous fleets begin taking trips and income out of the existing workforce,” O’Neill said.
The workgroup is preparing a final report for the General Assembly to consider by Nov. 1.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Loudoun to consider data center pause, removing by-right grandfather clause
description: Loudoun County, the epicenter of Data Center Alley, is set to take up two amendments that would curb data center development, at least temporarily, and permanently end by-right development of the power-hungry data warehouses. Led by the county board member Juli Briskman, who is running for board chair, the amendments could pause the processing of […]
text:
A view of a data center in Loudoun County next to Chick Ford & Ryan Bickel Fields. (Photo courtesy of Karen Graham/Loudoun Times-Mirror)Loudoun County, the epicenter of Data Center Alley, is set to take up two amendments that would curb data center development, at least temporarily, and permanently end by-right development of the power-hungry data warehouses.
Led by the county board member Juli Briskman, who is running for board chair, the amendments could pause the processing of all new data center applications while the county revisits its comprehensive plan’s zoning ordinances for data centers. 
County staff has been directed to develop a plan detailing what a data center pause would look like while the ordinances are being crafted. That report will be presented at Tuesday’s board business meeting.
“I decided it was time that we actually just pumped the brakes, listened to the community, and just put a pause on all of it until we can get our arms around some of these other standards that we’ve been working on,” Briskman said in a July interview.
Additionally, Briskman and board member Laura TeKrony have advanced a resolution that could reshape existing data center applications.
County staff are drafting an amendment to end the grandfather clause, which allows data center applications filed prior to the adoption of the March 2025 change that ended by-right permitting for data centers to keep the by-right status. 
That change to the application process came about after the first phase of reviewing the comprehensive plan. 
The newly proposed amendment would require data centers in the previously grandfathered group to obtain a special exception that includes public hearings and a vote by the full board, steps that are already required for all new applications. 
The revamped process would give the public more opportunity to weigh in on the permitting process for data centers in their county, TeKrony said. 
“Data center applications should never be approved by-right without a public hearing and Board review. I did not support the grandfathering resolution in March 2025 and believe we need to do the right thing for the community and expire this resolution now,” TeKrony said in a statement. 
“We’ve given the data center industry 25 years to build by-right. There is no legal requirement for grandfathering. It is a choice,” she added.
In Loudoun, several neighborhoods butt up against under-construction data centers, which has led to the rise in concerns around sound, backup generator use, and other complaints for the fence line communities.
The grandfather amendment report will be presented at the Oct. 6 board meeting. 
This comes as other localities such as Suffolk, Chesapeake, Front Royal, and others are also hitting the brakes on approving new data centers and taking a closer look at their zoning ordinances for the controversial projects. 
As election season ramps up, political ads have hit the airwaves from state Sen. Glenn Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, calling for a statewide moratorium on data center development. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger has repeatedly said she believes the state should honor its commitments to the data center industry, which self-reported a total contribution of about $40 billion to Virginia’s economy in 2024 and 2025. 
However, she has pushed for more regulations on the industry, including ones to bolster environmental policies and require the industry to pay more for their energy infrastructure.
Lawmakers have pledged to sponsor legislation in the General Assembly session that starts in January to continue cracking down on data centers’ environmental impacts and improve siting policies to aid localities in making application decisions, among other ideas. 
Del. Rip Sullivan, D-Fairfax, and Sen. Creigh Deeds, D-Charlottesville, said earlier this year that the legislature could address  potential loopholes in the Virginia Clean Economy Act, as the push for behind-the-meter power generation for data centers is leading to more gas turbine proposals. 
Bills for the 2027 regular session are starting to trickle in as part of the pre-filing process. More legislation proposals will flow in towards the end of the year.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island congressional delegation presses FEMA on its denial for blizzard aid
description: Rhode Island’s congressional delegation is demanding answers from the Trump administration over why the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) repeatedly denied the state’s request for disaster aid following the historic February 2026 blizzard. A Sept. 9 letter by U.S. Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse along with U.S. Reps. Seth Magaziner and Gabe A[...]
text:
Cars parked on an unplowed street in Newport as 4:15 p.m. on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s congressional delegation is demanding answers from the Trump administration over why the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) repeatedly denied the state’s request for disaster aid following the historic February 2026 blizzard.
A Sept. 9 letter by U.S. Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse along with U.S. Reps. Seth Magaziner and Gabe Amo asked the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA to preserve and provide all records related to the state’s request for a major disaster declaration in order to recover from the hurricane-strength blizzard that dumped more than 3 feet of snow.
FEMA is overseen by the Department of Homeland Security.
“To date, FEMA has not provided Rhode Island officials with a written, detailed explanation for why the state’s request was denied despite exceeding FEMA’s thresholds for assistance,” the delegation wrote.
Gov. Dan McKee submitted the state’s request for $19 million in aid on April 7 under the Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, which allows governors to either request support for disasters caused by severe weather or if “the situation is beyond the capability of the state.”
FEMA denied the state’s request on July 2. McKee appealed and the state was denied again on Sept. 2. 
McKee calls FEMA’s denial of Rhode Island’s blizzard relief request ‘a new low’

On both occasions, FEMA’s leaders offered no specific reason for their decision, only stating in their denial letters that “based on our review of all of the information available, it has been determined that supplemental federal assistance under the Stafford Act is not warranted.”
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton elaborated on the denial — which applied to similar requests from New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts — in an X post Sept. 3 stating neither state offered new information to consider and that “winter weather is not new to the Northeast.”
Rhode Island’s congressional delegates argue the storm “was not typical winter weather.”
 Over 3 feet of snow fell across many parts of Rhode Island, with 37.9 inches of snow recorded at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport when the blizzard hit on Monday, Feb. 23. That surpassed the 28.6 inches that blanketed the state during the Blizzard of 1978.
The blizzard had the magnitude of a Category 2 hurricane with 74 mph wind gusts. The storm knocked out power to thousands of homes and caused $19 million in damage and cleanup costs across the state, including about $9 million in state costs and another $10 million incurred by Rhode Island’s cities and towns.
“The facts could not be clearer,” the delegation wrote. “Downplaying this devastating blizzard as just ‘winter weather’ is an insult to those whose lives and businesses were upended by the historic blizzard.”
The delegation wrote that a review of communications and records about the state’s request would illuminate how FEMA reached its decision and determine whether Hamilton’s explanation was supported by the agency’s records.
“If you fail to preserve and provide this information, it is only reasonable to assume that claim is entirely without merit,” the delegation wrote.
Asked for comment, spokespeople for FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security reiterated Hamilton’s stance that “no new information was provided” by the states who requested blizzard aid.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia’s voter registration deadline is approaching. Here are five things you need to know.
description: The midterm elections are less than two months away, which means now is the time for Georgia residents to register to vote or ensure that an existing voter registration is up to date. A number of competitive seats are up for grabs this year, including one of Georgia’s two U.S. Senate seats, the governorship and […]
text:
Tiffany Barkley, a 28-year-old nurse who said she would like the Public Service Commission to be more accountable to energy consumers, shows off her "I'm a Georgia voter" sticker after casting a ballot in DeKalb County, Ga. on Oct. 14, 2025. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderThe midterm elections are less than two months away, which means now is the time for Georgia residents to register to vote or ensure that an existing voter registration is up to date.
A number of competitive seats are up for grabs this year, including one of Georgia’s two U.S. Senate seats, the governorship and numerous other state and local races.
Georgia’s voter registration deadline is Oct. 5, according to the secretary of state’s office. Here’s what you need to know to ensure that you’re prepared.
I’m not sure if I’m registered. Where can I go to find out?
The secretary of state’s My Voter Page is a good place to start. The one-stop portal can help you check your voter registration status, as well as preview sample ballots, check your voting history and locate your nearest early voting location or election-day polling place.
Where do I go to register to vote or update my registration?
Georgia residents have a few different options when it comes to registering to vote for the first time.
Voters line up outside Shiloh Hills Baptist Church in Kennesaw, Georgia on Election Day, May 19, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
The secretary of state’s office allows Georgia residents to register to vote online or by mailing a completed paper application to the secretary of state’s office. A valid Georgia driver’s license is required to complete the online application, but residents who don’t have a driver’s license can complete a paper application using the last four digits of their social security number.
Georgia’s Department of Driver Services also allows voters to automatically register to vote whenever they apply for a new driver’s license or state ID card. Any time you update the address that appears on your ID card, you can automatically update your voter registration as well.
Voters can update an existing voter registration at the secretary of state’s My Voter Page. You can also reach out to your county registrar for their assistance.
How do I know if I need to update my voter registration?
Georgia law requires voters to be registered at their current home address, meaning that if you have moved since the last time you cast a ballot, it’s time to update your voter registration.
Republican state lawmakers revise Georgia election rules in time for 2024 campaign season

Voters who are registered at a nonresidential address, such as a P.O. box, a church, a business or a homeless shelter will also need to update their registration under a 2024 election law known as Senate Bill 189.
Voters who are experiencing homelessness should register to vote at their county registrar’s office under the new law.
Voter registration data, including residents’ addresses, are public and are available for purchase on the secretary of state’s website. Georgia residents who have been the victim of stalking and domestic violence may be eligible for Georgia’s VoteSafe program, which allows participants to register to vote while ensuring that their addresses are kept confidential.
My voter status is marked as “inactive.” What should I do?
The short answer is, vote.
Registered voters are sorted into two categories, “active” and “inactive,” as part of standard voter list maintenance practices. Marking voters as “inactive” is the first step election officials must take in order to remove voters who they suspect have moved away, died, or otherwise become ineligible to vote.
However, federal law restricts how quickly states can remove voters from the rolls and how close to an election officials can conduct routine voter list maintenance, meaning that states must wait years before removing most inactive voters from the rolls. There are some exceptions, such as if a county registrar receives proof that a voter has died, or if a voter reaches out and requests that their registration be removed from the rolls. But in most cases, it takes about eight years for a voter to go from actively registered to eligible for removal.
If you haven’t voted in two consecutive federal elections (such as presidential or midterm elections), you may be moved to inactive status. Once a voter is marked as inactive, they aren’t eligible to be removed from the voter rolls unless they do not vote for the next two federal election cycles. 
However, inactive voters are still registered and are therefore eligible to cast a ballot. Showing up to a polling place and voting will automatically restore an inactive voter to active status.
My voter status is marked as “challenged.” What should I do?
In addition to conducting routine voter list maintenance, state law also allows individuals to contest the voter registration status of individual Georgians if they have evidence that someone is improperly registered.
Groups readying mass voter challenges in Georgia’s 2024 elections. There’s an app for that.

Any registered Georgia voter can challenge an unlimited number of voters who live in their county, and digital tools like EagleAI and ELLY make it easier for users to browse through a wide range of publicly available databases and lodge challenges against voters they believe to be ineligible. Over 63,000 voters were challenged within the span of a few months during the 2024 election cycle, according to an investigation from the Associated Press.
Joseph Kirk, the Bartow County elections director and past president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, said residents should receive a letter from their county election office to notify them if their registration is challenged. He also encouraged voters in “challenged” status to contact their county’s elections office to resolve any issues with their registration.
The solution, he said, “could be filling out a form, it could be a new application, it could be some kind of documentation,” Kirk said. “There are a few different reasons you could be in that status, and the best way to find out what to do next is to call your local office.”

name: National
title: Misinformation, hesitancy could blunt impact of new cancer vaccines
description: Nearly five years ago, Chase Johnson was cured of breast cancer — but not of the profound anxiety that it would return. When Johnson was originally diagnosed in 2021, the resident of Cary, North Carolina, was only 31 — nearly a decade away from the age at which regular mammograms are recommended — and she […]
text:
Chase Johnson of Cary, North Carolina, is among the cancer survivors and patients participating in a clinical trial for a new breast cancer vaccine. New cancer vaccines could be coming, but doctors and researchers are worried that rising vaccine hesitancy, fueled in part by the Trump administration, could blunt their impact. (Photo courtesy of Chase Johnson)Nearly five years ago, Chase Johnson was cured of breast cancer — but not of the profound anxiety that it would return.
When Johnson was originally diagnosed in 2021, the resident of Cary, North Carolina, was only 31 — nearly a decade away from the age at which regular mammograms are recommended — and she had no history of breast cancer in her family. She only got screened because her dog, Cato, kept poking her chest with his nose, which helped her discover a lump.
Doctors discovered that Johnson had stage 2B triple-negative breast cancer, a rare and aggressive form. They treated her with chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, and in 2022, they declared her cancer free. Her oncologist warned her, however, that there was a 40% chance the cancer would return.
Anxious about that prospect, Johnson enrolled in a clinical trial at the Cleveland Clinic testing a new breast cancer vaccine. That vaccine has shown positive early results: In nearly three-quarters of the participants, including Johnson, it has generated an immune response.
“It’s just so promising and as a patient, it gave me a lot of hope,” said Johnson, now 37. “I feel much more protected having done it.”
In the past two decades, there has been steady progress in developing vaccines for cancer. The vaccine Johnson is taking isn’t one of them, but researchers are especially excited about the potential of mRNA vaccines, which use synthetic genetic instructions to teach a person’s immune system how to recognize and destroy unique proteins found on cancer cells.
Just last month, pharmaceutical companies Moderna and Merck announced that a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, combined with an immunotherapy drug, had succeeded in a late-stage trial for skin cancer. The news raised hopes that a wave of new cancer vaccines could be just over the horizon.
But will Americans be willing to take them?
Many doctors and researchers are concerned that vaccine misinformation — amplified by the Trump administration — and the resulting increase in vaccine hesitancy could blunt the impact of the new vaccines. In particular, they cite the false claim, which originated with mRNA COVID vaccines, that mRNA vaccines can super-charge tumors, creating so-called turbo cancer. 
Many point to the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine is a cautionary tale.
Some strains of HPV, which is spread through sexual contact, can cause cancer of the cervix, vagina, vulva, penis, anus, mouth, throat, head or neck. In 2006, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved an HPV vaccine for girls and women ages 9 to 26, and three years later the agency expanded approval to include boys and young men. Ideally, vaccination should occur before a person is sexually active.
The HPV vaccine is safe and extremely effective. But decades of misinformation, some of it spread by state and federal lawmakers, has reduced uptake: For four years in a row, vaccination rates for teenagers have not budged, and there is wide variation among states.
“I don’t think we can overstate the impact that the pandemic and the misinformation and disinformation around vaccines has had on all vaccines, including HPV vaccine,” said Dannell Boatman, an assistant professor at the West Virginia University Cancer Institute.
Trump vaccine order takes aim at states that limit exemptions

A 2024 study Boatman co-authored, funded by Merck, found that the HPV misinformation on social media platforms was most pervasive in the users’ comments.
“There were some really wild conspiracy theories about girls in India being killed with the HPV vaccine,” Boatman said. “We also were able to identify a lot of mistrust of authority.”
Boatman said she expects a similar dynamic with breast cancer vaccines, especially since some people already are spreading misinformation that mammograms can cause cancer. But she hopes an ongoing study on “inoculation theory” will help researchers combat false claims.
“Basically, you forewarn someone that they’re going to be exposed to misinformation,” she said, “and then you refute it or provide them just a little bit of evidence about why it doesn’t work.”
History of lawsuits
Before he joined the Trump administration, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. filed complaints and lawsuits against Merck, the maker of the HPV vaccine, and claimed on social media that the “vaccine appears to be increasing the risk of cervical cancer in vaccinated age groups just as COVID vaccines raise the risk of COVID.”
Early in his tenure, Kennedy dismissed all 17 members of the HHS vaccine advisory panel, replacing some of them with vaccine skeptics. Under his leadership, HHS also has altered the child vaccine schedule for certain diseases, including HPV. So far, those changes have been blocked in federal court.
HHS did not respond to a Stateline request for comment.
Last month, after signing an executive order separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots, Republican President Donald Trump suggested, falsely, that each individual vaccine could fill a “bottle of soda.” The administration has also proposed cutting funding for vaccine research and studies on vaccine hesitancy.
Epidemiologist Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, said Kennedy’s appointment spurred the creation of the Vaccine Integrity Project, a partnership between the center and the American Medical Association that tries to bolster public trust in vaccines. The project has published evidence reviews of some of the vaccines criticized by the Trump administration.
“To a young parent today who wants to do the right thing, they want to protect their child, they’re so confused because they hear from the leaders in public health in their government talk about these vaccines killing people,” Osterholm said.
“The credibility of 80 years of public health work of vaccines in this country is threatened because of confusion.”
In May, the center published an evidence review showing that HPV vaccines are not associated with serious side effects and reduce the risk of cervical cancer by 80% in minors who are vaccinated by age 16, and by 66% in people vaccinated after 16.
Resistance from state lawmakers 
But the HPV vaccine has long faced resistance from some conservative lawmakers, who associate it with teen sex.
Last year, 78% of U.S. teenagers ages 13-17 had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine and 63% had completed the full HPV vaccination series. But in some conservative-leaning states, the rates were much lower: The complete vaccination rate in Mississippi was only 31%. Oklahoma (46%), Kentucky (50%), Arkansas (52%) and South Carolina (55%) also had particularly low rates.
At the other end of the spectrum were Rhode Island (85%), Hawaii (82%) and Massachusetts (80%).
Some states, including Alabama and Oregon, have made recent efforts to boost their  HPV vaccine rates.
But other states, including Iowa, have enacted laws limiting access to the HPV vaccine.  Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds in May signed a law prohibiting Iowans under 18 from consenting to vaccinations related to sexually transmitted diseases and infections, including HPV.
Democratic governors launch multistate public health alliance to counter Trump, RFK Jr.

Idaho Democratic state Rep. Brooke Green said anti-vaccine sentiment is increasing among residents of her state — and among her legislative colleagues. As a survivor of breast cancer, Green is excited about the prospect of new cancer vaccines, but she fears that rising hesitancy could be hurdle to widespread adoption.
She noted that Idaho Republicans introduced a bill this year that would have established a two-year moratorium on mRNA immunizations for children and pregnant women. Similar bills were introduced in at least a dozen other states, though none were enacted.
This year, lawmakers in 34 states introduced 209 bills seeking to loosen vaccination rules, limit access to certain kinds of vaccines or sow doubt about their safety, according to a recent analysis by The New York Times.
“We are seeing several attempts to address some of the scientific tools that are used to create vaccines, mRNA vaccines and so forth,” Green said. “As a cancer patient, these are life-saving tools that are helping us.”
“I’m thrilled to see these new innovative advancements in medicine for these vaccines. Now, is it going to be widely accepted?” said Green, who was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2024, a week before her mother was diagnosed with the same cancer.
“There will be some hesitation and some pushback. But look at the flip side: ‘Do you want breast cancer or do you not? Do you want skin cancer? Do you not?’”
Chase Johnson, meanwhile, said her anxiety has significantly decreased, especially after celebrating five years in remission this summer.
“I think I’ll always have some sort of low-grade anxiety about it,” Johnson said. “But it’s definitely at a much lower level than it was before vaccination. It’s given me a great, great amount of peace of mind.”
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Is Jackson’s ‘Intelligent Medicaid Expansion’ weak tea – or a revolutionary fix?
description: A high-stakes mystery is unfolding in the Georgia governor’s race, potentially affecting health insurance for hundreds of thousands of Georgians. Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson released a major policy announcement last week supporting “intelligent Medicaid expansion.” But Medicaid expansion to all a state’s poor is no longer possible under Pre[...]
text:
Republican candidate for Georgia governor Rick Jackson's health plan could modernize a system that many call dysfunctional, but experts await specific details, some worry it could spread that dysfunction to hundreds of thousands of Georgians insured under the Affordable Care Act. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderA high-stakes mystery is unfolding in the Georgia governor’s race, potentially affecting health insurance for hundreds of thousands of Georgians.
Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson released a major policy announcement last week supporting “intelligent Medicaid expansion.” But Medicaid expansion to all a state’s poor is no longer possible under President Donald Trump’s new One Big, Beautiful Bill law, and Jackson’s team says details are still undetermined. So what exactly will this do?
“We haven’t seen a detailed proposal yet; it’s not 100% clear how this is going to work,” said Leo Cuello, an expert in Medicaid expansion law at Georgetown University. He said that after viewing Jackson’s list of bullet points on the issue and some remarks by Jackson at the event sent to him by a reporter.
From what Jackson said, there is a range of possibilities, though, and they could help or hurt hundreds of thousands of Georgians trying to get or renew coverage.
It is clear that his plan will seek more federal money. In the process, will it seek to close the coverage gap of perhaps 200,000 poor Georgia adults who lack health insurance? Jackson said he would close the coverage gap, but federal law now makes the full scope of that impossible.
So, just a portion of those people? How big a portion?
Importantly, will his plan fix Georgia’s defective paperwork systems that help keep many poor adults who work from getting Medicaid?
Or – potentially a huge concern for coverage advocates – will it turn Georgia’s current work verification bureaucracy on hundreds of thousands of other Georgians, potentially knocking many off their private health insurance if their paperwork falls through the cracks?
Reporters for the Georgia Recorder drilled down on those questions in several exchanges with Jackson’s campaign spokesman, Garrison Douglas. Douglas replied in a text message, “The details of this will be worked out through the waiver negotiation process (with the Trump administration) and with the General Assembly.”
 The Jackson Action Plan

Jackson named his policies the “Jackson Action Plan,” and sketched them out at a campaign event last week at a Perimeter hotel conference room. The Jackson Action Plan included principles on taxes, housing, jobs, education, government, public safety, and three pages of goals on health care.
A headline moment came midway through his speech: “On day one, I will close the coverage gap with intelligent Medicaid expansion.”
Trump’s first Secretary of Health and Human Services, Tom Price, was in the audience, and afterwards called Jackson’s plan “exciting.”
“He believes he can close the coverage gap right away, and with a (state-specific plan), and I believe that that’s possible as well,” Price said.
Traditionally, that would mean Jackson would offer health insurance to all uninsured poor people who fall in a gap between other programs. It comes with a big extra federal check to pay for it. It’s been the quest of Democrats from Stacey Abrams, who ran against Gov. Brian Kemp on expanding Medicaid, to Keisha Lance Bottoms, Jackson’s opponent.
If she’s elected governor, Bottoms says she will fully expand Medicaid to cover Georgians earning about $22,000 a year for a household of one, or 138% of the federal poverty level.
Jackson did say he is requesting the extra check.
But there’s a snag. The One Big, Beautiful Bill law passed last year by Congress and President Donald Trump says that Medicaid expansion and the extra federal money that comes with it now must include work and activity requirements, similar to the ones Georgia already has in place under Gov. Brian Kemp. And in Georgia, history shows that requirement – as well as the mere paperwork it takes – is a barrier even for eligible people.
Under Kemp’s Pathways to Coverage Medicaid expansion with work and activity requirements, compared to perhaps 100,000 Georgians that Kemp aides thought would be eligible, 18,000 are actually enrolled.
People who navigate the Georgia system suspect a major culprit is the bureaucracy of the eligibility checking itself, with its glitchy computer system and swamped customer assistance.
“It’s important for people to understand how suppressive the Georgia Pathways model has been,” Cuello said.  “It’s an abysmal failure at covering people in poverty, by any measure. To say that we are going to bring that to somewhere else? That does not seem like a good idea.”
 Could ACA policyholders be subject to work verification requirements? 

The “somewhere else” Cuello referred to concerns another big group of Georgians, these ones on private insurance plans.
There are currently about 500,000 or so low-income Georgians on Affordable Care Act plans, private insurance subsidized by the government under the Georgia Access ACA marketplace. If Kemp had expanded Medicaid, they would have gotten Medicaid instead.
Those subsidized plans proved wildly popular as they got cheaper under pandemic-era subsidies. Even after the subsidies expired and low-income enrollment in the plans slid from 700,000 Georgians, it’s still substantial at 500,000.
Kemp and his aides have long pushed back at criticisms like Cuello’s by changing the focus to that group. Kemp points to those people getting federal help for private plans as part of the benefit he delivered with his restraint.
Those 500,000 ACA policyholders are not below the poverty line like the Pathways recipients, but just barely above it.  That means making, for example, more than about $16,000 per year but less than about $22,000 per year, for a household of one.
In the 40 states that expanded Medicaid, people in that income group are about to have to meet Trump’s work requirements to keep their Medicaid.
Not in Georgia. But would that change if Jackson got the Trump administration to call that group covered as part of Georgia’s Medicaid expansion strategy?  Jackson is asking for the federal government to put Medicaid dollars toward some private insurance plans. “Medicaid resources should help Georgians keep or obtain private coverage,” his proposal says.
Garrison, the spokesman for Jackson, did not say whether the ACA policyholders could be subject to filing work eligibility paperwork with the system.
“It is not something Rick has announced. Rick laid out a vision of closing the coverage gap, eliminat(ing) burdens that inhibit successful enrollment and ensuring that we do so in a way that does not  remove access to private coverage for half a million Georgians in the 100-138% FPL window,” Douglas said.
He noted that Bottoms’ plan to fully expand Medicaid would do exactly that, though, shifting them to Medicaid.
 Plenty of room for improvement to current system

Leah Chan, who closely follows Medicaid expansion rules and Pathways as director of health justice at the Georgia Budget and Policy Institute, echoed Cuello’s concerns with the functioning of the eligibility system.
But Chan, an advocate for Medicaid expansion, also cheered another possibility in Jackson’s plan. What if the notorious Georgia Medicaid computer portal and eligibility bureaucracy actually actually worked like a charm?
Chan homed in on a line deep in the Jackson Action Plan reading “Reduce paperwork barriers that keep eligible Georgians from care. Enrollment and renewal should be clear, modern, and accountable, not a maze that causes eligible people to lose coverage because a form was missed.” The problems with the system are well known.
“When we talk about day one priorities, that should be top of the list,” she said.
Chan said the current outdated system works to undermine Pathways and other Georgia public assistance programs.
For eligible people who are trying to enroll or renew, “it’s basically like having a part-time job to navigate,” Chan noted, from faulty technology to overburdened caseworkers who never call back, to rural offices that aren’t even staffed with on-site caseworkers but with people who take messages.
“We still don’t have, I think, a clear explanation for why everybody was kicked off the (Georgia disabled children category) at Medicaid earlier this year. Just some sort of technology glitch,” she said.
When it comes to renewing paperwork to show a person met the work requirement for the Pathways Medicaid program, Chan said, “a high proportion of them are being denied because of, like, a missing form.”
“A win for anyone coming into office would be modernizing that system,” she said. “It would help everyone,” the entire Georgia Medicaid population and the workers who deal with them, she said.
Leaders have chipped away at fixes to the system, and allocated some money to starting. But a replacement technology system to manage the 1.8 million-strong Medicaid population could be hugely expensive.
Chan stressed that she can’t be sure which level of fix Jackson is proposing – until more information comes out.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Budget officials ask agencies to tighten belts, including a 10% cut scenario
description: State agencies are being asked to tighten their belts ahead of a coming difficult fiscal year. Administration emails told agency heads to include reductions of roughly 3% in their fiscal 2028 requests, with two dozen agencies told to outline reductions up to 10%.
text:
Budget Secretary Yaakov "Jake" Weissmann, in a January photo with Gov. Wes Moore, said asking agencies for up to 10% in cuts for next year's budget planning is a "prudent approach" to the state's ongoing fiscal problems. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)State agencies are being asked to tighten their belts as they finalize budget requests for the coming difficult fiscal year.
Emails to every executive branch agency, as well as state universities, told them to prepare fiscal 2028 budget requests that include reductions of roughly 3%, with two dozen Cabinet-level agencies told to prepare budgets with up to 10% reductions.
The memos come as the state heads into a 2027 General Assembly session in January that will be dominated by efforts to eliminate a projected structural budget gap of about $3 billion in the coming fiscal year, with wider gaps predicted in coming years.
“We’re having these conversations and having the tough conversations, and we’re going to continue to,” said State Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann. “They’re going to have to be genuinely tough decisions that are going to make impacts on how the budget is taken. Hopefully, this sets us on course for the next 20 years if we do this right.”
Lawmakers left Annapolis after the last session with a balanced budget — a legal requirement. Even so, the state faces troubling structural gaps, with projected revenues falling short of expected spending.
Any cuts will have to come from the state’s general fund spending. For context, Weissmann said cutting everything but health, education, public safety and human services spending would not be enough.
State Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann speaks to Senate Budget and Taxation Chair Sen. Guy Guzzone in a March budget meeting. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“That’s the magnitude of the problem that we’re facing,” he said. “Asking agencies to share what a 10% cut looks like is just a prudent approach to figuring out how we solve this budget shortfall.”
Not all the news is bad. A recent report released by Comptroller Brooke Lierman showed the state closed fiscal 2026 with hundreds of millions more in surplus than expected.
Senate Budget and Taxation Committee Chair Sen. Guy Guzzone (D-Howard) said the better-than-expected report to end the last fiscal year could be an indicator of more good news to come. But fiscal leaders will still be monitoring a Sept. 24 Board of Revenue Estimates meeting to gauge how the state’s revenues are faring.
“It doesn’t have an effect on BRE [Board of Revenue Estimates],” Guzzone said of the comptroller’s report. “But what led to that? What led to the good closeout numbers should also play a role … as we move forward.”
Weissmann said the state has made “significant inroads” into the state’s recurring deficits “because of the work we’ve done over the last couple years. We have done that work. The obstacles we’re facing this year are different in that regard.”
The Department of Legislative Services in June projected a nearly $2.6 billion structural gap in the fiscal 2028 budget — about $150 million lower than a December estimate. The Department of Budget and Management’s email to agencies said budget officials are “carrying a (projected deficit) figure of closer to $3 billion.”
Pulling back on aspirations
Fiscal 2028 is also the first year in which costs of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future education plan will exceed dedicated revenues. To cover the balance, the state will have to dip into the general fund, as a first-in-the-nation digital ad tax meant to help pay for the education plan remains in legal limbo.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Maryland’s $71 billion total budget includes just under $30 billion in general funds — money collected directly by the state through sources including personal and corporate income taxes and sales taxes.
The amount needed from the general fund is expected to grow in following years, with gaps of roughly $3.4 billion projected in each of the following two fiscal years.
The state’s “sizable and growing out-year budget gaps” were cited by bond rating agency Standard & Poor’s in May when it downgraded the outlook on the state’s debt.
“It is our understanding that, ahead of the January 2027 fiscal 2028 budget introduction, the state intends to establish a consensus budget framework that will meaningfully address these gaps through structural adjustments that better align revenues with spending, which will be critical, in our view, to maintain the state rating,” S&P wrote.
Guzzone the state has “always lived within our means,” but that recent budgets “had higher hopes for where we would be by now.”
“The reality is, the economy, the federal government, lots of different forces have put us in a place where we are not where we thought we would be,” he said. “We thought we would have been better off.
Senate Budget and Taxation Chair Sen. Guy Guzzone (D-Howard). (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“We have to pull back on some of our expectations now because it is clear those aspirations are not going to be able to be met at the levels we had hoped they would be met,” Guzzone said.
Slowing spending on the Blueprint could be part of the discussion. Administration officials also point to salary growth as a driving factor in the budget growth.
A 10% solution?
Weissmann declined to say if the administration had a target amount it was looking for from cuts.
Individual targets were laid out in agency memos. For some, the reductions represent actual cuts to current budgets, for others, it’s a reduction of increased spending.
Budget officials will review each proposed reduction. Not all will be accepted.
Weissmann said such target memos are part of the annual budget drafting process.
“We did this last year, right? The 3% reduction isn’t new. The 10% reduction is,” Weissmann said.
“The 10% gives us this big picture so we know what we’re walking into and we can have those conversations,” he said.
A 10% cut would also close the $3 billion gap in general fund spending and close the structural gap.
Earlier this year, an email to those departments requested a “short memo outlining the reductions your agency would need to take to absorb a 10% reduction in your GF (General Fund) budget.” The emails said the department memos would “help provide some perspective on what balancing the budget solely through reductions would look like.”
Budget officials asked that the memos — due at the end of July — include information on how such cuts would impact programs, operations and staffing, and how they would affect “services and support provided to Marylanders.”
Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) welcomed the move, but said the 10% budget request could also be used as “political cover rather than a governing plan.”
“The governor can say, ‘I asked agencies for cuts,’ knowing the General Assembly would rather find another tax or fee than make many of those difficult decisions,” Hershey said. “If he’s serious about 10%, show us the plan, identify the programs that aren’t working, and then fight for those reductions during the legislative session.”
‘All options are on the table’
House Appropriations Chair Ben Barnes (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel). (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Del. Ben Barnes (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), chair of the House Appropriations Committee, said it’s “no surprise to the House that the governor is taking a look at cuts.”
“I believe that for the Speaker and for the entire House, all options are on the table,” he said. “I think that we are committed, and I think our partners in the Senate and the governor’s office are as well, to tackling not just any shortfalls this year, but the out-year shortfall head-on this session.”
One option — taxes — is difficult to discuss in an election year, but it is also one that can be politically tempting in the first year of a term, which 2027 will be.
There are a number of potential tax options.
Some, such as a sales tax increase, would be easiest to implement. New taxes, like the recently passed IT and data tax, take longer to implement, which means the money might not available for near-term problems.
Maryland has not raised its sales tax since 2008, when it went from 5% to 6%. Going from 6% to 7% — a penny on the dollar — could generate an additional $1.2 billion.
In 2020, lawmakers considered a bill to lower the sales tax to 5% but expand it to most services, which would have raised an extra $2.6 billion. That bill did not get out of committee. A 2024 bill to expand sales tax to all services also failed.
But sales taxes are seen as regressive, as they hit lower-income families harder, proportionally, than higher-income taxpayers. Progressives — who control the House — could revisit the Fair Share Act, a 2024 package that included changes to corporate income tax reporting, increased taxes on the wealthiest residents, more auditors and increased capital gains surcharges.
That package would have raised $1.6 billion, but while there was support in the House, the Senate dismissed it out of hand.
“Our first reaction is always, always to see what kinds of cuts, or slowing down of growth in various programs can be made,” said Guzzone. “That is number one.”
‘Acknowledging… a spending problem’
Gov. Wes Moore in past years rejected calls for across-the-board budget cuts, calling such cuts “lazy” last year and saying last year he favored a nuanced and targeted approach.
Senate Minority Leader Sen. Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore). (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
While that might seem at odds with the current set of budget memos, a spokesperson said both efforts are parts of an ongoing analysis that will help craft the spending plan that will be sent to lawmakers in January.
“This evaluation is a continuation of Governor Moore’s approach to fiscal discipline,” said  Rhyan Lake, the spokesperson, in an email. “After inheriting long-standing structural budget challenges compounded by the Trump administration’s hits on Maryland’s economy, closing next year’s deficit will require a targeted look at where the state can save — and this analysis is part of that process.”
Hershey said he was “glad the administration is finally acknowledging Maryland has a spending problem and meaningful cuts are necessary.”
An across-the-board cut “isn’t strategy,” he said, since it “treats every dollar of spending as equally valuable. It isn’t.”
Hershey called for an approach that examines spending to see what can be protected, reformed or eliminated.
“The goal shouldn’t be to make government 3% cheaper. It should be to make government smaller, smarter, and more accountable,” he said.

title: ‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all
description: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “autonomous collective” scene from the 1975 film “Monty Python and the Holy Grail.” The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the […[...]
text:
Left to right, Andrew Garfield as Ploughman, Jamie Bell as John Ball and Thomasin McKenzie as Alyce in director Paul Greengrass' 'The Uprising,' released Sept. 10, 2026. (Courtesy of Focus Features. ©2026. All Rights Reserved.)This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “autonomous collective” scene from the 1975 film “Monty Python and the Holy Grail.”
The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the lexicon of a modern political Marxist. When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!”
It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.
But far from being an age of unquestioning obedience, the Middle Ages – the period from roughly 500 to 1500 – witnessed a remarkable number of popular revolts and collective political action.
Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then held strong views about the working of political authority. And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites.
 Enough is enough

In the 11th and 12th centuries, northern French peasants famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed.
But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, the subject of the new film “The Uprising,” starring Andrew Garfield.
After the first wave of the Black Death in 1348 created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers were better positioned to negotiate for higher wages and better conditions. Serfs – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations.
But kings and lords resisted change. In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the Statute of Laborers, which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class. Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague.
Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time tax of 12 pence to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France. Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families.
The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords. They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king.
The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land.
He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising.
Left to right, Tom Hollander as Treasurer Hales, Woody Norman as King RIchard II and Katherine Waterston as The Countess in ‘The Uprising.’ (Betina La Plante/Focus Features. ©2026. All Rights Reserved.)
 A tradition of collective action

Insurrections like the English Peasants’ Revolt erupted, in part, because in cities across Europe, regular people had cultivated a strong tradition of collective action. There was broad membership in guilds, which were voluntary associations of merchants and craftsmen. Then there were neighborhood religious confraternities, which were akin to today’s religious mutual-aid societies. Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances.
Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority. People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford. Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats.

In 1358, the Jacques – a derogatory name for members of the lower French peasantry – razed noble estates and killed members of the aristocracy. They also joined forces with the Parisian bourgeoisie and the city’s chief political leader, Étienne Marcel, to fight for a greater voice in French government.
The rage underpinning the violence of what became known as the Jacquerie emerged from the fact that the same aristocracy that demanded so much of them could not fulfill their basic part of the bargain: protect them.
A little over a decade later, violence erupted in Florence, Italy. The city-state was an industrial juggernaut ruled by guilds, but their representatives all belonged to the urban elite. The lower classes of the textile industry weren’t represented by guilds and were largely disenfranchised. So the Ciompi – low-level woolworkers – demanded a role in the guild system. Those demands fell on deaf ears.
In June 1378, the Ciompi revolted and attacked government offices. Thanks to their efforts, they won participation in the guild system for four years, up until the city’s old powerful merchant elite dissolved their lower guilds.
 Contesting the church

Nor was the other main source of authority, the church, immune to attack.
When power vacuums emerged after the death of an abbot, bishop or even the pope, regular people routinely ransacked their property, taking with them a substantial amount of the dead’s movables.
As cardinal Peter Damian wrote in 1050:
“From various reports we are aware of the perverse and wholly detestable practice of certain people, who at the death of the bishop break in like enemies and rob his house, like thieves make off with his belongings, set fire to the homes on his estate, and with fierce and savage barbarity cut down his grape vines and orchards.”
Early Christian elections were initially open to entire congregations. Though these elections often gave the lion’s share of voting power to the wealthy and well-connected, there was the general understanding that everyone would play a role: “vox populi, vox Dei,” or “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”
However, by the end of the 13th century, the papacy had successfully established its authority over both ordinary people and secular rulers. On religious matters, there would no longer be public input. Instead, beginning in 1274, a conclave of cardinals elected the pope. The pope, sometimes still under the influence of higher lords, then nominated abbots and bishops.
The voice of the people had largely vanished. Nevertheless, they made themselves heard.
An April 1314 papal election in Carpentras, a small city in southeastern France, turned so violent that it delayed the naming of a new pope for nearly two years.
Deadlocked over the candidates, the cardinals dragged out the election for so long that frustrated locals attacked the episcopal palace where the conclave was being held. Cardinals and their staff fled and delayed until August 1316, when, under the protection of the French king’s forces, they nominated Pope John XXII.

A 16th-century engraving of Pope Urban VI by Onofrio Panvinio. (Wikimedia Commons)
Over 60 years later, in March 1378, Pope Gregory XI died. Amid threats from a crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected Urban VI, an Italian, the following month. But over the ensuing months, the cardinals soured on Urban and declared their election invalid on the grounds that they had acted under duress. They elected a rival pope, triggering the Great Western Schism, during which two competing papal courts existed from 1378 to 1417.
Violence could also erupt for seemingly minor affronts.
In October 1367, Pope Urban V was in Viterbo, Italy. The pope and his court were French. The Viterbese took offense when papal court officials washed a little dog in their fountain of Piano di Scarano, which served as a source of drinking water. A confrontation followed, which escalated into a two-day uprising. The fountain was destroyed, and the pope and his cardinals were forced to take refuge in the Rocca Albornoz, the papal fortress.
 Authority is a two-way street

Ideologies have evolved and technologies have advanced, but the fundamental struggle over who wields power, how authority earns legitimacy, and how compliance is enforced remains strikingly familiar.
The levers that leaders pull – taxation, welfare, infrastructure projects, propaganda, law enforcement – are largely the same, too.
Yet medieval folks understood that authority was a two-way street. When those in power didn’t hold up their end of the bargain, they were quick to resist, demand accountability and challenge authority.
In this sparring over power and consent, we can see, as one of Monty Python’s peasants put it, “the violence inherent in the system.”
 

  ‘Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses!’

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Here’s what goes into your electricity bill — and what could change
description: Amid fierce customer pushback to high electricity bills and increasingly frequent hikes, Indiana officials are reconsidering utility risks, profits and key charges in a bid to bring prices down — ahead of a major regulatory transition.
text:
Indiana utility bills have base charges, taxes and more. See how they might be changing in the future. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)What’s in your utility bill?
Amid fierce customer pushback to high electricity bills and increasingly frequent hikes, Indiana officials are reconsidering utility risks, profits and key charges in a bid to bring prices down — ahead of a major regulatory transition.
Five large investor-owned utilities serve roughly 80% of Indiana electricity customers: AES Indiana, CenterPoint Energy Indiana South, Duke Energy Indiana, Indiana Michigan Power Co. and the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. They are monopolies in their service areas in exchange for submitting to state regulators.
The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, or IURC, decides how much they’ll assess customers based on evidence from the companies themselves, customer advocates and other stakeholders.
Here’s what goes into what you owe.
Fixed charges
All residential customers pay a service or facilities charge that stays flat no matter the amount of electricity used.
It’s intended to spread out the cost of servicing ratepayers, like meter readings, bill preparation and customer service.
The charge ranges from CenterPoint’s $11 at the low end to AES’ $17 at the high end.
AES Indiana President Brandi Davis-Handy answers Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission questions on Tuesday, March 24, 2026, at the agency’s headquarters in Indianapolis. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Variable usage
Next up is the amount owed for the actual electricity consumed. This is the part of a bill impacted by base rates.
Regulators have agreed to reconsider the $71 million base rate increase approved for AES in June. CenterPoint, Duke and NIPSCO all received approval for base rate hikes last year, while I&M’s base rates date back to 2024.
Under the outgoing system, utilities generally can’t file for an increase to their base rates sooner than 15 months since their last request for a base rate hike was filed. But that’s changing.
Lawmakers and Gov. Mike Braun approved House Enrolled Act 1002 in March. Regulators will set base rates and schedule increases over a three-year period under the new system. Utilities may earn more or less money from customers depending how well they perform on affordability and post-outage service restoration metrics.
Duke Energy Indiana home energy use reports. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Duke, as the utility with the most customers, must petition first under this setup by mid-December. The rest will follow under a schedule laid out in statute.
“The worst-case scenario I envision under the multi-year rate making platform structure that we have now is adhering to the status quo,” said Sarah Freeman, who left the IURC last year after nine years as a regulator. 
She now works as a principal for the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nongovernmental organization focused on the U.S. and the world’s other largest energy markets.
“By that, I mean a situation in which a utility complies with the multi-year rate plan and performance incentive statutes and does not roll in all of their trackers,” Freeman continued. “That, on a bill, would very likely look the same as what bills look like now.”
Trackers
Bills also carry a list of rate adjustment mechanisms — also called trackers or riders — that allow utilities to recover costs from customers in between base rate cases.
Some providers offer a “detailed” bill with a list of every charge, including trackers; others don’t. But the breakdown must be provided upon request, Freeman said.
Trackers generally fall into capital and operational expenditures.
All five investor-owned utilities have a transmission, distribution and storage system improvement charge.
They’re part of five- or seven-year infrastructure plans, with 80% of the costs recovered from the tracker and the rest deferred to the utility’s next base rate case.
Freeman was a staff attorney working on utility law at the Legislative Services Agency when the TDSIC statute was enacted in 2013.
“When TDSIC came about, I would say that rate cases were more spread out than they are now,” she said. “And this was a way to incentivize a slightly tighter timeframe, while ensuring that projects intended to address reliability concerns were happening and being paid for in a timely manner.” 


Demand side management is another capital tracker that pays for the new lights, appliances and more offered to help customers reduce energy usage — and make up for the revenue lost to those efficiency measures.
The utilities also have trackers for federally mandated investments.
Some capital trackers could be rolled into base rates in the coming years, however.
In their first multi-year rate submissions, the utilities must submit plans for incorporating planned capital expenditures into their subsequent rate proposals.
The hardest-hitting tracker for customers, however, is an operational one called the fuel adjustment clause.
Utilities set fuel costs in their base rates, but jumps and dips beyond that are collected or returned to customers at levels that can change every three to six months.
It’s a passthrough, meaning that utilities don’t profit off the changes.
New Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission leader Anthony Swinger announces a pair of affordability investigations on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Other operational trackers account for the money utilities spend to be part of regional transmission organizations, as well as the energy they buy and sell on regional markets.
The IURC has launched two investigations to prepare for the onset of multi-year rate plans, including one on changes in risk — and therefore to regulated profits — and another on how both kinds of trackers will fit into the new system.
“The investigation … will consider the development of guidelines for the commission, utilities and additional parties to use in evaluating the role that expense trackers and capital trackers will play within the (new) regulatory framework,” IURC Chair Anthony Swinger said at a technical conference last month.
Utilities don’t have all the same variable costs.
CenterPoint, for instance, has several charges for securitization to retire generation plants.
Sales tax
Indiana’s 7% sales tax applies to utility service. This is another passthrough to customers.
The IURC, in an affordability report released in July, asked the General Assembly to consider repealing the sales tax for utility bills.
But such legislation, largely sought by Democratic lawmakers, has failed repeatedly in the past — despite supportive sentiment from across the aisle. Some officials, including Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, have publicly backed ditching it.
But that elimination would cost the state $615 million annually in tax revenue.
