name: Florida Phoenix
title: Still no answers from DeSantis administration on KidCare disenrollments, challenges
description: The administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis is still not giving firm answers on when — or whether — it intends to expand a safety-net healthcare program for low-income children that the Florida Legislature has approved. A bipartisan pair of state senators pushed a top official with the Agency for Health Care Administration Friday for answers […]
text:
The DeSantis administration continues to stall  the implementation of a 2023 law that would make Florida KidCare coverage available to more children. (Photo via Getty Images)The administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis is still not giving firm answers on when — or whether — it intends to expand a safety-net healthcare program for low-income children that the Florida Legislature has approved.
A bipartisan pair of state senators pushed a top official with the Agency for Health Care Administration Friday for answers on an two-year legal tussle between the governor’s office and the federal government over providing healthcare access to children in lower-income households.
At the heart of the debate is a requirement that children who qualify for Medicaid-funded healthcare remain continuously eligible for one year, including the children’s health insurance program, dubbed Florida KidCare. 
The delay in expanding eligibility started when Democrat Joe Biden was in office but has continued during the Trump administration, with Florida filing a new lawsuit, at least its third, earlier this year in the dispute.
Lori Berman (Photo via Florida Senate)
“What are you doing?” asked Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman. “What is AHCA doing to resolve this issue?”
Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Stuart Republican, noted “it has been more than three years” since the Legislature first signed off on expanding KidCare eligibility.
The issue came up during a meeting of the Joint Legislative Budget Commission, which approves mid-fiscal year budget amendments, because AHCA was asking to shift money around to conform the Florida KidCare program with current spending estimates.
But one top AHCA official, citing ongoing litigation, was unable to say when he expected the case to be resolved and when income eligibility for the program would expand per the law. Families must earn 200% of the federal poverty level to qualify, $66,000 annually for a family of four in 2026.
Championed by former Republican House Speaker Paul Renner, the law expanded income eligibility to children living in families that earn 300% of the federal poverty level, or $99,000 for a family of four. 
Several Democrats on the panel voted against the budget amendment being sought by AHCA.
“There’s too much uncertainty regarding what we are doing,” Berman said. “There’s a lot of unanswered questions.”
 What’s going on

The DeSantis administration has filed at least three lawsuits against  the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, one which still is being litigated in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida in Pensacola. 
“We’re working through that process as much as we can and working with the attorneys to resolve this case,” Jon Manalo, deputy secretary for AHCA, told members of the panel when asked about the litigation.
Another AHCA official was unable to answer Berman’s questions about whether the state is still removing children from the KidCare program for failing to pay monthly premiums — the issue at the center of the dispute between the state and federal government.
Top AHCA officials have been unable to publicly answer legislators’ questions about the number of children disenrolled during the legal dispute or, when they have answered questions, provided misleading or inaccurate information.
When senators asked in October 2025 how many children the state removed from KidCare for failing to pay premiums, Brian Meyer, who headed Medicaid at the time, said he didn’t know. 
The Florida Healthy Kids Corp. (which helps administer Florida KidCare) subsequently told the Phoenix that more than 17,000 children were disenrolled for failing to pay premiums. But that information was incorrect. The state removed more than 43,000 children over 12 months for that reason.
Meyer testified before the Senate six month later that he had been having conversations with CMS and that the state was “actively trying to get to an agreeable place between both parties so we can move this program.” 
The Phoenix reported last month that Crestview Republican Don Gaetz recommended Florida’s next governor take a close at the dispute and consider dropping the lawsuit.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Something has to change in Congress
description: No single election will repair Congress. No single election will restore public confidence. But democracy was not designed to prevent change.
text:
Here’s something on which Americans of nearly every political persuasion appear able to agree: Congress is not working.
Were Congress an employee sitting down for its annual performance evaluation, the meeting would be brief. Public confidence has collapsed. Basic responsibilities are routinely deferred until the last possible moment. Cooperation has become a liability, theatrics a professional skill, and measurable output an afterthought.
Congress would be fired.
Gallup’s latest measurement offers little room for a more charitable assessment. In July 2026, just 16% of Americans approved of the way Congress was handling its job. Technically, that represented a six-percentage-point improvement over Gallup’s April reading of 10%. But a rise from 10% to 16% is only a movement from catastrophic to abysmal.
The public’s judgment is not based solely on mood or partisan frustration. It is reflected in Congress’s work, or rather, the absence of it.
Reuters reported that Congress passed just 27 bills in 2023, “a record low.” Its analysis, tracking legislative production back to 1973, found a long-term decline not only in laws enacted but also in measures passed by each chamber and activity recorded on the House and Senate floors.
Raw bill counts, of course, are not a perfect measure of effective government. One consequential law can matter more than a hundred ceremonial resolutions. But when legislative output and the ability to perform basic responsibilities deteriorate together, the pattern becomes difficult to dismiss.
Congress has become remarkably productive at producing everything except legislation. It produces viral clips, fundraising appeals, partisan investigations, cable-news appearances and daily declarations that civilization will end if the other party prevails in the proverbial culture war. It is less adept at passing budgets on time, addressing long-term fiscal problems, conducting sustained oversight, or reaching durable compromises on matters that cannot be solved by executive order. This undoubtedly presents another problem, since the president is not a legislator of last resort, no matter how popular or unpopular the president may be. But that is a discussion for another essay.
Despite the obloquy, not every member of Congress is lazy, corrupt, or incompetent. Many are serious people working within a system that increasingly rewards the wrong things. Outrage attracts attention. Compromise invites challengers. Governing requires patience, while political media rewards immediate gratification. In this environment, members become divas competing for the limelight, encouraged to cultivate their own individual brands rather than build a functioning lawmaking institution that serves us all.
The result is a Congress in which experience can tacitly turn into entitlement, longevity can be mistaken for effectiveness, and incumbency can be treated as ownership. Together, these tendencies form a distinctly anti-democratic triad.
Experience and institutional memory are certainly important. And public service should not be dismissed simply because it has been lengthy. However, experience is valuable only when it is being applied to the problems of the present. A congressional seat is not a lifetime appointment, and gratitude for past service is not an obligation to provide permanent employment.
Recent primary results suggest that voters are increasingly willing to make that distinction.
Instead, they demonstrate something far more basic. Political outcomes are not ordained. Money, seniority, endorsements, and name recognition remain powerful, but they are not invincible. Voters can still interrupt the seemingly inevitable.
That possibility makes people nervous. Change always does.
A familiar representative, even an imperfect one, feels predictable. A new candidate introduces uncertainty. Will that person be effective? Will the rhetoric of the campaign survive contact with the realities of governing? Will change produce genuine improvement or merely a different kind of dysfunction?
Those are reasonable questions. But they must be asked of incumbents, too.
The status quo is not neutral. Retaining the same leadership, incentives, and habits is itself a choice. Moreover, when congressional approval stands at 16% and legislative productivity has fallen to historic depths, continuity should not automatically be regarded as the responsible option.
Change is not something a society can permanently decline. Economies change. Communities change. Technology changes. Political coalitions change. The problems confronting Congress change. Even Congress itself has already changed, becoming more centralized, more performative, more polarized, and less capable of legislating through regular order.
The question, then, is not whether change will come. It is whether citizens will help direct it.
Electing new members will not, by itself, repair Congress. The institution also needs structural reform: independent and empowered committees, a more rational legislative calendar, greater transparency, fewer opportunities for individual members to profit from public office, and rules that allow ideas to receive genuine debate rather than disappear into leadership-controlled packages negotiated behind closed doors. In a word, we need to elect public servants who actually serve the public.
But institutional reform rarely begins with institutions voluntarily surrendering habits that protect the people already in power. It begins with political pressure. And elections are one source of that pressure.
Connecticut voters will soon choose among candidates for Congress. They need not regard every challenger as a savior or every incumbent as an obstacle. They should, however, reject the assumption that change is inherently reckless while repetition is inherently safe.
No single election will repair Congress. No single election will restore public confidence. But democracy was not designed to prevent change. It was designed to make change peaceful, accountable, renewable, and ongoing.
Something has to change in Congress. The evidence for that is clear.
So let us not fear change because its destination is uncertain. Let us examine it, test it, and judge it by what it produces. Should it fail, democracy gives us the power to change course once again.
Robert T.F. Downes is a PhD candidate in the Department of Political Science at the University of Connecticut, specializing in political theory and public law. He is also an Adjunct Professor at Rhode Island College, where he teaches American Government.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Tom Tiffany recovers after plane makes emergency landing
description: U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau Saturday night after his plane lost power while he was on his way home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner. Tiffany and the pilot of the four-seat Bonan aircraft exited the plane and swam to […]
text:
Rep. Tom Tiffany condemned Capitol violence, but just days after the attack he appeared at a closed-door rally with right-wing radio house Vicki Mckenna who called for "war." (Tiffany.house.gov)U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau Saturday night after his plane lost power while he was on his way home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner. Tiffany and the pilot of the four-seat Bonan aircraft exited the plane and swam to a shallow area, where they were rescued by boat by emergency responders, Tiffany said in a statement. 
“I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly,” Tiffany said. “They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care. Thankfully, both the pilot and I sustained only minor injuries.”
“God was watching over us tonight,” he added in the statement released late Saturday evening. 
On Sunday morning, Tiffany’s campaign released another statement thanking “everyone across Wisconsin and around the country who has reached out with prayers and kind words.” 
Tiffany suffered a laceration above his right eye that required stitches and both he and the pilot were was released from the hospital Saturday night, according to the campaign.  
Tiffany and the pilot were the only two people on board the Beechcraft K35, according to the campaign. An investigation into the accident will be handled by the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, released a statement saying, “I’m grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot. I wish them and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks analyzing nonresident hunting impacts, seeks hunter input
description: Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks is collecting data on the impacts of nonresident hunters on deer, elk, upland game birds, and water fowl hunting in the state, and is asking hunters to provide feedback about how nonresident hunting impacts how licenses are allocated. The survey is part of a study bill — House Bill 568 […]
text:
During the 2025 session, Montana state lawmakers passed a bill increasing the base cost of a nonresident hunting fee by more than 500%, which is expected to raise nearly $7 million annually. (Photo by Getty Images)Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks is collecting data on the impacts of nonresident hunters on deer, elk, upland game birds, and water fowl hunting in the state, and is asking hunters to provide feedback about how nonresident hunting impacts how licenses are allocated.
The survey is part of a study bill — House Bill 568 — passed by the 2025 Legislature. The Montana Hunters First Act, sponsored by Republican Rep. Courtenay Sprunger, directed FWP to conduct an impact study on nonresident hunting.
National Elk Refuge plan calls for feeding Jackson Hole elk, even if CWD transmission skyrockets

The bill requires the department to look at how nonresident hunting impacts deer, elk and bird hunting in each of the seven regions across the state, as well how lands enrolled in hunter access program are utilized and game population trends.
During the 2025 session, lawmakers also passed a bill increasing the base cost of a nonresident hunting fee by more than 500%, which is expected to raise nearly $7 million annually.
While the final results of the study will be released in December, the department released some preliminary data this week showing that nonresident license sales have grown during the previous decade, “though some of that has tapered a bit in recent years,” according to FWP, while remaining higher than 2016 numbers.
Nonresident total elk license purchases, which includes deer-elk combo and elk only licenses, grew from 19,914 in 2016 to 22,092 in 2025, while deer licenses peaked in 2021 at 42,557 and dropped to 40,614 in 2025.
The share of nonresident deer and elk hunters climbed from around 17% in 2016 to a peak of more than 20% in 2021 before dropping off a percentage point in recent years.
Since 2016, the largest uptick in hunting license sales has been in migratory bird licenses, which rose from 3,490 in 2016 to 5,539 in 2025 — a 58% increase.
Nonresident upland game bird license sales increased 15% from 3,490 in 2016 to 5,539 in 2025.
In general, license sales are sold according to state law, which can change with every legislative session. The Fish and Wildlife Commission can also dictate how licenses are distributed and has cut back on some licenses for nonresident in recent years.

House Bill 568 requires FWP to identify “specific issues for consideration” for the legislature, the department and the Fish and Wildlife Commission about nonresident hunter impacts. However, the bill does not make any immediate changes to hunting seasons, license quotas, or resident/nonresident allocations.

Hunters can participate in the survey through FWP’s website.
The department will publish a publicly accessible report by Dec. 1.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Third measles-related death in Pa. reported in Jefferson County
description: Amid a growing measles outbreak, Pennsylvania officials reported the third measles-related death in the state so far this year in Jefferson County.
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley, California, in a 2015 file photo. (Photo illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Amid a growing measles outbreak, Pennsylvania officials reported the third measles-related death in the state so far this year in Jefferson County.
Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong confirmed the death of a 40-year-old female Jefferson County resident in a social media post early Sunday morning. Furlong said no further details will be shared.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said.
Measles outbreak has sickened 676 in Pa., including four fully vaccinated people

Jefferson County’s Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver said that severe illness with measles is uncommon. Still, he said, people should not take the disease lightly. Stiver urged people to recognize early symptoms and consult with healthcare providers.
“This tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly,” Stiver said. “Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community.”
The previous two measles-related deaths happened in Lancaster County, where a large portion of the state’s measles cases are reported.
As the outbreak grows across the state, Pennsylvania’s Department of Health is leading a vaccination campaign against the disease. DOH administered more than 3,500 MMR vaccines last month and nearly 1,000 this month.
According to the most recent data posted to a public dashboard, there are 676 total measles cases so far this year in Pennsylvania.

name: VTDigger
title: Rural Vermont is running out of places to give birth
description:
Vermont is losing rural birthing centers one hospital at a time, with no coordinated plan to stop the pattern.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont is running out of places to give birth.
text:
This commentary is by Selin Tukel, a medical student at the University of Vermont Larner College of Medicine who is an advocate for equitable healthcare with an interest in obstetrics and women’s health.
Access to maternity care in the U.S. has shrunk in recent years. Shockingly, more than half of U.S. counties do not have a hospital that provides labor and delivery services, according to the 2026 March of Dimes report. In Vermont, it took an average of about 22 minutes to reach the nearest birthing hospital in 2023. For births in the state’s rural community hospitals, average travel time was estimated at 37 minutes.
Why are specifically rural communities facing these challenges? Springfield began the trend; Copley closed its birthing center in November 2025, and Brattleboro Memorial Hospital came within weeks of joining it — reversing course on Sept. 10 only after securing state grant funding, with no long-term fix yet in place. Areas at risk of becoming obstetric deserts include Lamoille County, Windsor County and a large part of southern Vermont. Had Brattleboro Memorial closed its birthing center, it would have created a significant access gap to maternity services in Vermont and bordering states, a scenario the state now says it wants to avoid but hasn’t structurally ruled out. 
Commissioned through Act 167, the Oliver Wyman report, published in August 2024, suggests the answer to Vermont’s issues is a regionalized system, since it is not financially sustainable for every hospital to provide every service. In theory, reduction and centralization of certain services would make sense if there were completely reliable communication between facilities. In practice, without a concrete plan for timely transfer with confirmation of receiving center capacity and local emergency department preparedness, regionalization of obstetrics is not always safe. 
Significantly, this report also claims, “Free-standing birthing centers could be established to replace closed inpatient obstetrics units.” Act 19 defines these freestanding centers as those providing “midwifery care, low-risk deliveries, and newborn care immediately after delivery, and that are not part of a hospital.” These centers lack the equipment or personnel for obstetric emergencies and must stabilize and transfer patients beyond their care capacities. Solo birthing centers can serve patients with low-risk pregnancies but require timely access to hospital-based obstetric services for emergencies, which the Oliver Wyman report neglected to address.
The impact on the surrounding local communities would have been substantial. Annie Kaufmann, a 13th-generation Vermonter and Brattleboro patient, delivered four of her babies at the birthing center. With three other children at home, Kaufmann said she would have been unable to travel to another location for care if needed. Emily Martyn, a certified nurse-midwife at Brattleboro Memorial, said people would still show up in the emergency department and still have babies at the hospital. With patients already driving an hour to get to the hospital, adding an extra 30 minutes could have meant the difference between life and death. 

READ MORE

The planned opening of the freestanding Green Mountain Birth Center may be something to celebrate, but it won’t solve the lack of resources in the community. These closures increase travel burden, disrupt continuity of care, strain the workforce and wider community, and widen the gap in care access for marginalized groups.
Obstetrics is not just another service to consolidate because of low volume; maternity care requires highly sensitive and individualized treatment that should be safe and timely regardless of location. There is a clear need for a consistent, statewide process for evaluating the consequences of decreasing hospital-based obstetric care. Vermont doesn’t need another hospital-by-hospital scramble. It needs a statewide plan to keep mothers and babies safe — before the next birthing center closes.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont is running out of places to give birth.

title: Lawmakers examine Department of Corrections policy keeping more people in prison past their minimum sentences
description:
Some lawmakers and advocates have expressed concerns about the policy, which critics say keeps people incarcerated past their minimum sentences without adequate due process.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lawmakers examine Department of Corrections policy keeping more people in prison past their minimum sentences.
text:
Defender General Matthew Valerio testifies before the Joint Legislative Justice Oversight Committee at the statehouse in Montpelier in September 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Vermont lawmakers responsible for overseeing the Department of Corrections are taking a closer look at a department policy that has expanded the criteria the department uses to keep people incarcerated beyond their minimum sentence. 
The policy, known as risk containment, has prompted concern from advocates and lawsuits from incarcerated people. VTDigger first reported on the policy in July. 
Now, lawmakers are scrutinizing the policy, with some expressing concern. In a hearing last week, the Joint Legislative Justice Oversight Committee heard testimony about risk containment, and legislators indicated that they intend to examine it in the upcoming legislative session. 
The policy outlines the process for the department to designate individuals as “risk contained.” People who receive the designation are not released on furlough, a form of supervised release, and do not receive a positive parole recommendation from the department. To designate a person as risk contained, a committee of corrections employees has to determine that the individual “constitutes a threat to the life, safety, or physical or mental well-being of others.”
The department has broad discretion over when to release someone between their minimum and maximum sentence, but some prosecutors and defense attorneys told VTDigger that changes to the policy had altered norms in the system. In court documents, one judge wrote that the policy “had the likely effect of significantly increasing the length of the in-prison incarcerative portion of a to-serve sentence that a person with (the defendant’s) criminal history would serve.” 
Risk containment was first introduced in July 2024, when it replaced the department’s former “Level C” policy. It was then broadened in April 2025 to make anyone with a felony conviction eligible to be reviewed for risk containment. Prior to April 2025, only people convicted of a sex offense or a listed offense –– a category that includes some especially serious crimes –– could be considered for risk containment. 
The review process to receive the classification has also left some people incarcerated past their minimum sentence for months, as VTDigger previously reported. Corrections officials told lawmakers in the hearing last week that they had cleared “a good amount” of the backlog of cases for people who were incarcerated past their minimum while awaiting a risk containment determination. 
Corrections Commissioner Jon Murad defended the policy in his testimony to the committee. 
“It is in keeping with our obligation to protect the people and the property from offenders of the criminal law,” Murad said, “and it is in keeping with our obligation to provide treatment and care for those who are given to us by the courts, so that they may successfully return, eventually, to the community.”
Murad also said that he thought concerns may be out of proportion. 
“I think there is a certain element of people making this a more ominous and troubling program than it is, considering it is something that has been long the practice and prerogative of the Department of Corrections, even if under a different name,” he told the committee. 
Seventy-seven people were designated as risk contained as of Sept. 1, according to data presented by the department. That includes some people who had previously been classified as Level C. 
Defender General Matt Valerio, who also testified at the hearing, said that risk containment is causing people to remain incarcerated who previously would have been released. That includes some people who were sentenced before the new policy took effect. Valerio’s office is representing multiple people in cases challenging the policy, he said.  
“Clearly what has happened is that there has been a second look at sentencing by the department, which will hold these people longer than they would have reasonably expected at the time they were originally sentenced,” Valerio said.
He also expressed concern about individuals’ abilities to meaningfully challenge the classification without access to legal counsel. 
In interviews this week, lawmakers on the committee said they expected the Legislature to continue to scrutinize the policy in the upcoming session. 
“There are a lot of questions here,” said Sen. Ginny Lyons, D-Chittenden Southeast, who serves as vice chair of the justice oversight committee. 
“Why did it change? How did it change? What information was being sent out, if any at all, to folks who were affected? All of those things just are problematic,” she added. 
According to previous court testimony from Jordan Pasha, a corrections employee who oversees the risk containment process, the policy change was sparked by Gov. Phil Scott. 
“We had received direction from the Governor’s office to look at mechanisms that the department had to slow down releases in the interest of public and victim safety,” Pasha testified in December 2025, according to a hearing transcript obtained by VTDigger. 
Rep. Martin LaLonde, D-South Burlington, and Sen. Robert Plunkett, D-Bennington, two of Lyons’ colleagues on the committee, also said they wanted more information about how the department makes risk containment decisions.
LaLonde, who also chairs the House Judiciary Committee, said he is concerned about the department considering a person’s convictions in risk containment decisions, because that information is already taken into account in the sentencing process. 
“It’s the judicial process that determines what the length of incarceration should be, both the minimum and maximum,” he said in an interview. “They shouldn’t be considering those factors again and determining whether to hold the person past their minimum. That’s, you know, essentially that’s de facto resentencing.” 
Plunkett, who works as a prosecutor in addition to his role in the Legislature, said in an interview that he didn’t share the concern about considering a person’s convictions in a risk containment decision. 
“I’d be shocked if DOC didn’t take every factor into consideration when they made their determinations,” he told VTDigger. Plunkett also emphasized that there was no guarantee that a person would get released at their minimum sentence.
Last week’s hearing seems likely to be just the beginning. 
“I’m sure this is going to continue being looked at,” Rep. Alice Emmons, D-Springfield, who is chair of the oversight committee and leads the House Corrections and Institutions Committee, said during the hearing. 
“Be prepared once the new session starts.”

title: Pittsford Village Farm opens with new childcare operation and affordable apartments
description:
“It is going to house significant opportunities for citizens across our town and our surrounding towns,” said the Pittsford Village Farm Board chair. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pittsford Village Farm opens with new childcare operation and affordable apartments.
text:
The farmhouse restoration project at the Pittfsord Village Farm features two rental apartments, a childcare center and a retail operation. Seen in Pittsford on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
What began as a vision among Pittsford residents in 2018 will become reality Sept. 15, when a childcare center in the newly restored Pittsford Village Farm is set to open.
Already, two families have moved into new affordable apartments, and a new drink shop called Small Town Nutrition has moved into the Pittsford Village Farm, said Lorrie Byrom, the chair of the Pittsford Village Farm board of directors. It has been a “citizen effort” to see the town’s plan realized, and now a ribbon cutting ceremony is planned for Sept. 17, Byrom said. 
It all began about eight years ago when Pittsford residents gathered to ask what would be the best use for the historic Pittsford Village farmhouse after the sprawling farm had been preserved for local use. Townspeople prioritized developing a community center, childcare operation, affordable housing and fostering local business, Byrom said. 
The total restoration project cost over $4 million, Byrom said, with funding coming from citizen donations, state programs, the National Parks Service, Let’s Grow Kids and the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board, among other sources. 
Byrom said the Pittsford Village Farm is still fundraising around $200,000 to finish the community center portion of the project, which will be a gathering space for everything from potlucks to yoga classes.
The childcare center in Pittsford is licensed for 30 slots, open to children who are six weeks to 5 years old, with infant, toddler and preschool classroom cohorts, said Stephanie Carvey, the co-executive director of Rutland County Parent Child Center, which will operate the childcare facility. The Pittsford Village Farm’s campus has opportunities for nature programming, while also being centrally located near the Maclure Library and Kamuda’s Country Market in the village center, she said. 
Pittsford Village Farm partnered with Rutland County Parent Child Center in Jan. 2025 to open the childcare facility, after First Children’s Finance helped the nonprofit community group seek out a childcare operator.   
In Vermont, childcare is more affordable since the passage of Act 76 in 2023, which expanded the state childcare subsidy program, said Erin Roche, senior advisor for First Children’s Finance. The bill aimed to make wages higher for childcare providers and to increase childcare subsidies for families making up to 575% of the federal poverty line.  
There is still a gap between the supply and demand for childcare in Vermont, Roche said. First Children’s Finance helped Pittsford Village Farm secure a planning grant as part of the overall mission to expand childcare access across the state. 
Rutland County has among the highest demand for childcare in Vermont: Over 1,000 childcare slots are needed to meet the need, according to 2026 analysis by First Children’s Finance. 
The Pittsford Village Farm board decided to honor a Pittsford community stalwart, Breda Harnish, who died at 71 in 2013, by naming the portion of the building that will house the childcare center “Breda’s Place.” 

The view from the balcony at Pittford Village Farm after a restoration project seen on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

While owning and operating the Cortina Inn in Rutland, Breda Harnish mentored children through the New York Times Fresh Air Fund and Mentor Connector, among other efforts to educate and support children in the community, Bob Harnish said of his late wife in an interview.
“I hope that she would be very pleased to have her name on this portion of the village farm house,” Harnish said. “It’s becoming more and more well known that early childhood learning is important to overall success.”
Through this restoration effort supported by locals like Harnish, Byrom said she hopes the historic building in Pittsford will be a cross-generational gathering place for the region.
“It is going to house significant opportunities for citizens across our town and our surrounding towns to do many educational, cultural, recreational things together,” Byrom said.

title: Revealed in the river
description:
Local historians discover the remnants of a blockhouse on the Crown Point Road, Vermont’s first interstate highway.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Revealed in the river.
text:
Annette Spaulding prepares to dive in the Connecticut River on Aug. 15, 2025. Spaulding was a member of the team of historians that discovered a Colonial-era blockhouse built for the Crown Point Road that had been submerged in the river for many decades. Photo by Lonnie Lisai/The Commons

This story by Robert F. Smith was first published in The Commons on Sept. 8, 2026.
SPRINGFIELD — A trio of local history experts, working with historical records, personal exploration and eventually with archaeology staff and students from Dartmouth College, believe they may have solved a regional history mystery.
That mystery? The exact location of a blockhouse built in 1760 in the first few miles of New Hampshire’s historic Crown Point Road, near where it crossed the Connecticut River by ferry into Vermont.
Local historian Lonnie Lisai, of Westminster, along with fellow historians Annette Spaulding, of Rockingham, and Nicholas Levlocke, of Springfield, have pooled their research and skills over the last two years to try to pinpoint the Beaver Brook site using underwater sonar with the help of Dartmouth archaeologists.
They feel they have discovered, photographed and investigated the remaining stone foundation of that original blockhouse that guarded the first section of the Crown Point Road.
A blockhouse is essentially a tall (2½-story) structure, up to 32 feet square, built of stone and thick timbers. It is a house that doubles as a small enclosed fort.
Blockhouses were so sturdy and thick that they were impenetrable by the typical weapons and firearms of the period. They were built with small openings in all four walls for cannon fire, and numerous slots were built into the stone and timber walls and even the upper floors to allow for musket fire in all directions against enemy attackers.
In the Colonial era and through the Revolutionary War, dozens of these blockhouses were built along what was then the Colonial frontier — southern Vermont and New Hampshire.
It is well known that the military road, built in 1759 and 1760 during the French and Indian War, was constructed starting at Fort Crown Point on Lake Champlain, continuing for about 77 miles across Vermont.
The road ended at the Fort at No. 4 in New Hampshire, the fort built in 1744 in the recently surveyed township referred to as “No. 4” and ultimately chartered as Charlestown, New Hampshire, in 1753. A replica of the fort was built a short distance from the original in 1960 and serves as an open-air living museum today.
Starting at the end of the 1800s, interested parties, including the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Crown Point Road Association, began placing markers that traced the original road from end to end.
In Charlestown, New Hampshire, and Springfield alone, 21 historic marker granite posts and bronze plaques accurately detail the road’s route. More than 80 other markers trace the road across the rest of Vermont to Lake Champlain.
The frontier blockhouse
The Fort at No. 4 in New Hampshire was the farthest northern outpost of the Colonies in the 1740s. The 1891 “History of Windsor County, Vermont” refers to the area across the river from Charlestown — now Springfield — at that time as “a vast unguarded frontier, unsafe for occupancy.”
This isolated region survived Abenaki raids and skirmishes up into the early 1760s and the end of the war.
In April 1747, a force of just over 30 Colonists successfully defended the frontier Fort at No. 4 against a major three-day attack by a force of about 10 French soldiers and 60 Abenaki warriors. The fort would become known as Fort Stevens in honor of Capt. Phineas Stevens, commander of the force that defended the fort.
Lisai, a member of the Crown Point Road Association, said that historical records place the blockhouse at the Connecticut River ferry crossing at Beaver Brook, but some historians have confused the site with another point downriver, near the present Cheshire Bridge, where a later ferry crossed from Charlestown into Springfield.
“I think it was one ‘historian’ who did no research and determined that the Wentworth ferry/CPR (Crown Point Road) could not possibly be a mile up from Black River,” Lisai said in an email. “Then other historians assumed that to be a fact — and it became a fact.”
Where was the original blockhouse?
Levlocke, Lisai and Spaulding agreed that the evidence they’d accumulated over the past few years — from maps, old diaries, journals and personal exploration of the area — pointed to a site upriver from the Cheshire Bridge, not downriver, and much closer to the route of the original Crown Point Road.
Complicating the search is that two major changes have reshaped the Connecticut River and the region’s landscape in the last 266 years, and the three historians kept those changes in mind during their research.
First, in the mid-1800s, railroads were built along the sides of the river. The railbed was built atop large earthen berms, in some cases many yards high, with engineering that dramatically altered how smaller tributaries joined the Connecticut.
This was key, because early references about the blockhouse referred to it as being built at the place where Beaver Brook entered the big river. What had been Beaver Brook was cut off from the main river by the railroad bed.
But Levlocke, in studying maps and looking at the area where they thought the brook should be, noticed a large culvert at that point which emptied into the river. He thought that might be the place to start looking for remnants of the blockhouse.
Secondly, early in the 20th century, a series of hydroelectric dams were built on the upper Connecticut River, including the Vernon Dam in 1907 and the Bellows Falls Dam from 1926 to 1928. These dams at least tripled the width of the upper Connecticut from its original bed, expanding it into the low, open terraced farmland on both sides of the river.

The Connecticut River looking north from Putney Landing. Creative Commons Photo/Flickr user putneypics

The local historians knew that if any remnants of the blockhouse remained, they could be far from shore, toward the middle of the river, and perhaps buried under mud and silt.
On Aug. 15, 2025, they took a boat and scuba diving equipment to the point, now well into the river, where they predicted that Beaver Brook had originally met the Connecticut to see what they could find.
Surprise find
Spaulding has more than 35 years of experience as a master diver, with more than 3,400 dives around the world. She routinely makes in excess of 100 dives a year in the Connecticut River, her stated favorite place to dive, and has made numerous historical discoveries in other rivers and lakes.
The three knew that the original blockhouse had a cut-granite foundation and first floor 12 to 14 feet high. The foundation had been topped by an upper floor of heavy timbers, 9 inches to 12 inches thick. Those timbers were removed at one point and used for other constructions in the area after the threat of Abenaki and French army attacks died down and the blockhouse was no longer needed.
Spaulding began her dive at the site where their research told them Beaver Brook should be.
Despite muddy water with poor visibility, she spotted the foundation — but not way out in the riverbed as they expected.
To everyone’s surprise, she saw a “straight line of cut-granite stones underwater, not far off the present riverbank, in about 16 feet of water.”
“I was stunned when Annette found it!” Lisai wrote.
Spaulding said that what she could see of the foundation looked like “smaller cut stone that humans could handle, with drill marks.”
She took photos and measurements, and the three accurately marked the site. They were certain they had quickly found what they were looking for.
Levlocke contacted archaeologists at Dartmouth College about the find, and in July a group of three archaeologists and two technicians, under the direction of Jonathan Alperstein, a graduate student in the Department of Anthropology, brought sonar down to the site to look at what was buried under the silt there.
Along with Levlocke, Lisai and Spaulding, Alperstein boated to the site and began to search the riverbed.
“The sonar found the rest of the foundation,” Spaulding said. “Buried under feet of silt. It was a square of granite with an opening, about 8 to 10 feet from shore.”
Alperstein assured them that it was “a man-made site,” Spaulding said.
Since then, he has contacted the New Hampshire state archaeologist and made a report about the find, which begins a process that could lead to designation in the National Historic Registry. He said he will continue to follow its status.
Levlocke, Lisai and Spaulding said they plan on continuing their investigation of the area, including seeing if they can find more details on the original path of the Connecticut River, and that they will continue “working with Dartmouth College on evaluating and documenting the discovery further.”
Lisai wrote that “the Wentworth Ferry/Blockhouse will get much more attention next year” with the 250th anniversary of Gen. John Stark crossing the river from Fort at No. 4 along the way to the 1777 Battle of Bennington with 1,500 militia soldiers.
“I will be digging for military records,” he said.
Levlocke, Lisai and Spaulding each repeatedly credited the other two with doing the bulk of the investigation and work.
“I personally equate our team (Lonnie, Annette, and me) to an ant colony — everyone brought something unique to solving the Blockhouse mystery,” Levlocke said. “Together as one, we made this find happen.”
Vermont’s first interstate highway
It’s hard to overstate the impact and importance of the Crown Point Road in New England’s, and especially Vermont’s, history.
But it wasn’t exactly the case that the Crown Point Road was a Colonial trail carved out of a vast wilderness, as it is often referenced.
Native people had been living in this region for thousands of years, and the road followed and widened their well-established trails between the Connecticut River and Lake Champlain.
In fact, as soon as the Crown Point Road crossed the Connecticut River into Vermont it passed directly through the Skitchewaug section of Springfield and over a gap in Skitchewaug Mountain into the town’s historic Eureka area. This was already a well-established Native American trail.
Skitchewaug was the site of a large-scale archaeological excavation in the 1980s that showed it was a major Western Abenaki village and farming region that had been in use for hundreds of years before Europeans arrived in New England.
From the south end headed north, after leaving the Fort at No. 4 and crossing into Vermont, the Crown Point Road made its way north and west through Springfield, Weathersfield, Cavendish, Ludlow and Plymouth, and on across the Green Mountains, terminating across Lake Champlain from Fort Crown Point. It would eventually also connect with Fort Ticonderoga on Lake Champlain in New York.

The Fort at Number 4 in what is now the town of Charlestown, New Hampshire.  Photo by Ascended Dreamer – Own work, Creative Commons BY 4.0

The historic military supply route, built on the order of Gen. Jeffery Amherst at Fort Crown Point, was built by famed Colonial frontiersman Capt. John Stark, Maj. John Hawks and Col. John Goffe. It was cleared largely by Colonial militia and ranger military units like Rogers’ Rangers, who helped, as Amherst ordered, cut the “at least 20-foot-wide” roadway.
Trees were dropped to widen the Native American trail, stumps were removed, parts of the road were graded, sturdy bridges and causeways were built, and corduroy sections were laid over wetlands and swampy areas.
Every 15 miles, Amherst required log enclosures be built to hold the cattle that would be “drove through that road for the use of the troops.”
It was first used during the French and Indian War to move British and Colonial troops, cannons, supplies, and sheep and cattle between the English settlers on the New Hampshire frontier and the forts in New York.
Then, during the American Revolution 15 years later, regiments of Colonial forces used the road to reinforce and supply U.S. troops at Fort Ticonderoga in their fight against the British.
But the Crown Point Road’s major impact on Vermont emerged between the wars.
With the defeat of the French by Great Britain in 1763, and Britain now in control of Canada, the threat of Native American raids was nearly gone. British colonists flooded into Vermont along this main highway between the Connecticut River and Lake Champlain, establishing villages and towns on what had been Indigenous lands.
The Daughters of the American Revolution and the Crown Point Road Association have worked for decades to document and mark the original road as well as its changes and additions.
Some parts are well-known hiking trails, some parts have all but disappeared, some parts are now just vague forest paths, and a few short sections of the old military highway are still in use as town roads, such as Crown Point Road in Springfield.

title: Real Vermonters don’t milk goats. They laugh at newly revived books with that title.
description:
A 43rd anniversary edition of 1983’s “Real Vermonters Don’t Milk Goats” — the state’s all-time bestselling humor book — is debuting this month with a few 21st century tweaks.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Real Vermonters don’t milk goats. They laugh at newly revived books with that title..
text:
“Real Vermonters Don’t Milk Goats,” the state’s all-time bestselling humor book, is set to return to stores this fall in a 43rd anniversary edition. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger
Vermont political science professor Frank Bryan and writer friend Bill Mares were bumping along a muddy back road four decades ago when they spotted a pristine log cabin with a two-vehicle carport.
“Flatlander,” Bryan later recalled saying of a perceived out-of-state owner.
“And what are we?” Mares replied.
Mares was born in Missouri, raised in Texas and educated in Massachusetts. Bryan grew up as one of seven students in his class in the Upper Valley town of Newbury — after his delivery in a maternity ward in nearby New Hampshire.
“You’re not a real Vermonter,” Mares said.
Bryan, aiming to change the subject, pointed to a road sign advertising goat’s milk.
“Real Vermonters,” he declared, “don’t milk goats.”
And so begins the story of the 1983 book “Real Vermonters Don’t Milk Goats,” the state’s all-time bestselling humor title, which is set for a comeback this fall with a 43rd anniversary edition.
Back in the Reagan era, Bryan and Mares, inspired by the satirical book “Real Men Don’t Eat Quiche,” turned their back-road conversation into the introduction of a 94-page paperback.
“Real Vermonters don’t wear bib overalls,” the two went on to declare. “They don’t tie their sweaters around their necks. They wear hats when it’s cold, even if they have wavy hair. They never try to look like farmers. Most of all, Real Vermonters never, never try to look like Real Vermonters.”
That Christmas shopping season, the Bennington Bookshop sold 200 copies of the title — nearly 15% of its total holiday sales, according to the local newspaper. Manchester’s Northshire Bookstore reported even bigger success.
“We sold hundreds,” then co-owner Edward Morrow was quoted by the Bennington Banner. “We just kept on reordering and reordering it.”
The now-closed New England Press of Shelburne ultimately churned out 70,000 copies — one for every seven of the state’s 511,546 residents at the time — before curbing production in the 1990s.
Mares went on to write nearly 20 other books before his death in 2024. Bryan, 85, has retired from public life and press interviews after teaching at the University of Vermont for 36 years. And “Real Vermonters Don’t Milk Goats” has been out of print for three decades — a challenge for storekeepers who still receive requests for it.
Enter Michael DeSanto, owner of Vermont’s Phoenix Books and its Onion River Press. He recently approached Mares’ wife of 53 years, Christine Hadsel, about the possibility of another printing.
Hadsel reread the original manuscript she typed for her husband in the seemingly prehistoric age before personal computers. She smiled at its “Things Real Vermonters Are Born With.” First and foremost: “An ability to tell New Hampshire from Vermont.”
“Real Vermonters would never tear down a barn when they could let it fall down,” the manuscript continued. “Real Vermonters, of course, always park their cars pointing out — it’s easier getting out headfirst than backwards after a good snowfall. Finally, Real Vermonters don’t honk when the light turns green.”
The more things change, Hadsel saw, the more they stay the same.
“Fundamentally,” she said in a recent interview, “we still have a state where we have a lot of tensions between the incomers who have more money and the people who are already here who tend to have less.”
That’s why Onion River Press is rolling out a $13 reprint (up from the original $4.95) with a few other revisions.
“We don’t want to change what it was,” Hadsel said, “but it needs some updating.”

Vermont political science professor Frank Bryan and writer friend Bill Mares published “Real Vermonters Don’t Milk Goats” in 1983. Photo courtesy of Christine Hadsel

People not alive or around in 1983 can read one of several newly added “explainer” footnotes to learn that Burlington’s Oasis Diner — the place where Bryan and Mares wrote the book — was a Bank Street staple for a half-century before its recent reincarnation as Burl’s Downtown Kitchenette.
(Burlington, the book informs, remains “a large city that has the advantage of being very close to the Vermont border.”)
For those who question the book’s assertion that “Real Vermonters don’t believe in summer,” a second footnote points out that the original work was written before the advent of the term “climate change.”
And for anyone wondering why the authors told Bernie Sanders, then mayor of Burlington, to “(1) renounce socialism and (2) shed his accent” before they’d consider him a “Real Vermonter,” a third footnote simply deems that thought “Wrong!”
Readers of all ages can more easily appreciate the rest of the book, illustrated by Vermont cartoonist Howard Johnson.
“Real Vermont Women know the Women’s Auxiliary is anything but,” it says. “Real Vermonters’ kids don’t go to summer camp unless they work there. In the fall, you can find them ignoring the foliage almost anywhere.”
A list of “Items Not Found in a Real Vermonter’s General Store” begins with decaf espresso beans, suntan oil and contact lens fluid.
“Things Real Vermonters Recognize as a Waste of Time” include Interstate 91 north of St. Johnsbury, Interstate 91 south of St. Johnsbury and “advising a Flatlander not to burn white birch.”
As for “What Real Vermonters Dread the Most,” citations range from “change” and property reappraisals to any weather forecast that opens with the words “only a dusting is expected.”
Four decades ago, reviews of the book observed that its humor cushioned more serious commentary.
“The premise of the book is simple: Real Vermonters are dying out and people ‘from away,’ identified as Flatlanders, are moving in,” the late sixth-generation Vermonter Keith Jennison wrote in the Vermont Historical Society’s magazine. “Only by identifying their differences can they get along with each other — provided they feel like it.”
Today, Hadsel notes the irony of her and Mares moving to the state in 1970 for its bucolic charm: “There were so many people like us who came in and bought farmland — and didn’t farm it.”
As the late New Yorker cartoonist Edward Koren, who lived his last years in Brookfield, wrote Mares in 1983: “I do like the book, and it does raise serious issues about rural area inroads by the likes of us and how we change the nature of the nature we’ve come for in the first place.”
Hadsel is set to promote the reprint Sept. 18 at the Tunbridge World’s Fair, Sept. 20 at Brookfield’s Old Town Hall, Sept. 27 at Stowe’s Alchemist Brewery, Oct. 1 at Woodstock’s Yankee Bookshop, Oct. 11 at Burlington’s Saint Johns Club, Oct. 16 at Lyndon’s York Street Meeting House, Oct. 27 at Rutland’s Phoenix Books, Nov. 1 at Newbury’s Bailey Club, Nov. 7 at St. Albans’ The Eloquent Page, Nov. 8 at the Charlotte Grange and Nov. 9 at Guilford’s Broad Brook Community Center.
(She has time: “Anyone seen mowing the lawn after September 15th is not a Real Vermonter,” the book notes.)
The 43rd anniversary edition includes a “New Real Vermonters’ List” featuring Strafford “Gen Z’s rock star” Noah Kahan, Tony Award-winning “Hadestown” creator Anaïs Mitchell and fellow Vermont singer-songwriter Grace Potter.
But it ends with the same 1983 warning: “Before you get pretensions about how ‘real’ you are, we caution you to remember that Real Vermonters Don’t Read Books Like This.”
Disclosure: The late Bill Mares was a member of the governing board of the Vermont Journalism Trust, the nonprofit that owns and operates VTDigger.

title: South Dakota wildlife officials try to let anglers keep large muskies, but anglers say no thanks
description: When South Dakota wildlife officials tried to give anglers the freedom to keep their prize catches of a unique fish, something surprising happened. Many anglers said no thanks and convinced a state commission to reject the proposal. The Game, Fish and Parks Commission’s monthly meeting Thursday and Friday in Winner included consideration of a proposal […]
text:
Muskellunge are an ambush predator fish often found in vegetation or submerged trees. They feed on fish, insects, crustaceans, birds and small mammals. (Photo courtesy of South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks)When South Dakota wildlife officials tried to give anglers the freedom to keep their prize catches of a unique fish, something surprising happened.
Many anglers said no thanks and convinced a state commission to reject the proposal.
The Game, Fish and Parks Commission’s monthly meeting Thursday and Friday in Winner included consideration of a proposal that would have changed regulations protecting large, predatory freshwater fish known as muskellunge or muskies. The proposal would have changed the state’s current catch-and-release requirement for muskies, which was put in place after muskie anglers advocated for it in 2018 to allow muskies to live longer and grow bigger. 
The rule change would have allowed anglers to keep one of the fish per day, if the fish is at least 45 inches in length. Opponents feared the change would ultimately deplete the population of trophy-sized muskies. 
Thousands of South Dakota habitat license plates do nothing for habitat, due to two-part process

Scott Vander Meulen, of Sioux Falls, pointed the commission to a petition signed by more than 650 people opposing the change, while noting the more than 50 people who submitted written comments on the matter were overwhelmingly against it.
“The opportunity to catch a trophy muskie already exists under current regulations,” Vander Meulen said. “When a trophy fish is released, that fish can be caught again, allowing multiple anglers to experience that same opportunity. Once harvested, that opportunity is gone forever.”
The South Dakota Wildlife Federation also testified against the change, with Executive Director Dana Rogers saying the group’s members who fish for muskies were adamantly opposed. 
According to the state Department of Game, Fish and Parks, the fish “are an ambush predator often found in vegetation or submerged trees,” and they have a torpedo-like shape with a duckbill-shaped snout and sharp teeth. They feed on fish, insects, crustaceans, birds and small mammals.
Josh Karch, president of the Fargo-Moorhead chapter of Muskies Inc., submitted a letter opposing the change. He wrote that other states set the minimum harvest size for muskies at 50 inches. 
“Anglers who wish to commemorate the capture of a trophy fish have excellent alternatives available, including high-quality replica mounts that preserve the memory of the catch without removing the fish from the population,” Karch wrote.
Department fisheries biologist Brian Blackwell walked the commission through the science behind South Dakota’s muskie program, which began in 1975 and now manages five stocked lake populations at roughly one muskie per 5 acres, while the fish are also found in several other lakes and the lower Missouri River. He said the program has struggled with low interest from anglers, and allowing anglers to keep a large fish could spur more interest.  
Blackwell said relatively few muskies over 45 inches turn up in department sampling.
“The muskie anglers probably do to see some bigger fish than we’re seeing,” Blackwell said. “And perhaps partnering with them in the future would be a good thing to try to get our hands on some more information.”
After hearing the public comment and the department’s presentation, the commission voted to strip the muskie harvest provision out of a broader rule package, leaving the current muskie regulations unchanged.

name: Mississippi Today
title: 25 years later, even small events from Sept. 11 remain etched in the mind
description: A Mississippi Capitol Police officer walks past the new package scanner and metal detector at the south entrance of the statehouse in Jackson on Friday, Jan. 15, 2021. State capitols across the country were under heightened security after the siege of the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
text:
On Sept. 11, 2001, media members working in the fourth floor pressroom of the Mississippi Capitol were keeping an eye on a portable television on a filing cabinet.
The immediacy of the internet was not then what it is today, so the small box television was the only instant access to the outside world. It was difficult to stop watching the television.
A commercial jet had already been seen on national television in real time slamming into the south tower of the World Trade Center in New York. People watched as the twin towers tumbled.
Would another horrible event unfold on live TV?
Reporters covering the Mississippi Capitol did not have much else to do that horrible day. A meeting of the powerful Legislative Budget Committee had been scheduled for that morning but was canceled as the tragedy unfolded in New York, Washington and rural Pennsylvania.
Gathering the obligatory quotes on the unprecedented American tragedy from state politicians was the primary task of members of the Capitol press corps.
Democratic former Gov. Ronnie Musgrove speaks during an interview on Thursday, Aug. 14, 2014 in Jackson. Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
“We are deeply saddened and alarmed by these cowardly attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon,” then-Gov. Ronnie Musgrove said. “We are monitoring this situation closely and will take all necessary security precautions at the state level. Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of those killed and injured in these attacks.”
In reality, there was much that could be – perhaps needed to be – done on the state level, especially at the Mississippi Capitol.
Before that tragic day, people came and went unimpeded into state buildings, including the Capitol. No less than eight entrances into the building were never locked or secured by law enforcement during business hours and sometimes they were still unlocked after business hours.
In such a massive building, there was no way to monitor who was coming and going if all the doors were open without security.
Then-House Speaker Billy McCoy, a Prentiss County Democrat, said on that day that everything changed.
No longer, he predicted, would people be able to move freely into and out of public buildings and public events.
McCoy’s prediction quickly came true, and restrictions remain in place 25 years after four commercial aircraft were turned into weapons to kill nearly 3,000 people on American soil.
The general public’s entrances to the Mississippi Capitol are limited to two, and they are reinforced by security, metal detectors and scanners.
As McCoy predicted, stronger security was in place just a few days after the attacks, on Sept. 20, when Mississippi State hosted South Carolina in the first college football game played after  Sept. 11.
A story retelling the historic game, in the State newspaper in Columbia, South Carolina, described the security put in place, including a no-fly zone over Davis-Wade Stadium in Starkville.
“The placement of the security, the amount of security was all very important, but we didn’t want it to look like a military presence,” Musgrove said in the article. “We wanted the fans to enjoy the game and we wanted the nation through TV and other means to enjoy the game.”
Efforts to maintain balance – between security and convenience – continue today.
Late in the afternoon of Sept. 11, 2001, long lines formed at gas stations as Americans started to panic about whether more attacks were coming. Spikes were reported in the cost of gasoline.
Two political rivals, Musgrove and Attorney General Mike Moore, both Democrats, announced a joint news conference just outside of one of those once unguarded doors on the eastern side of the state Capitol. It was a rare site for a press conference, and that just added to the surreal feeling of the day.
The rivals announced jointly that Musgrove was declaring a state of emergency to prevent the spike in gas prices after it was reported that the attorney general’s office received more than 2,000 calls about price gouging that day as rumors circulated that the attack would impact the supply of gasoline.
Musgrove told Mississippi Today five years ago that his emergency declaration was to highlight that price spiking was illegal. “It seemed like an appropriate thing to do, though I was more focused on security risks related to 9/11.”
Musgrove and Moore’s press conference received a brief mention in national news, though in the scope of the  day, price gouging in Mississippi or events at a state Capitol far from the attacks on the East Coast seemed like small concerns.
