name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled. It’s Worse in States With Abortion Bans.
authors: Agnel Philip, ProPublica, Andrea Suozzo, ProPublica
description: The number of women who died after an ectopic pregnancy has spiked in recent years, a ProPublica analysis found. The mounting deaths in Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data have drawn little scrutiny or response. Such deaths typically occur in the first trimester, after a pregnancy fails to properly implant in the uterus and […]
text:
(Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)The number of women who died after an ectopic pregnancy has spiked in recent years, a ProPublica analysis found. The mounting deaths in Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data have drawn little scrutiny or response.
Such deaths typically occur in the first trimester, after a pregnancy fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The embryo grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.
With prompt and appropriate medical care, maternal health experts say, women should not die. Yet ProPublica’s analysis found a stark and baffling increase: Almost 200 women with the condition died from 2020 to 2025, compared with about 100 in the previous six years.
“A death related to ectopic pregnancy should really be a never event,” said Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia.
Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are presented as a rate within three-year intervals to meet data suppression thresholds. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. (LUCAS WALDRON/ProPublica)
While chaos and access issues at hospitals during the COVID-19 pandemic likely contributed to at least some of the deaths, the surge has persisted, raising serious questions about the role of the most significant disruption to maternal healthcare in the years since: state restrictions on abortion.
To treat an ectopic pregnancy, which is almost never viable, doctors must terminate it. But lawsuits and federal complaints have alleged that some medical providers are hesitating or flat-out refusing to do that in states where they face criminal penalties for performing an abortion. Patients described their terror.
“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.
“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in a lawsuit after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”
To determine whether these issues go beyond anecdotes, ProPublica analyzed the data collected from every state by the CDC to look for patterns. The analysis shows a growing divide for women in states with strict abortion bans compared with those without.
While the uptick in ectopic deaths occurred nationwide, the climb has been much steeper in states that banned abortion after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are grouped into three-year periods to meet data suppression thresholds. States with abortion bans that begin at six weeks of pregnancy or earlier are considered to have a strict ban. For the list of states in each group, see the methodology. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. (Lucas Waldron/ProPublica)
ProPublica shared its analysis with more than a dozen maternal health experts, including leaders in the field, who were unaware of the spike; early pregnancy complications are chronically underresearched.
While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies.
In Thurman’s case, despite clear signs of an ectopic pregnancy, two emergency departments sent her home without resolving the complication. Regulators in 2025 found that one of the hospitals, Ascension Seton Williamson, failed to properly screen Thurman for a suspected ectopic pregnancy and did not call in an OB-GYN, in violation of the hospital’s own policies and federal law that requires emergency departments to treat and stabilize patients before discharging them. Thurman has an ongoing lawsuit against Ascension Seton Williamson and the other hospital, Ascension Seton Highland Lakes, for medical malpractice.
Arkansas judge revives lawsuit challenging state’s near-total abortion ban

Thurman had to have her fallopian tube removed after it ruptured. (Thurman is not related to Amber Thurman, who died in Georgia, which also has an abortion ban, after doctors delayed treating different pregnancy complications in 2022.)
“I’ve never been in a situation where I didn’t get healthcare when I needed it,” Thurman told ProPublica, comparing the condition to having “a time bomb you can’t control.”
A spokesperson for the Ascension Seton hospitals said in a statement, “When a patient experiences a serious or life-threatening condition during pregnancy, our clinicians provide medically indicated treatment, including treatment for an ectopic pregnancy.” The hospital has denied Thurman’s malpractice allegations in a court filing.
Ectopic pregnancies, while rare, have long been recognized as the leading cause of maternal deaths in the first trimester. The condition impacts up to 2% of pregnancies in the U.S. Because government agencies don’t require hospitals to track or report overall ectopic diagnoses, it is impossible to know whether the condition itself is becoming more common.
While rates for other pregnancy-related deaths also increased during the pandemic, those climbs have largely subsided.
Experts aren’t sure why ectopic deaths have continued to rise. Ectopic pregnancies are more common among older women, but the increase in deaths has been even more stark among younger women, the analysis showed.
Anti-abortion groups have suggested that the use of abortion pills prescribed online is leading to more undiagnosed ectopics because telehealth patients don’t receive an ultrasound. But studies have found that ectopic rates are far lower among people who seek medication abortions than in the general population. Telehealth clinics ask questions that filter out patients at higher risk of ectopic pregnancy and follow up with those they treat to screen for symptoms, said Ushma Upadhyay, a researcher at the University of California, San Francisco, who studies telehealth abortion administration.
Lawsuit says Arkansas’ near-total ban on abortion violates state’s constitution

Experts told ProPublica that more research is required to determine the role of the abortion bans in the rise of ectopic-related deaths. Many states with bans, which generally provide less Medicaid funding and coverage to low-income women, have long had poorer maternal outcomes. “It’s a real challenge to try and tease out one thing out of the array of factors that undermine women’s health in these states,” said Eugene Declercq, a public health researcher at Boston University.
But experts said ProPublica’s data analysis, along with stories about delays in ectopic care, underscores the need to find out what is driving the deaths.
“Reproductive health is unusual across medicine when we consider how swiftly policy changes affect the care patients can receive,” said Dr. Courtney Schreiber, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology.
Caitlin Myers, an economist at Dartmouth College who studies abortion policy, said the deaths should be investigated: “This is a potentially profound consequence of the regulation,” she said.
How abortion bans interfere with ectopic care
Many state abortion bans include exceptions for ectopic pregnancies. But experts have worried that doctors are hesitating to offer treatment without an ironclad diagnosis, which clinicians say can take time and increase risks to the mother.
Ectopic pregnancy symptoms often begin with abdominal pain and bleeding, which send women to emergency rooms. There, doctors use ultrasounds to locate where the pregnancy has implanted.
However, embryos are often not visible on an ultrasound early in pregnancy. That could mean the pregnancy is ectopic, but it may also be a miscarriage or normal pregnancy that’s too small to see. Doctors can also assess whether the pregnancy is likely ectopic through blood tests over multiple days.
Abortion could return to Supreme Court, this time with a focus on women’s health

If the pregnancy is ectopic, the risk of rupture increases the longer treatment is delayed. In a state without a ban, a patient could decide at any point that that risk is not worth taking and opt to terminate the pregnancy.
In a state with a ban, however, that option may not exist. If doctors can confirm the pregnancy is ectopic through an ultrasound, they can protect themselves from having their decision to terminate questioned, perhaps by a zealous prosecutor. But waiting for this can delay treatment by days or even weeks.
“Seeing a mass is not the only reason to have high suspicion for an ectopic pregnancy,” said Dr. Rebecca Nerenberg, an emergency medicine doctor in New York and the clinical director at Access Bridge, which educates ER doctors on reproductive healthcare and has released evidence-based guidelines for diagnosing possible ectopic pregnancies.
Experts say that doctors should be able to offer treatment when other symptoms are present, such as plateauing pregnancy hormone levels, bleeding and abdominal pain. Patients can be treated with a procedure or a cancer drug that stops cells from growing.
But for women in states with abortion bans, getting that treatment can be difficult.
Lowrimore, who lives near the state border in Oklahoma, sought care at an Arkansas emergency department in February after experiencing abdominal pain and significant bleeding. She was sent home and told to return for more tests after being diagnosed with a “pregnancy of unknown location,” because an ultrasound could not show where her pregnancy had implanted, according to a lawsuit.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lowrimore visited three different hospitals across both states over the following week as she began passing blood clots and the pain intensified, radiating up the left side of her body, according to the lawsuit.
The fact that the states’ abortion bans make exceptions for ectopic pregnancies did not help her, even though doctors acknowledged that was a possible diagnosis. In each visit, they didn’t treat her for that condition. One told her that intervening in her pregnancy could land him jail time — “10 years in the poky,” according to the suit. “I felt like my life was a risk he couldn’t afford,” she said in the lawsuit filing.
After consulting a lawyer, Lowrimore finally drove to a hospital in Kansas, where abortion is legal, and got an injection of the cancer drug called methotrexate within hours of arrival.
Arkansas abortion ban gets tweaked; pro-choice advocates plan “immersive” event

Lowrimore’s lawsuit, in which an OB-GYN and six women who were denied care are seeking to block the Arkansas abortion ban, is ongoing. Lowrimore also filed complaints under the same emergency medicine law as Thurman against the three hospitals. Regulators cited Mercy Hospital in Fort Smith, Arkansas, for failing to provide care during the eight hours Lowrimore waited to be seen. The other two hospitals were not found to have violated that law, and they did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Mercy Hospital declined to comment on the case, saying that, “in tragic situations when a mother suffers from an urgent, life-threatening condition during pregnancy, Mercy provides all medically indicated treatment to save her life.”
Many experts predicted that ordeals like the ones Lowrimore and Thurman described would occur when abortion bans took effect. To see if more women with ectopic pregnancies are experiencing severe health outcomes, ProPublica analyzed hospital data from Texas, the most populous state to ban abortion.
In this new analysis, ProPublica found that 310 more patients in Texas experienced substantial blood loss after an ectopic pregnancy in 2023 and 2024 compared with 2018 and 2019, an increase of about 29%. Similar to ectopic deaths, the rise appeared to begin during the COVID pandemic, but the rate of complications remained elevated after hospital systems stabilized and the state passed its restrictive law. ProPublica is working to acquire similar data from states without abortion bans.
In response to ProPublica’s reporting on the deadly impacts of Texas’ abortion ban, the state passed the Life of the Mother Act in 2025, which attempted to clarify what kinds of abortions are allowed by the state’s law, explicitly adding ectopic pregnancies to the list.
But new guidance from the Texas Medical Board includes only a case study with an ectopic pregnancy that can be seen in an ultrasound, remaining silent on the difficulty of early ultrasounds to detect where a pregnancy has implanted. This leaves open the possibility that a prosecutor could question whether such a case was really ectopic, in a state where doctors face up to 99 years in prison for performing illegal abortions.
A spokesperson for the Texas Medical Board said the course is not intended to cover all scenarios and that it “explains that imminent harm is unnecessary and specifically states that physicians who follow evidence-based medicine, standard emergency protocols, and proper documentation face minimal risk.” Asked whether a conclusive ultrasound image is necessary for an ectopic diagnosis, the spokesperson said, “The Board has consistently stated that providing commentary on every possible situation would be impractical.”
But Michelle Maloney, an attorney who represents Thurman and 13 other Texas women or their families who say they were denied care — including seven with ectopic pregnancies — said she still gets frequent calls from women who say they were denied care for pregnancy complications. “I don’t think specific exemptions address the massive gray areas that arise in pregnancy,” she said.
Solutions are unlikely to come from the states themselves. A previous ProPublica investigation found that states with strict bans are not studying whether their laws are contributing to maternal deaths. And others have not followed Texas in attempting to amend their bans.
Gaps in research, training and awareness 
One of the biggest challenges to reducing ectopic pregnancy deaths nationwide is the lack of awareness, research and data.
No one, for example, is tracking whether women who experienced ectopic pregnancies also had one or more common risk factors, like a history of ectopic pregnancies, infertility or use of hormonal intrauterine devices, according to ProPublica’s review of maternal health statistics and interviews with experts.
Nor has any published research addressed the connection between recent ectopic pregnancy death rates and untreated infections like gonorrhea and chlamydia, which increased substantially during the first years of the pandemic before declining again. Those infections can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which causes fallopian tube scarring and raises the long-term risk of developing an ectopic pregnancy.
It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. But experts say the country’s capacity to respond to it has been greatly reduced under President Donald Trump.
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, told Congress in April that improving maternal health outcomes is a priority. But the Trump administration has eliminated much of the staff devoted to researching the topic and cut hundreds of millions of dollars in government funding for healthcare research.
The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year. The entire division that ran the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System, a significant source of data for state and local governments as well as maternal health researchers, is on paid administrative leave. That includes many researchers who would have been responsible for investigating the rise in ectopic pregnancy deaths, according to current and former CDC employees.


Let us know what you think...


 

“You’re losing the capacity to know what’s going on with pregnant women,” Lee Warner, the former chief of the Women’s Health and Fertility Branch at the CDC, said of the cuts at the division. “It’s going to take decades to build this capacity back.”
Funding cuts have also impacted efforts to raise awareness about the condition. Because ectopic pregnancies usually cause complications before standard prenatal care begins around 10 weeks, patients often rely on emergency departments, where doctors don’t typically have specialized training in pregnancy care. Experts say more training on high-risk early pregnancy conditions could help combat rising maternal mortality rates.
The CDC in 2025 also stopped funding a partnership with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists to educate emergency medicine doctors about reproductive healthcare. The initiative, “Obstetric Emergencies in Nonobstetric Settings,” offers resources for emergency departments on caring for pregnant patients with cardiovascular disease, hypertension and eclampsia. An ACOG spokesperson said its foundation now funds the project, and that the organization is working on a set of guidelines for diagnosing and managing tubal ectopic pregnancies in the emergency department.
A spokesperson for HHS said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research. “This important work is being accelerated across the Department to support healthy mothers, healthy babies, and strong families,” the spokesperson said.
The United Kingdom’s response to a similar spike in ectopic deaths during the pandemic shows just how much the U.S. is failing to do.
Reproductive health care restrictions likely to repel provider workforce, research shows

Researchers and officials there identified a surge in deaths in 2021 and 2022 in the U.K. and Ireland; 12 women died of an ectopic pregnancy during those years, which, as in the U.S. during this period, represented a near doubling of the death rate compared with previous years.
They investigated the causes and found a range of culprits, including overstretched emergency services and inadequate early pregnancy screenings, says Marian Knight, a professor at the University of Oxford who leads the U.K.’s maternal mortality reporting.
In 2024, Knight co-authored a maternal mortality report that focused on those deaths and offered policy recommendations. Knight worked with policymakers and a U.K. charity to raise awareness and help doctors and the general public recognize ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Officials also changed how patients experiencing ectopic pregnancy symptoms are prioritized when they call for an ambulance, leading to faster response times.
But the first step, said Knight, was identifying and investigating the issue. “If we’re not tracking and not just understanding the numbers, but understanding the why behind the numbers, we have no ability to respond,” Knight said.
The U.S. doesn’t do national maternal mortality reviews, said Boston University’s Declercq, who serves on the Massachusetts Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Review Committee. Instead, CDC epidemiologists review death and birth records to establish accurate national totals of pregnancy-related deaths, largely leaving state and local maternal mortality committees to take an in-depth look at individual cases and make recommendations to lawmakers and medical providers.
Miscarriage patients have fewer treatment options in states with abortion bans, study shows

Declercq said his committee has not identified a notable increase in deaths from ectopic pregnancies in Massachusetts in recent years. In most states, these deaths are sporadic enough that they don’t, in isolation, show a notable trend.
It’s only at the national level that this increase in avoidable deaths becomes visible.
ProPublica’s analysis “raises concern that young women are dying from a preventable cause at an increasing rate,” Schreiber, the professor of OB-GYN, said. “That is not what we should be seeing in the United States of America.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How this CT ceramic artist applies AI to an ancient art form
description: Adam Chau uses AI to apply imagery to porcelain, creating traditional-looking work that couldn't have existed in ancient times—but does now.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

Adam Chau makes tangible what once seemed impossible, reimagining an ancient art form by pairing it with digital technology to depict — and celebrate — queer subjects.
Chau brings these subjects to life through ceramics, working with his hands, machines and, lately, artificial intelligence. To Chau, the technology is one of many artist’s tools that assists him in rendering images of people and histories that couldn’t otherwise exist.
“I want to work with technology, not against it,” Chau said. “Most of my work, there’s a little bit of hand. There’s a little bit of machine.”
Chau, who is Asian American and queer, is known for blending traditional blue-and-white porcelain with digital technology. 
Last year, Chau joined the Hartford Art School as the Edith Dale Monson Gallery director and curator. He manages the on-campus art program, and he’s responsible for maintaining the school’s art collection, coordinating art loans and presenting works by emerging mid-career and established artists throughout the U.S.
Chau’s interest in ceramics came about organically.
Born in Stamford and raised in Greenwich, Chau spent years learning the act of molding, baking and decorating in his family’s bakery. Those early lessons in shaping raw materials would soon follow him into his ceramics career. 
He first earned his BFA in studio ceramics from the Maine College of Art & Design and later a master’s degree from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, where he took courses in digital manufacturing and learned to use tools such as 3-D printers and lasers. 
The combination of handwork and machinery has since become central to Chau’s artistic practice, which is simultaneously traditional and contemporary. While crafted from clay, using skills developed by humans thousands of years ago, Chau’s pieces convey a modern awareness of a world in which digital technology is woven into every aspect of day-to-day life.
In “MESSENGER: a 21st Century Love Letter,” Chau used ceramics to craft a cellphone, which he inscribed with intimate messages to his husband, who was his long distance boyfriend at the time. The series was debuted in 2021 at the Northern Clay Center in Minneapolis.
“MESSENGER: a 21st Century Love Letter” by Adam Chau featured porcelain tiles in the shape of smartphones with messages exchanged with his future husband after they met in Italy.  Credit: Courtesy of Adam Chau
Art in the AI age
Ten years ago, Chau was wondering what his child might look like if he and his husband could conceive. Chau tried to answer the question with the technology available to him at the time, but eventually set the idea aside. The results couldn’t capture what he envisioned.
Then, about three years ago, a fellow artist inspired him to try AI.
Chau was interviewing Canadian ceramics artist Carole Epp on his podcast, Trade Secret. Epp was using AI in her work — which helped her find a new way to make art while she was undergoing treatment for breast cancer.
“It allowed me to still feel like I was being creative and sort of processing what I was actually going through at the time,” Epp said. 
For Epp, AI has almost become nearly inseparable from everyday life, much like the internet did years ago, she said. And she thought artists shouldn’t shy away from it.
“You can’t tell artists not to use a language or a technology that is being used all over the world,” she said in an interview with The Connecticut Mirror. “We want to play around with it too, and we want to figure out the boundaries of it, how it can be incorporated in different ways, and how it can be used positively.”

Credit: Courtesy of Adam Chau
Credit: Courtesy of Adam Chau
“Generated Love” by Adam Chau rendered in a blue-and-white Ming Dynasty porcelain style. The series reimagines a counterfactual history celebrating gay romance.
Epp’s experience inspired Chau. His first series of work using AI, “Generated Love,” explored an alternate ancient history — one in which queer love was celebrated.
Using an AI image generator called Midjourney, Chau created romantic images set during the Ming Dynasty, featuring men in traditional attire embracing and kissing. The images were then integrated into plates that resemble the kind of ancient artifacts one might see in a museum — but depicting people and lives that weren’t commonly portrayed at the time.
Chau’s artistic endeavors, bringing together ancient and modern, go beyond the pieces he crafts. 
Throughout his career, Chau has worked with several art organizations including Hudson Valley MOCA, ArtsWestchester, and Clay Art Center. He has also curated more than 20 exhibitions and has given lectures across the country and around the world about the relationship between the traditional craftsmanship of ceramics and digital technology. 
Chau’s work has also earned him international recognition. In 2018, he received the National Council on Education for the Ceramic Arts Emerging Artist Fellowship and since 2019, has been a member of the International Academy of Ceramics, a UNESCO partner organization.   
Since joining the Hartford Art School, Chau has produced six exhibitions. He is now curating a yearlong exhibition for the art school’s 150th anniversary next year. 
Hand and machine
One element remains consistent across Chau’s work: a blue-and-white palette rooted in the centuries-old history of Asian ceramics and his own Asian heritage. 
“AI afforded me the ability to make the images look old,” Chau said. “I can paint fairly well on ceramics but AI allowed me to have a different characteristic of the image.”
In 2024, “Generated Love” was shown in “Flights of Fiction,” an exhibition Chau curated at the Stonewall National Museum and Archives, one of the largest LGBTQ+ museums in the United States. Chau was the first Asian artist featured at the museum.  
As part of the exhibition, Chau chose to include works by Howard Kottler, a gay artist from the 1960s who was among the artists to begin putting images on plates. Chau wanted to honor the mentor he has never met, but whose works have also greatly influenced his own.  
When Robert Kesten, president of the museum, first saw one of Chau’s plates on a postcard, he said he was immediately struck by Chau’s creativity and intelligence. 
“He uniquely pulls together history, culture, and when I say history and culture, I mean we’re going back maybe a thousand years, maybe more than a thousand years, to Asian pottery and design all the way and then bringing it from a classic tradition in the Asian mindset to an LGBT mindset in the 21st century,” Kesten said. 
After “Generated Love,” Chau returned to the question he’d wondered about years earlier, envisioning a child he and his husband might conceive. He now had a tool to explore that vision.
Chau blended childhood pictures of himself and his husband, using Midjourney, and the result was Billie, a fictional son born from Chau’s imagination. 
Chau then brought Billie into the physical world, hiring a designer to create a 3-D model. After printing the model, Chau turned back to the traditional ceramic process of shaping the clay, allowing it to dry, and eventually painting it piece by piece. 

“Billie,” a blue-and-white porcelain sculpture by Adam Chau, from “The Joy and Sorrow of Imagining.” Chau created a fictional child using AI-generated images based on childhood photographs of himself and his husband. On view at the Northern Clay Center from September 19 to November 1.  Credit: Courtesy of Adam Chau

The three-year long project, “The Joy and Sorrow of Imagining,” will debut at the Northern Clay Studio in Minneapolis in September. Billie is the centerpiece of the exhibition.  
“The part that I find the most human is this introspective component that has led him to use AI in this way,” said Lauren Tucci, the studio’s exhibitions and collections manager. “It’s the desire of two people wanting to have children and only maybe one person being able to contribute to a biological child.”
Chau’s work, Tucci added, speaks to what it means to be human today while contributing to a larger conversation about art in the digital age.  
“Ceramics is a very traditional and at times stuck in traditions,” she said. “I think acknowledging our digital time is necessary. It’s a unique contemporary lens for ceramics specifically.” 
An imagined world
A few months ago, Chau started working with Michael Biello on the “Semiqueercentennial” exhibition at the Biello Martin studio in Philadelphia. The exhibition was part of “Radical Americana,” a large initiative organized by the Clay Studio in Philadelphia that paired artists and organizations to respond to America’s 250th anniversary. 
For Biello, 74, a ceramic and theater artist, and his partner, music producer Dan Martin, 73, the 37-year old Chau initially seemed to have come from a different world. 
The two grew up in a different generation and a different world where the technology that Chau incorporates into his work didn’t exist and where art meant a slow and physical process — one that can take weeks or years of creating. 
As Biello spent more time with Chau’s work, he began to see what their art had in common: queer love and intimacy.
But seeing how Chau used AI to imagine what queer love might have looked like in China made them a little less fearful of the technology. 
“I don’t use AI and I don’t even want to see it and I don’t really care about it,” Biello said. “But he changed my feeling of that because of the way he’s using it.”
Martin echoed that sentiment.
“I don’t think people are going to AI with that particular question. It’s his guiding of the technology that makes it beautiful.”
For Biello, the AI behind Chau’s work became less important than the stories he was using it to tell. 
“His work just generates love,” Biello said. “The AI piece of it and all of that becomes not that important to me anymore.”

Credit: Courtesy of The Clay Studio
Credit: Courtesy of The Clay Studio
Credit: Courtesy of The Clay Studio
“Presidential China” by Adam Chau, 2026, on view at the Philadelphia Museum of Art through December.
For “Radical Americana,” Chau turned to the long-running tradition of presidential china — the custom tableware each president selects for use in the White House. After researching the presidential china collection at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, he created a set of plates for a conceptual gay president. 
Like his other bodies of work, Chau’s presidential china involved digital technology, but no AI.
Jennifer Zwilling, curator and director of artistic programs at the Clay Studio who helped organize “Radical Americana,” said she appreciates that Chau’s work illustrates political ideas while imagining possibilities that have yet to exist. 
Zwilling, who has known Chau for a decade and is skeptical of the use of AI in the art field, said that Chau approaches technology differently. 
“There are people who sometimes get interested in new technologies and they let the new technology take over the process,” she said. “But Adam was doing it in a very smart and creative way to allow him to push his ideas forward rather than letting the tool kind of take the front seat.”
Recently, Chau published an article, “Our Obsession with Reality,” in Studio Potter that considers AI through the history of collage. Chau argues that AI is doing something artists have been doing for generations: taking existing images and elements and turning them into something new.  
“AI is doing the same thing,” Chau said. “It’s just doing it in a more seamless way.” 
But where AI will take the art world, Chau said, remains an open question.
“I really don’t know,” he said. “That is the question. I haven’t figured it out.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Who bankrolls Emporia’s data center bid is the $3 million question. The answer is sought in court.
description: Thank God for open courts. Secrecy has been a hallmark of the data center assault on rural America, and few subjects have been as secret — or as enigmatic — as the money behind the proposed “digital campus” for my town of Emporia, at the edge of the Flint Hills in east central Kansas. The […]
text:
A notice could be seen in June 2026 near the intersection of G and 190 roads at the west edge of Emporia, with Interstate 35 in the distance. The site is part of a proposed hyperscale data center that has sparked furious debate. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Thank God for open courts.
Secrecy has been a hallmark of the data center assault on rural America, and few subjects have been as secret — or as enigmatic — as the money behind the proposed “digital campus” for my town of Emporia, at the edge of the Flint Hills in east central Kansas. The stakes are enormous, and the fight over a thousand recently annexed and largely pastoral acres at the western edge of the city is representative of a conflict taking place just about everywhere.
The local land in question is the site of a proposed hyperscale data center that has broken local politics since the project was announced June 2. I don’t know any better word than broken to describe how a furious public backlash to the plan collided with defiant city officials to create an atmosphere of mutual distrust and suspicion. The result has been an unsettling of the municipal order that had kept Emporia a relatively stable, if somewhat dull, town for decades. The political froth has smeared just about every aspect of civic life here, rattling allegiances, challenging friendships and creating a general sense of unease.
It’s difficult to feel secure when the national conversation has been overtaken by experts warning of the existential threat to humanity posed by artificial intelligence. It’s as if thousands of privately funded Manhattan Projects are being plunked down in people’s backyards, with no government regulation, no oversight, and few answers about who exactly owns or controls the artificial brain bombs.
Small towns once felt like a haven from national news.
Now they are the headlines.
Despite days of public hearings, there has been little substantial information released about the investment behind the Emporia project. It’s difficult to tell if the city actually knows who put up the money behind Kanza Park Place, because it has denied or slow-walked open records requests seeking information. It’s disconcerting, considering the resources the city has thrown into annexing the land and creating special zoning regulations for the data center (and at present there is only the single proposal), all the while fending off an angry public. An enormous municipal machine has been built, yet we don’t know who really is behind the project.
But a recent filing in a sprawling Chapter 11 bankruptcy case in Georgia may eventually shed light on the ownership structure and finances of Kanza Park Place LLC, the Kansas entity that is the applicant of record. The debtor in the case, Gary Pinkston, has been touted as a benevolent neighbor and developer, but in sworn testimony in June, he said he had “no interest at all” in the project and received no compensation.
Just two days later, on June 25, Pinkston received a wire transfer of $3 million from Kanza Park Place, according to court documents. He had also received $20,000 from the same source a week earlier.
In addition, Pinkston had personally signed the rezoning applications.
The apparent inconsistency between Pinkston’s testimony and his actions is what prompted Meridian Pacific Holdings to ask the bankruptcy court on Sept. 4 to allow it to examine documents and other material held by Kanza Park Place and other non-debtor parties associated with Pinkston.
What is known about Kanza Park Place, the legal entity behind the Emporia Data Center project, can be summed up with a few lines: Kanza Park Place is a limited liability company, formed in October of last year, with a business address that is a lawyer’s office in downtown Emporia, and its registered agent is Garrett Nordstrom. That information comes from the Kansas Secretary of State, whose website requires you to identify pictures of handbags or other common items to prove you’re not a robot when searching for a business listing.
Nordstrom, the registered agent, is a governmental grant specialist from Lawrence and, from the outset, has been the spokesman for the Emporia project. Pinkston, the self-identified “master developer,” is an 84-year-old West Coast condo and shopping center developer who grew up in nearby Chase County. His home address is Tiburon, in Marin County, California.
On Tuesday I asked Nordstrom, via email, some questions.
Was Pinkston still connected to Kanza Park Place? 
If so, could he be trusted when he apparently lied under oath? 
Is Kanza Park Place still the developer of the Emporia data center and, if so, how would being subject to discovery in the bankruptcy proceeding affect the project?
“I appreciate the opportunity to explain and provide clarification,” Nordstrom responded. “I am aware of this but unfortunately will not be able to comment on this ongoing legal proceeding.”
Pinkston did not respond to a voicemail request for an interview.
The bankruptcy case seeks Chapter 11 protection for Pinkston personally and at least 17 limited liability companies or family trusts owned or managed by him. The bankruptcies were filed May 14, just weeks before the public announcement of the data center project.
Meridian, which Pinkston founded in 1988, is a group of investment and development companies with offices in California and Hawaii. It is now in conflict with Pinkston over Waikoloa Village Lofts West, a development project in Hawaii. Pinkston and Meridian have accused each other of fraud in cross claims associated with the bankruptcy, with a $28 million loan to Pinkston at the center of the dispute.
“Since the inception of this case, it has been clear Mr. Pinkston has used his numerous corporate entities as his personal piggy-bank,” according to Meridian’s motion. It seeks, under Rule 2004 of the federal bankruptcy code, the authority to subpoena the documents of Kanza Park Place and other non-debtor entities associated with Pinkston.
In the months before the bankruptcy filing, Meridan alleges, Pinkston transferred millions of dollars to himself or company insiders, and did not initially disclose those amounts to the bankruptcy court. The transfers appear to be “part of a convoluted shell game” among various Pinkston entities and trusts.
Meridian, the motion argues, “is clearly entitled to investigate, among other things, the transfer of funds between Kanza Park Place and Pinkston and the nature of such transfers” and “the ownership and capitalization of Kansas Park Place.”
Meridian also seeks to determine whether Kanza Park Place should be deemed part of Pinkston’s property in the bankruptcy proceeding.
In July, Emporia City Manager Trey Cocking said Pinkston’s bankruptcy case was a “non-factor” in the city’s consideration of zoning and other applications from Kanza Park Place. Cocking said it was his understanding that Pinkston had no financial interest in the project.
In June, Pinkston told a local radio station the bankruptcy would have no bearing on the Emporia data center. Nordstrom, the spokesman for Kanza Park Place, also said the bankruptcy did not reflect Pinkston’s career in real estate and would not determine the “feasibility” of the Emporia project.
Really?
It is difficult to believe individuals who are presumably familiar with business and law could not anticipate that creditors in Pinkston’s bankruptcy filing would be curious about the nature of his interest in the data center project. Such official myopia has been a civic contagion in Emporia, because not a single city official publicly questioned Pinkston’s background or his current financial troubles.
But the general public was clear-eyed.
The bankruptcy was a red flag for anybody paying attention.
A hearing on Meridian Pacific’s motion to examine Kanza Park Place is scheduled for Tuesday, Sept. 29, at the federal bankruptcy court in Gainesville (the cases were filed there because some of Pinkston’s business interests are in Georgia). If the motion is granted, we may finally get answers about the money behind the Emporia data center. A court has the power to compel responses and seek documents that ordinary citizens and journalists don’t.
But even if the motion isn’t granted, there’s value in those queries becoming part of the court record.
It is shameful that those questions weren’t part of every public meeting Emporia officials have had on the data center since June 2. But the city commission has voted unanimously to advance the data center at every step so far, ignoring pleas from the public for caution.
A citizen petition driven by Emporia Neighbors United has successfully placed a city data center ban on the November ballot. Similar petitions have been circulated in communities across Kansas, including El Dorado and Edgerton, with mixed results. Some cities, including Emporia, have sought declaratory judgments to block the petitions. If the Emporia petition is found to be primarily administrative in nature, the public vote will be moot.
Even if a judge determines the ban is a proper issue for voters to determine, it is not expected to impede the Kanza Park Place project, as city officials approved it before the petition was certified.
There’s more to the story of what has happened here since June 2, and it includes a recall petition against a city commissioner and a movement to change the structure of government from a commission to a council, to better represent working-class neighborhoods. I’ve already written about the protestor who was arrested during a city meeting for clapping and how an unexpected coalition formed to fight the data center.
For decades, Emporia has been a pleasant if sleepy college town whose legacy was that of a “heartland utopia” envisioned by editor and author William Allen White. In recent years it has lost hundreds of manufacturing and meat processing jobs, creating economic desperation of historic proportions. Civic leaders sought a big fish solution, and Pinkston and Kanza Park Place must have seemed like a whale. The choice, we’ve been repeatedly told by business leaders since early June, is to embrace progress or to wither away.
But the conversation cannot be reduced to progress versus provincialism. Those who engage in the expected arguments about environmentalism or economic development soon find they have lost the larger narrative driving people to action. The question is: who are we as a community?
The question is made sharper by the growing alarm over the speed at which AI is progressing. The irony is that rural America’s quest for jobs may ultimately contribute to a cataclysmic disruption for workers nationwide, as jobs are lost to technology at an unanticipated rate. Advances in computing technology can be a boon for humanity, but we’re not seeing revolutionary cancer cures. Instead, we’re witnessing an uncontrolled cyber arms race. The time for governmental regulation, international cooperation and strategic limits on AI is now.
We stand at a pivotal, if not terminal, moment in human history, taken by surprise at the speed at which it arrived. Just six years ago, we were paralyzed and separated by COVID. Now things are moving so fast it seems impossible to keep pace with a changing political, cultural and technological landscape. Yet we must not give in to exhaustion or despair, because the decisions we make now will either shape our communities for generations to come — or hasten their demise.
Some readers have objected to my referring to Emporia as “my town” in these columns, pointing out that I wasn’t born here. Others have said I don’t understand the community because I didn’t go to high school here. But citizens are more than accidents of birth or survivors of shared secondary education. After 20 years on Constitution Street, I can confidently say it is my town.
Just as the town where you live is your town, too.
Give me a community that values humanity over machines, compassion over profits, and fact over folksy fictions. Let us use technology with restraint and pursue economic development with wisdom. Give us competent judges and lawyers and open courts, transparent government and responsive lawmakers, reliable health care and food for all. Give us art and music and love. Let us make communities that are worthy of our best and most engaged selves. We cannot revisit the past, but we can imagine a future worth striving for.
No machine can, or should, do that for us.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The museum that owns its own railroad
description: It was in 1996 that the museum, which now has almost 100 rail cars in its collection, made its first passenger runs.
text:
Happy 30th birthday to the largest railroad museum in Connecticut, the Railroad Museum of New England in Thomaston.
It was in 1996 that the museum, which now has almost 100 rail cars in its collection, made its first passenger runs.  To celebrate there will be special excursion runs Saturday and Sunday Sept. 26 and 27, filled with happy rail fans.



What makes this railroad museum so different is that it owns a freight railroad, the Naugatuck Railroad, the proceeds from which help fund the museum and its extensive restoration efforts.
“The ‘Naugy’ began running in 1849,” says its president and railroad veteran Howard Pincus who also serves as Chairman of the Board for the Museum.  “The railroad played a major role in the development of industry in the Naugatuck Valley.”  Though the railroad’s tracks are now owned by the Connecticut Department of Transportation, the Naugy operates its trains over them, hauling construction debris and occasional freight as a short-line railroad connecting with CSX and Norfolk Southern.
“The CDOT Office of Rail has been a wonderful partner,” says Pincus, “especially on infrastructure repairs like bridges.”
Pincus says it’s a long haul up a steep grade to run any railroad — let alone one funding a museum.  Restoration of a single freight car can cost up to $40,000.  Repairing the old Thomaston train station has already cost the museum more than $100,000.  “It’s insanely expensive,” says Pincus, “especially to do it right.”
And it’s the artistry of the restoration work that sets the RMNE apart, even compared to the rail cars in the fine collections of the Danbury and Essex railroads.
The RMNE has its own restoration shops with six full-time artisans, many of them in their 20s.  “I want to make sure there’s some continuity [in our mission],” says Pincus.  “I’m absolutely thrilled when I walk in that shop and see young people doing such amazing [restoration] work.”

The RMNE restoration shop. Credit: Howard Pincus / RMNE.ORG Railroad Museum of New England

Like the 26-year-old self-taught metal fabricator and welder who rebuilt an old Canadian National passenger coach “down to iron oxide and thin air” and two weeks later rolled it out of the shop “looking like it just came from the Canadian Car and Foundry in Montreal,” said the proud Pincus.
As with any non-profit, the museum couldn’t function without a dedicated cadre of volunteers who do everything from catalog their archives to serve as train hosts.  So popular is the Thomaston site that volunteers journey from as far away as Long Island for the chance to lay hands on this living memorabilia.
Shop tours will be available for museum members with tour guides to manage down the enthusiasm of the “foamers” (a pejorative term used by railroad people to describe rabid rail fans who they believe may actually foam at the mouth when seeing old trains).
Both rail excursions (Saturday 9-26 and Sunday 9-27) will include “rare mileage”… the first time a passenger train has rolled over some of these tracks in many, many years.  But the stars of the trips will be the equipment including old Canadian passenger coaches and a GE U23 freshly painted to celebrate America’s 250th birthday.
The only question is, where will they mount the birthday candles.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa, national politicians court voters at CyHawk tailgates
description: IOWA CITY — Candidates vying for Iowa state and federal government positions joined football fans in Iowa City Saturday to engage with supporters before the football game between the Iowa Hawkeyes and Iowa State Cyclones. U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks held her annual Triple-M Tailgate with supporters and several guests, including U.S. Secretary of Homel[...]
text:
U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, left, Rep. Ashley Hinson, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and U.S. Sen. Rick Scott speak at Miller-Meeks's tailgate event on Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)IOWA CITY — Candidates vying for Iowa state and federal government positions joined football fans in Iowa City Saturday to engage with supporters before the football game between the Iowa Hawkeyes and Iowa State Cyclones.
U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks held her annual Triple-M Tailgate with supporters and several guests, including U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, Rep. Ashley Hinson, gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer, congressional candidate Joe Mitchell and others.
Republicans argued that if they aren’t elected, Democrats will make changes to the policies that they believe are common sense — supporting law enforcement, strengthening border control, stopping big government and providing tax relief to citizens.
“We know why we’re running. We know we’re here to serve you, and we know what we’re going to do,” Miller-Meeks said. “You also know what the other side is going to do. Don’t give them the opportunity to take away your opportunity.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Turek says Iowans want change
Democrat Josh Turek, facing off against Hinson in the U.S. Senate race, said at a tailgate near Kinnick Stadium that the football fans he’s spoken to expressed excitement for both the Hawkeyes and his campaign. Turek wore a Hawkeye shirt at the tailgate.
Polls from Rasmussen Reports and YouGov have reported Turek ahead of Hinson, with the first placing Turek at 45% of the vote and Hinson at 40% and the second reporting Turek as just one point ahead of Hinson at 44%.
Rep. Josh Turek speaks to tailgaters in Iowa City on Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
While Republicans at Miller-Meeks’ event said Democrats are seeking to change the foundations of the U.S. for the worse, Turek said he’s fighting for the American dream that young people have told him they’re afraid of never achieving. Iowans have said they’re tired of what they’re seeing in the state and federal government and are ready for a change.
One young Republican Turek said he spoke to told him he was worried about never being able to own a home. Young people are “worried about the same things that we all are,” Turek said, including rising costs, corruption, affordable housing and healthcare, earning a livable wage and having access to clean drinking water.
“I want to make sure that the American dream continues, and I want to make sure we’ve got someone in D.C. that is fighting for the people, not just the billionaires and large corporations,” Turek said. “Or not going up to D.C. to make yourself more wealthy but actually doing the work of the people.”
Hinson, among Republicans supporting Miller-Meeks Saturday, said she’s ready for the challenge of filling retiring Sen. Joni Ernst’s shoes. Wearing an Iowa State shirt, she said she is still focused on the three things she identified when she first ran for office — protecting taxpayers, ensuring rural Americans have a voice and ensuring “we have a safe and secure country.”
Republicans emphasize importance of Iowa races
Miller-Meeks, who sported a Hawkeye shirt on Saturday, is running for reelection in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District — which includes Iowa City — against Democrat Christina Bohannan.
Democrats no longer believe in Iowans or “in the beauty and the promise and opportunity of our nation,” Miller-Meeks said, but she and other Republicans are not “ashamed” but proud of America and being “American-made.”
Lahn said Democrats have been focusing on just bad things going on, and while he acknowledged there are things “we still need to work on,” he emphasized that “change is not a campaign platform.”
Gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn spoke to voters at U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller Meeks’s annual tailgate event on Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Democrats’ goal is to make voters believe that “your life is terrible and it’s somebody else’s fault,” he said, but there are many good things, including Iowa’s high rankings in affordability, opportunity and quality of a place to retire. However, he said, there are things that need to be improved, and his priorities include keeping kids in Iowa, increasing and supporting family farms, ensuring quality education and “the health of our people.”
U.S. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, who said he won races after recounts just like Miller-Meeks, told the crowd of supporters Miller-Meeks is the “epitome of the American woman” — someone who worked hard their whole life, has served people in her role as a doctor and will keep fighting to serve them in her government role.
Miller-Meeks shared the story of her upbringing and said the reason she decided to run for office was that she was tired of “big insurance companies and big government” hurting the patients she worked with.
If Iowa had a Democrat in the governor’s office during the start of the COVID-19 pandemic and not a Republican, Scott claimed, they would have ruined the state’s economy and kept children from attending school entirely. He added that all Democrats are socialists, although no Iowa Democrats running for statewide or federal office accept that label.
“These statewide races matter,” Scott said. “If you want more jobs, you want school choice, you want to live in a safe community, if you don’t elect your statewide candidates, it’s going to change.”
Miller-Meeks’ and Hinson’s races are also incredibly important in ensuring Republican majorities in the U.S. House and Senate, Scott said. If there aren’t Republican majorities, he said “nothing good will happen for two years.” Supporting law enforcement, school choice and growing jobs would all go away under Democrats, he said.
Republicans attack Democrats on immigration 
Mullin went further than Scott and called all Democrats “communists,” a point he said President Donald Trump has made before. Democrats are trying to turn the U.S. into a communist country by sowing chaos, which he said former president Joe Biden did by allowing illegal immigration. He said Trump has provided the tools to fix things through policy and law enforcement but Iowans must do their part in the voting booths.
Communism involves the seizure of the means of production and other resources by the government — something no Iowa candidates are advocating.
Reading an artificial intelligence-generated summary from an internet search on how to turn “a red state blue,” Mullin said one would need to shift demographics through encouraging migration and investing in voter registration efforts for new and returning voters. The plan isn’t to change people’s minds with good ideas, he said, but to bring enough people in to drown out others.
Republicans are the party of “common sense,” Mullin said, as it makes sense to not support criminals, to secure U.S. borders, to support law enforcement and provide “tax breaks for everybody.”
“By them allowing or wanting open borders, and then not deporting those that are in this country (illegally), it’s because they’re trying to change the fabric of our country, the foundation of our country, and it starts and races just like Miss Miller-Meeks’,” Mullin said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts political parties stand by as their membership rolls evaporate
description: Why Massachusetts parties are allowing the slow-moving self-destruction to continue is anyone’s guess.
text:
NEW PARTY REGISTRATION figures released by the secretary of state’s office once again show Massachusetts party membership withering. The newly released data show about 62,000 fewer party members compared to 2025 data, continuing the slide that began in 2020. At the same time, the number of unenrolled voters not affiliated with any party grew by over 220,000.  
Contrary to what seems to be the gathering consensus, these trends do not reflect voters’ growing contempt for parties or distrust of institutions. Although party leaders and others regularly cite these factors as driving the decline in registration, there’s a much more prosaic explanation: What’s happening instead is new voters are being funneled into the “unenrolled” category due to the design of the state’s registration system. 
In 2018, the Massachusetts Legislature passed a law automatically registering to vote any eligible resident who interacted with various state agencies. That includes anyone getting or renewing a driver’s license, applying for a state ID, applying for MassHealth benefits, or applying for health insurance through the state health connector. Crucially, these automatic voter registration systems do not collect party preference data at the time of registration, instead putting all new registrants in the unenrolled category. The system went into operation in 2020.  
The result has been a predictable flood of unenrolled voters while new party registrants have slowed to a trickle. This has been happening since 2020, and it continues today, even while many of these same voters hold strong party preferences and partisan views and would undoubtedly register with a party if presented with a clear opportunity. 
We can see a partial view of the impacts of automatic voter registration by looking at the Massachusetts state voter file and comparing party registrations in pre- and post-AVR years. As the chart below shows, Democrats tumbled to 19 percent of voters registering or reregistering since AVR, while Republicans are down to just 6 percent. Both of these are precipitous declines.  



But it’s actually far more severe than this. A large, but unknowable number of these Democratic or Republican registrants are actually voters re-registering at a new address. When voters move within the state, they carry their party membership with them to their new address when they re-register. This has the effect of making it look like more post-AVR registrants are joining parties than actually are. Unfortunately, we do not have data that allows us to isolate only first-time registrants from the pre- and post-AVR periods.  
The closest we can get is by looking at voters who turned 18 and registered in the five years since AVR, and comparing them to the cohort that turned 18 and registered in the five years before AVR began. Doing so produces the table below, which is perhaps the clearest display of the destruction AVR has brought to the Massachusetts parties’ membership. A full 87 percent of young, first-time registrants are unenrolled, a 23.5-point jump from immediately before AVR.  



There’s another wrinkle. AVR is by far the most common way to register. According to a separate report from the secretary of state’s office, 75 percent of registrations between 2022 and 2024 were through the AVR system. But voters can still register at their local town halls, by mail, or online, all of which offer opportunities to join a party. It is possible, even likely, that what few new voters are registering with parties are using one of these methods, while new AVR registrants are almost entirely unenrolled. We don’t know for sure, as that level of detailed data does not appear to be tracked.  
As voters leave the Massachusetts rolls, either through death, inactivity, or leaving the state, the party registration numbers will continue to decline. As voters join through AVR, the unenrolled number will continue to increase. What we are seeing is the result of a mechanism that is running unchecked. If left unchanged, it will end party registration as we’ve known it.  
This outcome is not predetermined, even if we embrace the goal of registering voters automatically. There are ways to run AVR systems that are less destructive to party rolls.  
In California, for example, eligible voters are also added to the rolls when they register for a driver’s license, just like in Massachusetts. Crucially, they are also asked for party preference, which does not happen in Massachusetts, where voters are sent a postcard at a later date telling them how to register for a party if they want to. The impacts are clear. For the four years of new registration data California has reported, party preferences for DMV registrants are nearly identical to overall state voter rolls. In fact, slightly more DMV registrants have chosen to register with a major party compared to the state’s overall voter population.  



Here in Massachusetts, legislators have taken no action to plug the leak in their own party membership. Party leaders themselves responded to the release of new membership data without addressing the actual issue.  
“Party registration is changing because Massachusetts is changing. Voters are looking for something different,” said Massachusetts Republican Party executive director Haley Jones, taking a swipe at one-party rule by Democrats. Meanwhile, Steve Kerrigan, chair of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, said “partisan politics has become a pretty ugly business,” and “[a]verage, everyday voters out there are trying to find leaders to vote for who are going to try to solve their problems.”  
Why Massachusetts parties are allowing the slow-moving self-destruction to continue is anyone’s guess. One might imagine both parties would rather have more members than fewer. But without clear intervention, party membership will continue to evaporate, and not because of any choices voters are making. 
Steve Koczela is president of the MassINC Polling Group.

Doing so produces the table below, which is perhaps the clearest display of the destruction AVR has brought to the Massachusetts parties’ membership. A full 87 percent of young, first-time registrants are unenrolled, a 23.5-point jump from immediately before AVR.  



There’s another wrinkle. AVR is by far the most common way to register. According to a separate report from the secretary of state’s office, 75 percent of registrations between 2022 and 2024 were through the AVR system. But voters can still register at their local town halls, by mail, or online, all of which offer opportunities to join a party. It is possible, even likely, that what few new voters are registering with parties are using one of these methods, while new AVR registrants are almost entirely unenrolled. We don’t know for sure, as that level of detailed data does not appear to be tracked.  
As voters leave the Massachusetts rolls, either through death, inactivity, or leaving the state, the party registration numbers will continue to decline. As voters join through AVR, the unenrolled number will continue to increase. What we are seeing is the result of a mechanism that is running unchecked. If left unchanged, it will end party registration as we’ve known it.  
This outcome is not predetermined, even if we embrace the goal of registering voters automatically. There are ways to run AVR systems that are less destructive to party rolls.  
In California, for example, eligible voters are also added to the rolls when they register for a driver’s license, just like in Massachusetts. Crucially, they are also asked for party preference, which does not happen in Massachusetts, where voters are sent a postcard at a later date telling them how to register for a party if they want to. The impacts are clear. For the four years of new registration data California has reported, party preferences for DMV registrants are nearly identical to overall state voter rolls. In fact, slightly more DMV registrants have chosen to register with a major party compared to the state’s overall voter population.  



Here in Massachusetts, legislators have taken no action to plug the leak in their own party membership. Party leaders themselves responded to the release of new membership data without addressing the actual issue.  
“Party registration is changing because Massachusetts is changing. Voters are looking for something different,” said Massachusetts Republican Party executive director Haley Jones, taking a swipe at one-party rule by Democrats. Meanwhile, Steve Kerrigan, chair of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, said “partisan politics has become a pretty ugly business,” and “[a]verage, everyday voters out there are trying to find leaders to vote for who are going to try to solve their problems.”  
Why Massachusetts parties are allowing the slow-moving self-destruction to continue is anyone’s guess. One might imagine both parties would rather have more members than fewer. But without clear intervention, party membership will continue to evaporate, and not because of any choices voters are making. 
Steve Koczela is president of the MassINC Polling Group.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Clamorous crowd dominates first Kansas U.S. Senate debate between Marshall, Hamilton
description: HUTCHINSON — Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, confronted a raucous crowd Saturday defending their stances on tariffs, the war in Iran and partisan politics. The two major party candidates running for U.S. Senate appeared in their first post-primary debate together in front of hundreds of people who […]
text:
Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton and Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall debate Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)HUTCHINSON — Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, confronted a raucous crowd Saturday defending their stances on tariffs, the war in Iran and partisan politics.
The two major party candidates running for U.S. Senate appeared in their first post-primary debate together in front of hundreds of people who filled the bleachers at the Kansas State Fair. 
The scales of attendance at times tilted in Hamilton’s favor, as people booed, jeered and heckled Marshall’s answers.
Marshall defended his record on agriculture and was forced to reckon with his loyalty to President Donald Trump, though he said he disagreed with Trump’s promise to offer $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans won the midterms.
“This is not the first time I’ve disagreed with President Trump, and it probably won’t be —” Marshall said before he was cut off by shouts from the crowd. “You know, instead, I’m going to be focused on Kansas jobs. I’m going to be focused on protecting Kansas agriculture and the Kansas cattle industry.”
Hamilton said: “This is exactly what’s wrong in Washington, D.C., right now.”
The debate was hosted by WIBW 580 Radio and featured questions from a panel of three journalists, including Kansas Reflector senior reporter Tim Carpenter. Absent from the stage was David Graham, a Libertarian candidate for U.S. Senate from Overland Park, who wasn’t invited to participate.
Marshall is finishing his first term in the U.S. Senate, having previously served two terms in the U.S. House and working as an obstetrician gynecologist in Great Bend before that. Hamilton is the founder of one of the largest United Methodist churches in the country, Church of the Resurrection, which is a multi-campus operation headquartered in Leawood.
Adam Hamilton, a Democrat running for U.S. Senate appears Sept. 12, 2026, on the Kansas State Fair debate stage in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Hamilton beat out nine other Democratic candidates in the August primary and out-fundraised Marshall.
Marshall tried to paint Hamilton as anti-agriculture, against the cattle industry and against oil and gas. 
“If he had his way, he’d go put a plastic bag over the mouths of these dairy cows back here,” Marshall said, motioning to the livestock building on the state fairgrounds.
Hamilton slammed Marshall’s record in the U.S. Senate, criticizing his support for Trump’s tariffs, inaction on the war in Iran and cuts to healthcare and food assistance.
He said the Trump administration’s recent decision to import beef from Mexico was “a slap in the face” to Kansas cattle producers and “came exactly at the wrong time.”
He said Marshall was voted to be a champion for Kansans, not “a spokesperson for the White House.”
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a Republican, appears on Sept. 12, 2026, at a debate at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Marshall said the decision was because of drought, the “smallest cattle herd of my life,” and “government overregulation.” The Democratic party has “strangled the ag industry,” he said.
“My opponent is too woke, he’s too weak and he doesn’t stand for anything,” Marshall said.
But Hamilton was firm in his belief that the country is going in the wrong direction.
“You’ve got to have courage,” Hamilton said, “and courage is when you stand up to your president and your party, and you say, ‘This is hurting people back home.’ And you say it even if your president’s going to bully you, pick on you, primary you, and call you names. You still say, ‘This is not OK.’ ”
Graham, the Libertarian who will appear on the November ballot as an option for U.S. Senate, watched the debate from the pavilion’s bleachers.
He said he is a better option for voters than either Marshall or Hamilton because he wouldn’t be beholden to leadership of either the Republican or Democratic party. That would allow him to do what’s best for Kansans, he said.
Graham, who noted that he doesn’t own a home outside of Kansas, said if he could have appeared onstage, his opening statement would have been about the need for less government and more freedom.
“When we do that, we’ll have free enterprise that takes care of a lot of these problems for themselves,” Graham said. “Problems involving inflation, which is due to overregulation. Problems involving the cost of health care. We’ve never really tried the free enterprise system, so that would be my opening statement. I believe in transparency in government, and I think we ought to have serious criminal justice reform.”
Hamilton and Marshall also answered questions about their multiple homes — Marshall’s vacation property in Florida and Hamilton’s vacation home in the Missouri Ozarks — controversies that have arisen during their campaigns, health care, the job market, immigration and the national debt.
Sherman Smith contributed to this report.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In scorching Kansas State Fair debate, governor candidates fight over taxes, data centers, vouchers
description: HUTCHINSON — Candidates for governor engaged in a veritable bare-knuckle brawl when they took the stage Saturday at the Kansas State Fair for a debate punctuated by the chants and jeers of an enthusiastic crowd of dueling supporters. Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee, and state Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee, largely [[...]
text:
Supporters of Republican Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson and Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher cheer and jeer during a raucous gubernatorial debate Sept. 12, 2026, at the state fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)HUTCHINSON — Candidates for governor engaged in a veritable bare-knuckle brawl when they took the stage Saturday at the Kansas State Fair for a debate punctuated by the chants and jeers of an enthusiastic crowd of dueling supporters.
Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee, and state Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee, largely sidestepped pointed questions from a news media panel as they argued over who was more extreme and how to make life affordable for state residents.
The crowd that filled the Heartland Credit Union Pavilion at times drowned out the candidates. Holscher supporters carried signs that poked fun at Masterson’s “no-show” job at Wichita State University, where he was paid nearly a million dollars since 2017 as director of “GoCreate, a Koch Collaborative.” Masterson supporters waved signs that read “Cue card Cindy,” a reference to Holscher’s preference to bring notes with her on stage at the debate.
Masterson, of Andover, said he was running for governor to make sure working families can afford to live in Kansas and stop people from being taxed out of their homes.
“I will be the most pro-ag, pro-business, pro-oil and gas governor this state has ever seen,” he said. “That is how we bring opportunity to our people.”
He repeatedly defined Holscher as a socialist and the “most radical liberal progressive that’s ever been on a ticket” in Kansas.
“I am no socialist,” she responded. “But Ty keeps saying ‘socialist’ and ‘extreme.’ Do you know what’s extreme? Opposing health care when people are struggling. That’s extremist. What else is extreme? Opposing raising the minimum wage for our people while he’s collecting a million dollars from a no-show job. That’s extreme.”
Greg Akagi of WIBW 580 Radio moderated the debate with questions posted by Kansas Reflector senior reporter Tim Carpenter, KWCH-TV’s Michael Schwanke, and Gras and Grain editor and publisher Donna Sullivan.
Holcher, of Overland Park, said she was running for governor because of the affordability crisis that is hitting everywhere in the state. She said property taxes are so high because a Legislature led by Masterson keeps giving tax breaks to corporations and the wealthy. She pointed out that Masterson has led the state Senate for six years with a GOP supermajority, and she blamed him for failing to lower property taxes.
“He either doesn’t want to do this or doesn’t know how,” she said. “I will get it done.”
She also called for the state to invest more in public schools to ease the local tax burden.
“Just listen to the words coming out of her mouth,” Masterson said. “You think the answer to affordability is more government spending? You think that’s the answer? That’s the opposite of what is true. The truth of why your taxes are so high is because people like Cindy have not met one of your tax dollars she didn’t want to spend two of.”
Holscher said there was a “very big difference” between the two when it came to tax policy. Masterson, she said, favors tax breaks for his donors while she favors tax breaks for working people. She promised to invest more in communities.
Masterson at times shouted down a chorus of boos from Holscher supporters.
“You guys think you’re going to get more affordability by higher taxes?” he said. “I mean, process that through your brains.”
 
Republican Ty Masterson attacks Democrat Cindy Holscher’s position on tax policy during the Sept. 12, 2026, state fair debate in Hutchinson. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Abortion rights
Masterson asserted during the debate that the constitutional amendment that voters rejected in August wasn’t about abortion. The amendment would have made Kansas Supreme Court justices elected officials, and Masterson previously argued in favor of the amendment because he said it would allow the court to overturn abortion rights in Kansas.
Masterson’s additional assertion that “abortion is an 80-20 issue” was met with chants of “liar, liar” from Holscher supporters. He said people want fewer abortions, no late-term abortions and no taxpayer-funded abortions.
Holscher said Kansas voters made their position known in 2022 when they shot down a different constitutional amendment that was purely about eliminating the right to terminate a pregnancy. After that failed by a 59-41 margin, she said, Masterson decided to try again with this year’s amendment, which failed by a 61-39 margin.
“He keeps attacking reproductive health care, and that’s what he will keep doing if you elect him governor,” she said. “The attacks will be unrelenting on your rights.”
Masterson responded by accusing Holscher of supporting elitists.
“She wants the power of the smallest group of people possible,” he said.
“When did 60% become the smallest group?” Holscher answered, referring to the popular vote.
Masterson then pivoted to a new topic, accusing Holscher of wanting to allow children to undergo “transgender surgeries” without their parents’ knowledge. Her supporters booed in response.
“It’s in the record! Look it up! Look. It. Up,” Masterson shouted at the crowd, which booed louder. “This is not up for debate. It’s in the record. You’re denying the truth.”
 
Democrat Cindy Holscher says during the Sept. 12, 2026, state fair debate in Hutchinson that Republican Ty Masterson will keep “attacking reproductive health care” if elected governor. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)
Data centers
Holscher, who has called for a temporary moratorium on data centers, attacked Masterson for supporting for their development. She said artificial intelligence companies spent $800,000 on advertising to support Masterson during the primary.
“Ty is gonna put a data center on every corner and every cornfield,” Holscher said.
Masterson said his position on data centers had never changed, a dig at Holscher, who voted with him in favor of legislation last year that provides a tax exemption for large data center developments. He said data centers will bring property tax dollars to communities.
“Let the locals make the decision,” he said.
 
From left, KWCH-TV’s Michael Schwanke, Grass and Grain editor and publisher Donna Sullivan, and Kansas Reflector senior reporter Tim Carpenter question candidates during the Sept. 12, 2026, state fair debate in Hutchinson. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)
School vouchers
Masterson said he supports private school vouchers because it isn’t fair to leave kids in a position where their only option is a failing school.
“They’ll learn generational welfare, or they’ll learn crime pays,” he said.
Pointing at Holscher, he added: “All this is blindness to those kids that are trapped.”
Holscher highlighted his support for former Gov. Sam Brownback’s failed tax experiment and cuts to public education spending.
“I don’t know what you’d expect,” she said. “You defunded our schools to the crisis point. You’re the person who made it difficult for these children to do well.”
