title: Newark Charter Football Improves to 2-0 in Second Varsity Season
description: The Newark Charter Patriots (2-0) defeated the Odessa Ducks (1-1), 13-0, in a road game played on September 11. It’s the program’s second win against a Class 2A opponent and first against Odessa.   TOWNSEND, DE — Newark Charter quarterback Chase Kennedy lined up in the pistol formation five yards behind where the ball was being snapped at the Odessa ... Read[...]
text:
Newark Charter junior Lucas Erunchak jumps in the endzone following one of his two touchdown runs against Odessa. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
The Newark Charter Patriots (2-0) defeated the Odessa Ducks (1-1), 13-0, in a road game played on September 11. It’s the program’s second win against a Class 2A opponent and first against Odessa.
 
TOWNSEND, DE — Newark Charter quarterback Chase Kennedy lined up in the pistol formation five yards behind where the ball was being snapped at the Odessa 31 yard line. Standing two yards behind Kennedy was junior running back Lucas Eruncak, the lone touchdown scorer in the game.
Senior center Brayden Scannell snapped the ball to Kennedy who handed the ball off to his left. Erunchak took the handoff and found running room up the middle of the field, running full speed past the outstretched arms of Duck defenders. Erunchak made it past the Duck defense and ran 31 yards for his second touchdown of the game with less than three minutes remaining in the third quarter.
Erunchak finished the game with over 100 rushing yards, the game’s only two touchdowns and a pair of sacks helping Newark Charter defeat Odessa, 13-0, Friday night.
“Honestly it’s amazing,” Erunchak said after the game. “We came out here with the right energy like we do all the time and I’m just like so excited.” 
Erunchak’s first score came in the second quarter on a run from the Odessa nine yard line. The first touchdown run came from a similar play call as the Patriots’ second score, with Erunchak lined up behind Kennedy in the pistol formation and the handoff to the quarterback’s left side. Instead of running up the middle, Erunchak broke to the outside and ran into the endzone for the touchdown.
“I’m so proud of how our [offensive] line handled everything,” Erunchak said. “I give all the praise to them.”
The touchdown run was the only points scored in the first half despite both teams working their way down the field and earning red zone opportunities. Odessa drove into the red zone twice in the first half, but penalties and strong defensive play by the Patriots defense inhibited their ability to score. Newark Charter’s other first half red zone opportunity was thwarted by an interception from Odessa senior Thomas Ngateh.
Odessa senior Thomas Ngateh celebrates with his teammates after his interception in the first half. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
Erunchak’s second touchdown run late in the third quarter completed the game’s scoring. The Patriot defense held the Ducks out of the endzone and helped the Class 1A program earn its first shutout victory against a Class 2A opponent. The Patriots defense finished the game with four sacks and two interceptions.
“Heart, we all got heart,” Newark Charter senior Alexander Burrows said postgame about what makes the Patriots defensive line dynamic. “Coaching, players, we all want it, we want it really bad.”
Newark Charter’s defense has allowed six points through the first two games of the 2026 season.
“We’ve been talking about kind of all week, you know, trying to find something we can hang our hat on and very encouraging tonight to watch these guys come out and how they swarmed defensively,” Patriot head coach Jody Russell said postgame. “I think we might have found something that we can hang our hat on which is good.”  
Newark Charter’s win improves its record to 2-0 on the season as the Patriots try to return to the Class 1A title game as they did a year ago. Last year, the Patriots finished their inaugural varsity season as the runner-up to Class 1A champion, Seaford. The Patriots only losses during that season came against the aforementioned Blue Jays and Odessa.
The Patriots next game will be at home against another Class 2A opponent, the Tatnall Hornets. Newark Charter and Tatnall matched up last season and the Patriots emerged victorious, 22-21, earning the program’s first win against a Class 2A opponent. This year’s iteration of the game will be played on September 18, at 7:00 p.m.
The Ducks will return to action on September 19, in a road matchup against the Glasgow Dragons. That game will be played at Glasgow High School and start at 11:00 a.m.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Galvin defends ballot questions as a ‘safety valve’ amid reform push
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: Lawmakers this year could move forward with changes to how initiative petitions get on the ballot. Now, other voices are also starting to weigh in, amid a particularly active election cycle for citizen-led petitions.
text:
AS LAWMAKERS WEIGH REFORMS to the ballot question process, the state’s top election official called it a “safety valve for democracy,” and said “you might change some of the procedures, but you shouldn’t change the concept.”
The House passed a bill in July to expand disclosure rules for ballot question campaigns and impose new requirements around paid signature gathering. That version was an expansion of a bill the Senate passed in January to require more public reporting on ballot question fundraising and spending.
The House bill calls for a special legislative commission to review the entire initiative petition process as laid out in the Massachusetts Constitution, with an end-of-2027 deadline to recommend statutory and constitutional amendments to change the process. The bills picked up momentum as lawmakers have grown frustrated with the process that allows citizens to get around the Legislature to make new laws.
They are now in House-Senate negotiations, and lawmakers could produce a compromise before the end of the year that changes how initiative petitions get on the ballot. Now, other voices are also starting to weigh in, amid a particularly active election cycle for citizen-led petitions.
There are nine questions going before voters in November — a tie for the most in state history. Secretary of State William Galvin, the state’s top election official, said they stand out even more this year for how diverse and complex the measures are.
Asked Tuesday if he worried voters might stop voting before getting to the end of their lengthy ballot in November, Galvin said, “I hope that doesn’t happen.”
“People have an opportunity here. However it came about, because of legislative inactivity, whatever it is, nevertheless, I think it’s important that people have the opportunity to understand these questions,” he said.
“This process of citizen lawmaking is really something … that emerged from the so-called reform effort of the last century, and it was a national effort that basically said, yes, it’s great to give the Legislature authority, but there was a distrust of the Legislature, and they wanted to make sure that people retain that authority,” Galvin added.
Used to controlling the lawmaking process, legislators have expressed discontent with the number and content of ballot questions this year.
House Speaker Ron Mariano said this summer that the Legislature’s efforts to change the process are a response “to widespread concerns.”
“Over the past several years, we have seen a growing number of well-funded special interest groups turn to the ballot to advance their agendas through one up-or-down vote, bypassing the negotiation and compromise inherent to the legislative process,” Mariano said. “Oftentimes, the opposition is equally well-resourced, which has led to high-stakes litigation and, in some cases, judicial removal of questions from the ballot.”
Galvin said Tuesday that the process is “meant to empower the people. It’s meant as an alternative to legislative action when there either has been none or it’s not popular.”
“So it gives people that safety valve for democracy,” he said. “There’s been discussion about, is it something we should change? Well, maybe you might change some of the procedures, but you shouldn’t change the concept, and you require a constitutional amendment to change the concept. I don’t think that’s going to happen.”
The Pioneer Institute released a study last week that recommended a different set of reforms to the ballot initiative process.
The conservative think tank was one of the main sponsors this year of a measure to cut income taxes, which the Supreme Judicial Court knocked off the ballot after it found Attorney General Andrea Campbell wrote a summary of the measure that was “significantly misleading and likely to influence voters.”
“In 2026, the SJC ultimately struck down three petitions, which if passed would have reinstated rent control, reformed stipend allocations in the Massachusetts Legislature, and reduced the income tax rate,” the Pioneer Institute wrote in its report.
It continued, “Combined, these campaigns raised more than $2.7 million and spent at least $1.6 million in 2025 alone. The SJC deemed the rent control and stipend reform petition language unconstitutional. The income tax cut measure was thrown off the ballot not because of a flaw with the petition itself, but because the SJC deemed the Attorney General’s summary misleading after it had already been presented to voters during the signature gathering process.”
The report said lawmakers’ proposed reforms would not fix issues with the process, but instead “severely restrict it,” by “increasing geographic signature requirements, increasing campaign finance disclosures, restricting paid signature collection, raising vote thresholds for certain ballot items, and expanding the Legislature’s ability to override voter-approved measures.”
The Pioneer Institute recommends, instead, earlier judicial review for all of the questions, as well as a lengthened period available for signature collection.
“In cases where the petition’s flaws are truly the fault of proponents, an earlier rejection may be a more fair and efficient outcome,” it says. “In cases where the petition summary is at fault, earlier judicial review of the petition would also make it easier to justify amending the summary language rather than keeping the measure off the ballot.”
For the first round of signature collection — the highest threshold a measure faces — campaigns have 64 days to collect signatures equal to 3% of votes cast for governor in the most recent gubernatorial election.
“Giving campaigns more time would reduce the incentive to hire outside signature-gathering firms and allow campaigns greater opportunity to collect signatures through their own supporters while preserving existing signature requirements and safeguards,” the report says.
Since Massachusetts adopted the initiative and referendum process in 1917, it said, voters have considered 231 statewide ballot measures and approved nearly 70 percent of them.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: $10M Omaha residential facility for combat-maimed vets aims to heal wounds medicine can’t
description: OMAHA — The scene was seared into John Folsom’s mind. On a visit to Bethesda Naval Hospital around 2010, he met a young soldier severely brain-damaged by a war device that exploded near his head during a mission in Iraq. The patient’s mom was at his bedside, holding her son’s hand. He was unable to speak, […]
text:
A dedication event for the Dunham House in Omaha, a long-term assisted living facility for veterans severely maimed in combat, kicked off Friday with a flag ceremony. The 30-unit residential complex is in the background. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner) OMAHA — The scene was seared into John Folsom’s mind.
On a visit to Bethesda Naval Hospital around 2010, he met a young soldier severely brain-damaged by a war device that exploded near his head during a mission in Iraq.
John Folsom, executive director of the Dunham House, calls to the podium Katie Saybolt, a Navy nurse who helped treat mortally wounded Jason Dunham in 2004 when both were stationed in Iraq. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
The patient’s mom was at his bedside, holding her son’s hand. He was unable to speak, but his eyes seemed to light up when a guitarist started to serenade a familiar tune, recalled Folsom, a retired U.S. Marine colonel. Also a parent, Folsom couldn’t shake his worry for the impaired soldier’s future, wondering what would happen once aging caretaker parents were gone. 
“I call it my epiphany,” said Folsom, a Nebraskan who recently relocated to Florida. “That’s what moved me to say, ‘We’ve got to do something here.’ It’s taken years and years and years … ”
But on Friday, coinciding with the anniversary of 9/11, Folsom and a few hundred supporters gathered to dedicate the “long time coming” project he helped plan and raise roughly $10 million to build: an assisted living care facility tailored for veterans severely maimed in combat. 
Folsom calls the 30-unit Dunham House a pioneering place that also will tend to spiritual wounds that medicine can’t heal.
The idea, said Folsom, its executive director, is to provide a residence and activities where younger generations of vets with shared experiences can bond and have a dignified, better quality of life. 
The 27,000-square-foot complex sits on about nine acres of a 40-acre rural setting property near 60th and State streets. It is expected to open to tenants before the year’s end, after final touches. 
 ‘Incredible day’

All funding came from private donations, Kate McCauley, president and CEO of the nonprofit Wounded Warriors Family Support told those gathered for the outdoor event.  She called the Dunham House a legacy project that will become part of programming and operations of Omaha-based WWFS, which Folsom founded in 2003.	

Dunham House namesake
Marine Cpl. Jason Dunham was conducting vehicle searches near Husaybah in Iraq’s Anbar province on April 14, 2004, when a driver in a stopped vehicle leaped out and attacked him.
Dunham wrestled the insurgent to the ground and saw him release a grenade. According to a commendation, Dunham did not hesitate to cover the explosive with his helmet and body, bearing the brunt of the explosion and saving the lives of at least two other Marines.
He died eight days later at age 23. 
In recognition of the selfless act, John Folsom, executive director of the newly dedicated Dunham House, said he named the facility to honor the young man’s service and sacrifice and to set him as an example for future Marines and soldiers.
Dunham, a rifle squad leader who served with the 3rd Battalion 7th Marines, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions.



The Dunham House, organized as an independent nonprofit with its own board of directors, is accepting rental applications. Leaders hope to attract vets from across the country dealing with multiple amputations or traumatic brain injury. 
Friday’s event drew out-of-state guests including retired U.S. Army Lt. Gen. John Sylvester of Texas, a WWFS board member who declared it “an incredible day.” 
He noted that military ceremonies for fallen soldiers feature upright rifles stuck in the dirt and topped with a helmet — a somber sign that “we lost somebody.” In comparison, Sylvester said, the groundbreaking last year for the Dunham House spotlighted upright shovels topped with construction hats.
“That means we’re here to help somebody,” he told the gathering. “We’re here to see if we can’t make life better for these kids that come home with traumatic brain injuries and other kinds of injuries that mean they’re unable to care for themselves and oh, by the way, they no longer have a caregiver.”
Scheduled to coincide with the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Friday’s event kicked off with a flag ceremony. Folsom said the 9/11 terrorist strike that stole nearly 3,000 lives and destroyed two signature skyscrapers was a jarring reminder of enemy forces intent on hurting the U.S.
“Our country was forever changed,” he said. “September 11 woke us up to the fact that there are people out there who would do us harm. … We found ourselves in a world that was quite unsettled and really dangerous.”
Folsom said 9/11 also marked the rise of the IED, or improvised explosive device — the “scourge” of modern conflicts that left many younger service members deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan with traumatic brain injuries and multiple amputations. 
It’s that post-9/11 veteran suffering from catastrophic combat wounds that the Dunham House was made for, he said.
The facility itself is named after Cpl. Jason Dunham, who, at age 23, threw his body over a grenade to save fellow Marines. Portraits and other mementos of Dunham were unveiled at the event.
Many cited the Dunham House mantra, which is rooted in a Bible verse: “No greater love than this — that one lays down his life for his friends.”

 Unexpected but welcome guest 

An unexpected guest summoned to the mic drew applause. Katie Saybolt was a Navy nurse who treated the mortally wounded Dunham in Iraq when he was brought to the trauma bay.
A dedication ceremony at the Dunham House Friday in Omaha coincided with the anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The official opening is expected later this year. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
She and her family moved to Omaha from another state last year and she said she was shocked to read about the local Dunham House project in a veterans-related newsletter. Saybolt emailed Folsom to talk about the connection. She said she felt “called” to attend Friday with her husband, Greg.
“This is just really beautiful,” Saybolt told Sylvester after the ceremony. Sylvester said he would continue to “hound” Saybolt until she agreed to work at the facility.
“It’s going to be more beautiful when we fill it up,” Sylvester added.
Other speakers included former Omaha Mayor Hal Daub, who is on the Dunham House board. He acknowledged other former and current officeholders at the event, including former Omaha City Councilman Garry Gernandt and current City Councilman Brinker Harding, who he said helped pave the way for various city permits and a street naming. The campus’s official address is 6000 Jason Dunham Drive.
Daub said he envisions growth on the property, including additional residential units for wounded vets.
Folsom, in an interview, recounted the challenging path leading to Friday. He said capital campaign fundraising was lengthy, as many donors prefer to invest in projects with a quicker turnaround.
Despite reaching the dedication milestone, Folsom said he remains unsettled and turns his thoughts to resident recruitment, programming and “what will happen inside the facility.” 
“It’s not mission complete yet,” he said.
 Still in the works

Still in the works is a plan to create a permanent national memorial at the Dunham House to honor American soldiers killed in action. Folsom and his board want to construct the tribute to service members who died in combat between October 2001 and 2021, including in Operations Enduring Freedom, Iraqi Freedom and other missions connected to post-9/11 wars.
Rendering of the Dunham House campus, which sits on nearly nine acres of a pastoral 40-acre site near 60th and State Streets. (Courtesy of Dunham House)
Estimated by Folsom to cost up to $700,000, the memorial is to be constructed using sunset granite quarried in South Dakota, with each name engraved into the stone.
Research is ongoing to identify the service members. 
Folsom, 73, started his military career as a CH-46 helicopter pilot, serving in multiple overseas deployments. In 1986, he left active duty and remained a Marine Corps Reserves member but was called back after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. He served in Iraq as “Air Boss” in western Anbar province, oversaw Marine attack helicopters and Army Black Hawk medevac air birds. 
Upon retirement, the Bronze Star recipient focused on the Omaha Dunham House.
Folsom said his longer-term wish is to see a chain of Dunham Houses across other states. Sylvester agreed.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi teen overcomes health challenges to harvest 12-foot alligator
authors: Justin Glowacki, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and Michelle Pinto, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center
description: Zoe Pell, 15, poses with the 12-foot, 4-inch alligator she harvested during a Southern Outdoors Unlimited hunt in Gautier.
text:
GAUTIER — When a 12-foot, 4-inch alligator jumped out of the water, Zoe Pell realized the hunt this year would be much different from the year before. 
“As soon as he drove up out of the water, he jumped and we realized that this wasn’t a little like we thought,” Zoe said. “We realized that it was a lot bigger than what we imagined.”
The 15-year-old from Utica had caught a 6-foot, 7-inch alligator during her first hunt with Southern Outdoors Unlimited, a nonprofit that connects disabled youth with guided hunting opportunities through volunteer hunters, in 2025. In 2026, she brought in an alligator nearly twice that size. 
“It was a really big fight,” Zoe said. “He, he kept going to the bottom and staying at the bottom. He was not coming up at all.” 
For Zoe and her mother, Ashley Pell, the hunt represented more than the size of the alligator. It was another sign of how far Zoe has come since an illness changed her life.
Only hunting remained 
When Zoe was 3 years old, she was diagnosed with Behcet’s disease, a rare inflammatory disorder that can affect blood vessels throughout the body. 
“It’s a painful disorder,” Ashley explained. “It kind of has the same symptoms of arthritis, so you have the inflammation and the blood pain of an arthritic in the joints.” 
Zoe Pell, left, stands with her mother, Ashley Pell, after Zoe’s Southern Outdoors Unlimited alligator hunt in Gautier.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
Even though Zoe was diagnosed with Behcet’s, she was still able to go to school, play softball and basketball and ride horses. But three years ago, Zoe woke up one morning and was partially paralyzed on her right side. 
After she was rushed to the doctor, medical staff determined Zoe also had ANCA-associated vasculitis, a group of rare autoimmune disorders that cause inflammation in small and medium blood vessels. 
“(The doctor) told me that what I have is rare, and that it would put me in, probably a wheelchair one day,” Zoe said.
Behcet’s disease has no cure, although treatment can help control symptoms. ANCA-associated vasculitis can be treated into remission but may relapse. As part of her treatment, Zoe had to start a regimen of chemotherapy, steroids and IVs and stop doing activities that caused stress on her body. 
“My doctor basically told me that I had to give up everything, that hunting and stuff was probably about the only thing I could do,” she said. “I gave up school, softball, basketball. I gave up all my sports. Almost gave up horse riding with it.” 
Since her diagnosis, Zoe has recovered enough to go hunting. Through Southern Outdoors Unlimited and G6:2 Outdoors Ministry, another nonprofit that provides hunting opportunities for children with disabilities, hunting has kept her active. 
“That’s the one thing that she’s not had to give up, is her hunting,” Ashley said. “And that’s why I’ve been very grateful for (Southern Outdoors Unlimited), because even though she’s been battling chemo and she’s been battling this disorder, she’s still able to go hunt and do the things that she loves to do.” 
Finding a place to hunt 
Zoe has since hunted alligators, deer, hogs, squirrels and rabbits through Southern Outdoors Unlimited.
“I was invited to start doing it by deer hunting, and then they told us that they had the gator hunt, and I was like, you know what? I want to try that one,” Zoe said. 
Ashley said hunting gives her daughter a chance to get outside despite her health challenges. 
“So you just enjoy the outdoors and being able to hunt, because that’s the one sport that she’s able to do, even though she has the disabilities that she has,” Ashley said. 
Zoe also tries to help other young hunters. Ashley said Zoe harvested two deer during a hunt last year and gave one to a participant who didn’t get one. 
Returning to the field 
Three years after stepping away from sports, Zoe recently began playing softball and basketball again. 
“When I put everything down, I put it down and didn’t expect to pick it up,” Zoe said. “I’m very, very rusty on it, but I’ve done pretty good.” 
Zoe’s ability to return to sports followed 11 rounds of chemotherapy, steroids and persistence. 
Ashley described her daughter as someone who continues pushing even on difficult days. 
“She’s strong. She’s a strong girl. She’s a fighter,” Ashley said. “Even on her worst days, she is still up trying to push through it.” 
Hunting hooks remain inside the mouth of the 12-foot, 4-inch alligator harvested by Zoe Pell during a Southern Outdoors Unlimited hunt.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
Her persistence was tested again as Zoe worked to bring the alligator to the surface. She credited Mike Macko, the organization’s alligator coordinator, and others on the hunt with helping place a second hook into the animal. 
Zoe said she was proud of the result. 
“When I put my mind to it, I don’t give up and I’m going to succeed,” Zoe said. 
For Ashley, the 12-foot, 4-inch alligator was further proof of the strength she has seen throughout her daughter’s life. 
“When she was born, she came into this world as a fighter,” Ashley said. “Everything she does, she gives it all. And she fights with every minute she has in her.”

name: VTDigger
title: Upper Valley Haven readies its new year-round shelter for its first guests
description:
“When someone unexpectedly needs a place to go, it can be hard to figure out the next steps,” said the executive director. “Shelters across the state are often full, with waitlists that stretch for months.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Upper Valley Haven readies its new year-round shelter for its first guests.
text:
An artist’s rendering of the Upper Valley Haven’s low-barrier shelter to be built at the intersection of Routes 5 and 4 in White River Junction, Vt. Courtesy Studio Nexus Architects + Planners

This story by Alex Ebrahimi was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 10, 2026.
WHITE RIVER JUNCTION — The Upper Valley Haven dedicated its new year-round shelter and resource center Wednesday, with an opening date for the 20-bed facility expected to be announced in the coming weeks.
The Haven, which has served the region since 1980, cut a ceremonial ribbon to mark a milestone of the progress made at the Patrick and Marcelle Leahy Shelter and Resource Center at 608 N. Main St.
“When someone unexpectedly needs a place to go, it can be hard to figure out the next steps,” said Will Towne, the Haven’s executive director, in a statement. “Shelters across the state are often full, with waitlists that stretch for months.”
The center is designed as a place where people can find immediate relief, including bed reservations, meals and staff support, Towne said.
Following over a year of construction, the building — on the site of the former 25,000 Gifts building — houses a 20-bed, year-round emergency shelter on its second floor and a daytime resource center on the first.
Guests will sign up nightly rather than holding a bed for a set period. Each person spending the night will get a semi-private pod with three-quarter walls, a cot, a small table and a light. The building will be staffed around the clock, and guests can connect with Haven service coordinators on site, according to the Haven’s staff.
The first-floor resource center is intended to serve more than just those staying upstairs.
“Community members who are precariously housed, living on a fixed income, or navigating a hard stretch will be able to meet with a Haven Service Coordinator and use computer workspaces for job applications and benefit enrollments,” information released by the Haven stated. “Partner organizations will also be able to provide services in the building.”
The Leahy center replaces the Lebanon Seasonal Shelter, a three-year arrangement with the city of Lebanon, New Hampshire, that has reached the end of its intended term. The Lebanon shelter had 14 beds and operated about three months a year; the city-owned building is slated for demolition to make way for a roundabout. Sixty-six people stayed there over roughly 100 nights this past season, and an average of two people a night were turned away for lack of space, with overflow placed in hotels at public expense.
The Haven raised $10.2 million for the project in just under nine months, with $7.5 million going toward construction and at least $2 million set aside to cover operating costs for the first five years. Public funding included $2 million from USDA Rural Development, $1.5 million from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board, $500,000 from the Vermont Office of Economic Opportunity and $125,000 from the city of Lebanon.
Studio Nexus designed the building, and Estes and Gallup constructed it. The property sits within walking distance of employment centers, healthcare and government offices.
It was named after the Leahys to recognize their longtime public service to Vermont. Marcelle Leahy devoted her career to nursing, while then-Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vt., secured $2 million in funding for the project before retiring from the U.S. Senate. 
The Haven supports more than 130 households across its housing programs and helped 108 families move into permanent housing in the past fiscal year, according to the release. It expects the Leahy center to provide more than 5,000 bed nights annually and serve over 100 individuals a year in the shelter alone.
“Now we turn to using this building to be an agent of lasting change for the people we serve, with our staff based here, room for our partners, and a calming environment for the guidance our guests require,” said Kathy Welling, board president of the Upper Valley Haven.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Make a low-risk bet, then brag: Explaining Trump’s endorsement of South Dakota’s governor
description: In politics, as in comedy, timing is everything. That brings us to the curious timing of President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Gov. Larry Rhoden. Any of the four candidates in the Republican primary for governor would have welcomed a Trump endorsement and ridden it to victory. While the president’s poll numbers are at an all-time […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during a rally Sept. 8, 2023, at The Monument ice arena in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)In politics, as in comedy, timing is everything. That brings us to the curious timing of President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Gov. Larry Rhoden.
Any of the four candidates in the Republican primary for governor would have welcomed a Trump endorsement and ridden it to victory. While the president’s poll numbers are at an all-time low nationally, he has carried South Dakota with more than 60% of the vote all three times he’s been on the ballot. There’s little doubt that his endorsement could have influenced the outcome.
None of the four candidates were in closer proximity to Trump than U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson. His few disagreements with the MAGA party line were used against him in primary election attack ads. Despite their few differences, it sure looked like Johnson was trying to curry favor with the president when he sponsored legislation that would have allowed Trump to purchase the Panama Canal. (After all that has happened in the second Trump administration, his early statements about the pressing need to buy the canal now seem quaint.)
After primary and runoff, Trump endorses Republican nominee for South Dakota governor

Yet the president kept his powder dry during a primary that saw a newcomer to politics, a Trump mini-me, finish first. Throughout the primary and the runoff, Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden gave off a Trumpian vibe that suggested in the vaguest of terms that his mere presence in Pierre would raise the level of competence in state government, boost the state’s standard of living and enhance economic development.
During the runoff between Rhoden and Doeden, Trump once again stood by mute. Trump and Rhoden even shared the stage at the Fourth of July fireworks at Mount Rushmore. In the end, Trump made his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of Rhoden in a Truth Social post. It would have seemed so much more personal and genuine if, there in the shadow of the monument to democracy, he had just put his arm around Rhoden and declared that this is the guy who should be your next governor.
Obviously, the best time for Trump to issue his endorsement was during the primary or the runoff. Thousands of South Dakotans suddenly became Republicans — including yours truly — because they knew that the real contest to choose the state’s next governor was the Republican runoff, not the general election.
It’s ironic that Trump should endorse Rhoden. In the runoff, Republican voters rejected the notion of a Trump clone in the governor’s office. The word landslide comes to mind.
As heavily influential as Trump’s endorsement can be, Rhoden doesn’t need it to win his first full term as governor. In South Dakota, Democratic Party registrations lag behind independent and no-party-affiliation registrations by more than 21,000 and trail Republican registrations by almost 196,000. The numbers just don’t add up for a victory by Democratic candidate Dan Ahlers. Against numbers like those, it’s doubtful that JFK himself could get elected governor of this state.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Part of the reason for Trump’s late but “Complete” endorsement of Rhoden is his high-profile hobby of endorsing candidates. According to the website VoteHub, at this writing Trump leads the league in political endorsements with 221. No one else comes close. (It’s odd that there’s actually a website devoted to this sort of thing.)
A New York Times analysis noted that Trump has a reputation for picking winners, but there is a method that makes his winning percentage less than stellar. Trump has a penchant for picking incumbents, like Rhoden, who are more likely to win and then bragging about the power of his influence within the Republican Party. “Superficially, the math supports his claims,” the Times analysis said. “But by favoring incumbents and candidates running in uncontested races, Mr. Trump’s primary wins are built largely on low-risk bets.”
Perhaps the Rhoden camp should feel good about being considered a “low-risk bet.” That translates into a high probability of being elected.
It’s easy to wonder why Trump waited so long to make his endorsement. It’s certainly something that Rhoden doesn’t need at this point in the process in a safely Republican state like South Dakota. Maybe the president truly believes that Rhoden is the best man for the job. Or maybe he’s just hedging his bet in order to enhance the number of winners he picks during this election season.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri should make medical respite part of its health care infrastructure
description: Missouri’s healthcare system routinely pays for a hospital stay, a surgery or a course of treatment, then reaches the edge of its own plan when the patient has no home in which to recover. For a person experiencing homelessness, “discharge” can mean returning to a shelter, vehicle or street while managing a wound, infection, cancer […]
text:
(Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Missouri’s healthcare system routinely pays for a hospital stay, a surgery or a course of treatment, then reaches the edge of its own plan when the patient has no home in which to recover.
For a person experiencing homelessness, “discharge” can mean returning to a shelter, vehicle or street while managing a wound, infection, cancer treatment, new dialysis schedule or medication regimen. The predictable result is not only suffering. It is fragmented care, missed follow-up and avoidable use of emergency departments and inpatient beds.
Medical respite care offers a practical alternative. The National Institute for Medical Respite Care defines it as short-term residential care that allows people experiencing homelessness to rest, recover and access medical care and supportive services when they are too ill to recover on the street but no longer require hospitalization. National guidance describes medical respite as a bridge between acute care and housing, with hospital collaboration essential to referrals, data collection and sustainable funding.
Missouri should recognize this bridge as healthcare infrastructure rather than an optional charitable add-on.
At Haven Recovery in St. Louis, recuperative care serves people with serious wounds, infections, cancer, heart disease, trauma and other medical conditions. Staff provide a safe place to heal, three meals a day, transportation to follow-up care, medication support, nursing coordination, case management and connections to housing and benefits.
The financial signal is notable. Data provided to our program on 27 Missouri Medicaid members served in 2024 compared spending in the 12 months before recuperative care with spending afterward. Average inpatient and outpatient spending declined from $3,091 per member per month to $956. Pharmacy spending declined from $515 to $457. The combined observed reduction was $2,193 per member per month, equal to approximately $710,532 when annualized across the 27-member cohort.
This is a small before-and-after analysis, not a controlled evaluation. It cannot prove that every dollar of the observed change resulted from recuperative care. That limitation is precisely why Missouri should invest in both capacity and rigorous statewide evaluation. The appropriate response to promising early data is not to ignore it; it is to test it at scale.
Evidence from other communities also supports the model’s potential. The Center for Health Care Strategies has highlighted medical respite as a pathway to better health and housing outcomes and noted that Medicaid policy can help finance it. A Commonwealth Fund case study similarly describes medical respite as short-term residential care for people who need a safe place to recover after hospitalization.
Missouri can act in four ways.
First, the state and its Medicaid managed care organizations should establish consistent reimbursement pathways for qualified medical respite services. Programs cannot responsibly add beds or retain specialized staff when payment depends on temporary grants or one-time agreements.
Second, Missouri should define quality standards. Medical respite must be more than a bed. Programs should demonstrate safe operations, care coordination, transportation, medication support, connections to primary and specialty care, and pathways to housing.
Third, the state should require shared outcome measurement. At a minimum, programs and payers should track hospital readmissions, emergency department use, total cost of care, connections to primary care and housing status after discharge.
Fourth, public and private capital partners should support facility development. Demand cannot be met without appropriate physical space. Haven currently operates 11 recuperative care beds and is planning an expansion to approximately 35 at its Davis Street location, but our referral demand already far exceeds available capacity.
Medical respite will not solve homelessness by itself, nor should it replace permanent housing. It solves a specific and urgent problem: where a medically vulnerable person can safely recover today while longer-term supports are arranged.
Missouri already pays when that gap goes unfilled — through extended hospital stays, repeated crises and human suffering. A structured medical respite system would allow the state to spend more intelligently while treating people with dignity.
The question is not whether Missouri can afford to build this part of the continuum. The current pattern shows that we are already paying for its absence.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: As data centers expand, advocates call for regulations on lights
description: The United States has the most data centers in the world. More than 3,000 are already up and running, as demand for infrastructure that can power artificial intelligence and store digital information continues to grow.
text:
The United States is seen at night in a composite of satellite images. (Photo courtesy of NASA)When it comes to data centers, Vayujeet Gokhale has but one ask.
“If you are going to have lights on at night, then let’s do it in a responsible way,” he said.
Gokhale is a physics professor at Truman State University and a board member for DarkSky Missouri — the state chapter for an international non-profit aimed at reducing artificial lighting at night. The broader organization has taken a similar stance.
Gokhale acknowledges that his cause might not be the first or second priority for most communities. It might not even be third, he said. Yet, he argues that it may be the easiest of environmental problems to solve.
“You don’t need to light up the place for these computers and memory banks to work. They’ll still work even if it’s completely dark,” Gokhale said. “You need light for certain other things, but you can minimize the pollution without affecting the quality of the data center product. You can’t make that same case with water and energy.”
Rather than allowing data centers and the companies running them to operate their lighting on an individual basis, Gokhale said he wants to see his organization’s principles for responsible outdoor lighting get adopted. This would include installing lighting that is pointed downwards, motion detectors so that light is only in use when needed, and warm-colored lights to reduce unnecessary brightness.
These kinds of deliberate choices might benefit the data center companies by reducing their spending on lighting while improving safety and security at their facilities, according to Gokhale.
“Many times, in these environmental issues, pollution-related issues, it’s a zero-sum game. You have to give up something in order to gain something. Not so with light pollution. It’s a win-win,” Gokhale said.
Dark skies for humans, birds and insects
The United States has the most data centers in the world. More than 3,000 are already up and running, as demand for infrastructure that can power artificial intelligence and store digital information continues to grow. Three-quarters of the data centers planned are in the South or Midwest, according to a report from the Pew Research Center.
Louisiana currently has 23 data centers active, under construction or planned, according to Data Center Map, the company that supplied data for the Pew report.
With regulations in place, Gokhale believes the U.S will be better equipped to preserve the night skies for human observers and wildlife — such as migrating birds or insect species that work as night time pollinators. While many people might first think of butterflies and hummingbirds as pollinators, nocturnal insects play a key role for both local ecosystems and agriculture.
“A lot of the pollinators are actually active at night,” Gokhale said. “If you have too much artificial light, they get confused or disoriented.”
The job of a pollinator is an important one, said Nicole Flowers-Kimmerle, a horticulture educator for the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Extension. About one out of every three bites of food produced in the U.S. is dependent on insect or animal pollinators, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
The East Campus chilled water facility at the University of Missouri sits next to the Hellbender data center on Thursday, Feb.12, 2026, in Columbia, Missouri. (Le Chen)
Artificial light at night not only disrupts a nighttime pollinator’s ability to navigate, it also changes their feeding and mating behaviors, she said. “So if we see that we’re having a declining number of moths, then that’s going to affect pollination, but it also affects the food web,” she said.
A decline in moths and other nighttime pollinators could impact the bird species that rely on them as a source for food. That’s a problem that is further compounded since many migrating birds are themselves affected by artificial light pollution at night, according to Murry Burgess, an assistant professor at Mississippi State University who specializes in ornithology and urban ecology. In recent decades, scientists have found that some migratory birds use the stars as a compass that helps orient their travel paths.
“So with light pollution, it’s really obscuring the stars and throwing them off course, making them expend more energy kind of circling around trying to find where they’re supposed to go,” said Burgess. “That’s when you start to see a lot of window collisions and increased mortality as well.”
The Mississippi River Basin, in particular, is a key flyway for approximately half of all North American bird species, which need to travel as far as South America and back each year. Those include song birds, waterfowl and even raptor species.
“It’s really important to preserve dark sky areas, the same way that you would have a wildlife refuge, like the sky is part of the environment, part of their habitat,” she said.
Like other environmental advocates, Burgess agrees that the harm from artificial lighting at night should be mitigated in a responsible way. She said that unlike the larger issues surrounding data center developments, such as land usage and environmental pollution, lighting could be less complicated to solve.
“With light pollution, it really can be as simple as just turning off the lights or changing the types of lights that you use,” Burgess said.
Regulations along the river?
Throughout the Mississippi River Basin, local communities are picking sides in the battle over data centers.
In January, elected officials for the city of Warrenton, Missouri, voted unanimously to approve a data center plan that would include two buildings — each of them four times larger than a Costco warehouse or Walmart supercenter — along Interstate 70. Yet, not all Missouri communities are eager to see these high-profile projects in their town and counties. Earlier this summer, the St. Charles County Council passed a six-month moratorium on large-scale data center development. On the other end of the state, voters in the city of Independence have recalled a number of city council members for approving a data center’s construction with tax breaks.
With both approval and pushback for data centers growing across the state, legislators have tried to address key issues for their constituents. Like Rep. Colin Wellenkamp — a Republican for St. Charles County — who introduced House Bill 3362 in the previous legislative session. The bill sought to regulate data center electricity usage by making them pay for costs, as well as any necessary power grid upgrades. It also would have created a permit requirement for high water usage from the state Department of Natural Resources, which does not currently regulate data centers or even have a standard definition for such businesses.
“The AI economy is growing in Missouri which is a good thing as long as Missouri communities are protected and empowered to lead the way,” Wellenkamp said in a late-June Facebook post.
Ultimately, none of the legislation aimed at regulating Missouri’s data center advanced, nor did they address environmental advocates’ concerns for light pollution and how it could affect local wildlife.
Gokhale, the Truman State professor, said he’s not in favor of data centers, but he’s not exactly opposed to them, either. He just has a lot of questions.
“At the most fundamental level, we need to define what these things are, what their purpose is,” Gokhale said.
Gokhale said a first step toward regulations would be to categorize data centers beyond the vagueness of artificial intelligence and cloud storage. To him, the need is urgent. More and more data centers will spring up around the country — and with them, an increased concern for limited land and water resources from local communities.
“This has to be done by the people, by council members, by politicians, and effectively enacted into some sort of policy,” he said.
This story is a product of the Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk, an independent reporting network based at the University of Missouri in partnership with Report for America, with major funding from the Walton Family Foundation.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: A journalist coined ‘the Bible Belt’ 100 years ago. It’s been oversimplifying the South ever since.
description: “Look No Further!” a billboard on the side of the highway beckons, drawing my gaze toward the red cover of a Bible. “You Are Worthy of Redemption!” Not far away, another sign urges me to “Keep Christ in Christmas.” Then farther down the road a third appears: “Jesus: COMING SOON” its bright colors announce. Signs […]
text:
(Photo by John Hayes/The Conversation)“Look No Further!” a billboard on the side of the highway beckons, drawing my gaze toward the red cover of a Bible. “You Are Worthy of Redemption!”

Not far away, another sign urges me to “Keep Christ in Christmas.” Then farther down the road a third appears: “Jesus: COMING SOON” its bright colors announce.
Signs like these are familiar to me: I’m a historian who studies the U.S. South and lives in it. I know how easily they can evoke the South – or, I should say, a certain image of it. As that image pictures it, the South is “the Bible Belt”: a place where people are really religious, and, as a result, socially and politically conservative. Indeed, in this year of midterm elections, you’re almost certain to hear pundits invoke “the Bible Belt” as shorthand explanation for Southern political behavior.
The phrase has been around for a century. Its endurance, however – and the “evidence” behind it today – could use some serious scrutiny. I spotted those roadside signs, for example, in Ontario, Canada, a thousand miles from what anybody would think of as the South.
Of the many things said about the South over the years, “Bible Belt” is the cliché that just won’t die.
Skewering the South

	
“Bible Belt” entered the lexicon in 1924, in the pages of The American Mercury, a magazine co-founded by H.L. Mencken. Based in Baltimore, at the upper edge of the South, Mencken was one of the nation’s most prominent journalists in the decades between the world wars.
The acerbic satirist had skewered the South in his much-discussed 1919 essay “The Sahara of the Bozart,” depicting it as a vast cultural wasteland. In 1925, he closely covered the Dayton, Tennessee, trial of biology teacher John T. Scopes, who had been charged with violating the state’s law against teaching Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution. Mencken famously lampooned it as the Scopes “monkey trial.”
He coined “Bible Belt” in his regular column of short news items, then employed the phrase routinely. By it he meant a place where two Protestant groups, the Baptists and the Methodists, dominated not just religious life, but also the mores of the whole society. The whole region, Mencken argued, was a Baptist-Methodist stranglehold where fun and free thought were banished.
Whose Christianity?

	
It’s true that in the early 20th century, Baptists and Methodists dominated the South in a way that they didn’t anywhere else. To trace the bloc of states where over 50% of religious congregation members were Baptist or Methodist was to trace the region’s boundaries with uncanny precision.
But beneath commonalities, religious life was divided by both race and class. Black Baptists and Methodists met in their own churches: autonomous institutions that came to be known, collectively, as “the Black church.” The region’s poor Christians drew on inherited traditions and their own hardships to craft a folk version of Baptist-Methodist faith – what I’ve written about as “hard, hard religion.”
These religious divisions paralleled political ones. Through techniques like poll taxes and literacy tests, Southern states severely restricted the franchise, effectively stripping Black and poor white Southerners of their voting rights.
The social order that Mencken described as the Bible Belt, then, expressed the culture of elite and middle-class white people, the ones with the political power to enforce it.
“Bible Belt” joined other phrases that expressed how the early 20th-century South differed from national patterns. Amid industrializing, urbanizing America, the South was “the Cotton Belt,” the world’s leading cotton producer, with a predominantly rural, agricultural population. Political contests marked the nation, but in the “Solid South,” the Democratic Party monopolized politics. With high poverty, low wages and limited capital, the South was the prosperous nation’s “No. 1 economic problem,” as President Franklin Roosevelt put it in 1938. And the violent racial oppression of the “Jim Crow South” was what many Black Southerners eagerly fled when doors of opportunity opened in other regions.

(Photo by John Hayes/The Conversation)
A new South

	
A century later, so much has changed.
Most Southerners, like most Americans, live in suburbs and work in a service economy. Republicans hold a political majority in the region, but they have to compete for it. Southern-based corporations like Walmart, McKesson and Exxon Mobil are in the top 10 of the Fortune 500. And what legal scholar Michelle Alexander calls “the New Jim Crow” – the system of mass incarceration that disproportionately criminalizes people of color – is not confined to the South, but nationwide.
Old lines of difference between the South and the rest of the nation have faded. So have the once-common nicknames that described them – with the stubborn exception of “Bible Belt.”
A quick glance at the news shows its persistence, with headlines discussing “The Bible Belt’s Beliefs About Women,” or describing one Arkansas town as “the Bible Belt’s LGBTQ Oasis.”
The cultural issues reported in stories like these are no doubt real, but framing them as expressions of an enduring Southern Bible Belt seems to imagine religion as unchanging, timeless.
In reality, both the region’s people and their religion are changing dramatically. More Black, Latino and biracial people live in the South than in any other part of the country. White people make up just 52.5% of the regional population. The rapidly changing South is dynamic, second only to the West in demographic diversity.



Let us know what you think...


 


This shapes religion, too. As the 2023-2024 Pew Religious Landscape Study showed, Black and Latino Americans are more likely than white Americans to identify as Christian. The faith of Black Southerners (predominantly Baptist) and Latino Southerners (predominantly Catholic) is a reminder that the South is not a religious monolith.
Meanwhile, white Baptists and Methodists are not the force they used to be. Their main institutions, the Southern Baptist Convention and the United Methodist Church, have been declining in membership for decades. The same Pew study showed that a mere 12% of Southerners identify with either denomination.
From ‘Bible Belt’ to ‘culture wars’

	
Internally, both denominations have had major splits on whether women can be leaders and whether to recognize LGBTQ identities. Such splits reflect divides that sociologist James Davison Hunter diagnosed in 1991 as “Culture Wars.”
Consider his book’s subtitle, though: “The Struggle to Define America.” In these culture wars, the battlefield is the nation. The fighters are not regions, but political factions. What they’re fighting over is the legacy of the social movements of the 1960s: civil rights, women’s rights, gay rights, the environment.
The fact that the culture wars for America can be found in the contemporary South is a testament to just how much the once-distinct region participates in the dynamics of national life. Those wars may sound louder in the South than elsewhere, but that’s not the expression of a changeless Bible Belt; rather, it is the historical pattern that reactions are often strongest where change is most pronounced.

title: Trump drone tariffs target a technology still used unevenly across US farms
description: Drone use remains limited among most U.S. farms, but larger farms have adopted the technology at a higher rate than small farm operations, federal data show. In 2023, 12% of large-scale family farms used drones, compared with 9% of midsize farms and 2% of small family farms, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic […]
text:
A farmer on a tractor sprays soybean crops. (Photo by Westend61/Getty Images)Drone use remains limited among most U.S. farms, but larger farms have adopted the technology at a higher rate than small farm operations, federal data show.
In 2023, 12% of large-scale family farms used drones, compared with 9% of midsize farms and 2% of small family farms, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic Research Service report, America’s Farms and Ranches at a Glance: 2024 Edition.
Among farms that used drones, 40% cited increased yields as a reason for using the technology, and the same share cited saving labor time, according to the USDA’s report. Another 29% cited improving soil or reducing environmental impacts, a quarter said reducing purchased input costs was a reason, and more than one-fifth reported reducing operator fatigue.
The data provides a snapshot of agricultural drone use as the federal government changes the economics of buying the technology.
President Donald Trump announced new tariffs on imported drones and components Aug. 13, pointing out that reliance on foreign suppliers poses a national security risk. The main tariffs took effect Sept. 3.
The highest tariff — 100% — applies to drones weighing more than 25 kilograms, or about 55 pounds, and those equipped with thermal imaging capabilities. The tariff also applies to their docking stations and certain critical components.
The new policy imposes a 25% tariff on certain smaller drones that lack capabilities considered particularly relevant to national security.
Drones and components from the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan face a 15% tariff. Drones from the United Kingdom face a 10% tariff, provided that substantially all of their hardware, software and technology originate in those countries or the United States.
On farms, drones are used for a range of tasks. USDA has reported that farmers use aerial imagery provided by aircraft, drones, and satellites for crop mapping, livestock monitoring, land surveying, and spraying, among other uses.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Stigma begone: If you’re in your mid-40s, schedule a colonoscopy without delay. It’s fine! Really!
description: I don’t like to preach in these columns. I’d rather poke fun and spoof craven politicians. This world contains many people who believe many different things, and I like to acknowledge that wondrous diversity.  But sometimes, circumstances demand a bit of the old fire and brimstone. If you are 45 or older — or if […]
text:
While a colonoscopy might sound unpleasant, writes opinion editor Clay Wirestone, it both screens for and prevents cancer. (Getty Images)I don’t like to preach in these columns. I’d rather poke fun and spoof craven politicians. This world contains many people who believe many different things, and I like to acknowledge that wondrous diversity. 
But sometimes, circumstances demand a bit of the old fire and brimstone.
If you are 45 or older — or if you’re someone who has a family history of colon cancer and related conditions — for goodness’ sake, get a colonoscopy. The procedure is generally covered by insurance and could save your life or the life of someone you love. If that’s not worth a bit of pulpit-thumping, I don’t know what is.
We’re talking about this today because I had my first colonoscopy Sept. 4. It went about as well as such a procedure could go, but I still dillydallied for a year or two longer than recommended. Please: If you or anyone has been sitting on the fence about the procedure, just go do it.
Listen, this subject makes me a little uncomfortable, too. No one likes to dwell on their lower digestive system, much less the preparations necessary to clean that system out for thorough examination via mechanical snake. On the other hand, we’ve all had a terrible stomach bug at one point or another in our lives. We know what it’s like to have abdominal discomfort and diarrhea.
That small amount of discomfort — it takes at most a day or two — is a small price to pay to screen for an illness found more and more often in younger and younger people.
You might have heard the names of some recent victims. Actors Chadwick Boseman and James Van Der Beek both died of colon cancer in their 40s. Actress Catherine O’Hara died after a battle with rectal cancer. 
According to the American Cancer Society, colorectal cancer is “now the No. 1 cause of cancer-related mortality. In 2026, an estimated 158,850 new cases of colorectal cancer will be diagnosed, and 55,230 people will die from the disease, including 200 diagnoses each day in people younger than 65.”
Because of all this, the ACA now recommends that those at average risk receive their screening at age 45.
Colonoscopies don’t just screen for cancer. They also prevent it. If the doctor performing the procedure spots a polyp — a small growth on the lining of the colon — he or she can snip it off during the procedure. Removing polyps prevents them from growing, changing or otherwise mutating into cancer.
During my colonoscopy, the doctor found a single, 3-millimeter polyp. It turned out to be benign, and I can wait a decade until my next appointment with the scope. If the polyp had been precancerous, removal would have stopped it cold.
There are other options, of course. Various tests look for DNA changes or microscopic amounts blood in patients’ stool. For those who want to avoid the fraught preparation and anesthesia of a colonoscopy, such tests can be a worthwhile alternative.
However, these tests can produce false positives. The next step for any positive results is to undergo — you guessed it — a full colonoscopy.
My personal advice is to avoid such half measures and just go for the full-blown procedure. Depending on your results, you may be able to wait as long as a decade until your next screening. You may need to go back in three or five or seven years, but you will have still gained peace of mind and prevented any growths from causing havoc.
Yes, the whole procedure sounds a bit gross.
No one likes to think too much about their bathroom visits or having doctors scope their nether regions. But the more that we avoid these topics — the more that we act as though there’s something embarrassing or awkward or shameful about them — the more we prevent people from obtaining the care they need.
That’s why I chose to preach today. There’s nothing weird or bad about taking care of your health and receiving routine preventative care. Push past any awkwardness, get yourself checked out and move ahead.
Then we can all get back to making fun of Roger Marshall.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” comes out Sept. 29 from the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Dreamers as cops: Danbury’s legal gamble
description: A DACA Dreamer is not a permanent American resident. There residency must be renewed every two years.
text:
Danbury taxpayers deserve to understand the full risk behind Mayor Roberto Alves and his Democratic majority council’s decision to hire Deferred Action Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients as police officers– a move most states won’t touch.
A DACA Dreamer is not a permanent American resident. There residency must be renewed every two years. If renewal is delayed or denied, the city must terminate the officer immediately. That alone destabilizes the force.

Warren Levy

But policing adds two major legal problems:

Firearms: Federal law bars individuals without lawful immigration status from possessing guns. DACA does not grant lawful status. The city’s “we’ll issue the gun each shift” workaround has never been tested in court.

And here’s the part Danbury taxpayers need to hear:

Training a police officer costs well over $250,000 and takes 18–24 months before the officer is fully deployable. That includes academy training, salary, benefits, equipment, field training, and supervision. If DACA status lapses, every dollar of that investment is lost instantly.

Meanwhile, DACA’s legality is still being fought in federal court. No one knows how that case will end.
Only a handful of states have tried this, and even they’ve moved cautiously. Danbury’s leadership chose to jump first, putting personable and political beliefs ahead of legal clarity, insurance liability, and the stability of our police force.
This isn’t about any individual. It’s about protecting Danbury from avoidable legal exposure and wasted taxpayer dollars.
Danbury deserves decisions grounded in law, not personal or political beliefs.
Warren Levy lives in Danbury.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What we could gain from Cuba
description: We should be demanding our government reverse course, and promptly normalize relations with Cuba.
text:
Probably everyone has encountered a family member or friend who suffers from Alzheimer’s disease.
A recent opinion piece in the CT Mirror urges Congress to fund research that would produce diagnostic tests to detect Alzheimer’s onset early so that the progression of the disease may be slowed by existing drugs and the family has time to prepare for the inevitable decline of the patient and its effects on loved ones.
Having an accurate diagnostic test is no doubt very valuable. But its value is limited if there are no effective treatments.
The existing treatments available in the U.S. may slow the progression of the disease but fail to improve the patients’ conditions. They result from important basic research that is expensive and time consuming to carry out, but important for this country to continue to invest in.
Yet, unbeknownst to most of us, there exists today a treatment that improves or stabilizes Alzheimers. But it isn’t coming from the multibillion dollar U.S. pharmaceutical industry, or the U.S. government. Most critically it isn’t today available in the U.S.
The reason we don’t have access to this treatment has nothing to do with medical research. Rather it results from longstanding U.S. foreign policy.
In Cuba a drug that was used to help patients recover from brain trauma was tested on several sets of Alzheimers patients. It’s called NeuroEPO or NeuralCIM. The results in controlled clinical trials were remarkably encouraging to say the least. In mild to moderate Alzheimers patients, cognitive abilities improved in over 50% of patients receiving the Cuban drug in just 48 weeks. In another 30% of patients cognitive abilities stabilized. In the control patients, however, cognition continued to deteriorate. These were double-blind trials and included 170 individuals. The studies are documented in a video, “Teresita’s Dream,” related documentaries and scientific publications. There are efforts in Canada and China to replicate these trials. Why not the U.S.?
How is it possible that this incredible medical development that promises to dramatically improve the lives of millions of Alzheimers patients in our country takes place and most of us don’t know about it?
What do we know about Cuba in general? Today it can’t keep the lights on. It can’t pick up the garbage. We’re told it’s a dictatorship. Well, that’s the narrative that has been driven into us  for over 60 years by our government and the corporate media.
The back story is that the U.S. has imposed a strangulating siege on Cuba. For over six decades the U.S. has worked overtime to overthrow the Cuban government. It has invaded, it has sanctioned, it has sabotaged, it has assassinated. President Trump has intensified this siege so that Cuba now has no access to oil. It can’t run its electric grid. It has no gasoline for garbage trucks or trucks to deliver food. It can’t keep infant incubators running. Its infant mortality rate, among the best in the world, has spiked in the last few years. Hospitals can’t carry out important surgery or hydrate sick patients. Under threat of secondary U.S. sanctions the international banks refuse to do business with Cuba.
The Trump administration is publicly threatening to invade Cuba, which likely means bombing its civilian infrastructure including its astounding biotech industry. It claims that this island nation of 11 million souls is a threat to the 340 million population of the United States of America with the biggest, most advanced, technically-armed military in history and an economy a hundredfold or more greater than Cuba’s.
What nonsense demands that this great country needs to be afraid of the small Cuban island? Really?
To the contrary, we should be asking how it is that Cuba appears to have developed a successful treatment of Alzheimers, or a number of successful disease treatments. We should be asking why we aren’t allowed access to NeuralCIM. 
We should be demanding our government reverse course, promptly normalize relations with Cuba and find ways to mutually benefit from Cuba’s success in treating Alzheimers among other medical conditions.
Henry Lowendorf lives in New Haven and belongs to the Greater New Haven Peace Council.
